item.title: Coding agents
item.description:
Running an agent

An agent runs where you start it, so you start it in the VM’s shell, not on this machine. On this machine, devvm opens the VM’s shell, and the VM’s prompt starts with (devvm):

~/some-project $ devvm
(devvm) ~/some-project $ claude

In the VM the agent sees only your project folder, and your agents’ settings from devvm’s agent store, which it gets read-only. Whatever it runs, such as a script a package installs, runs in the VM too. You don’t install any agent on this machine, because devvm installs each one in the VMs that have it.

The guide in every VM

Every VM has a guide to devvm for the agents in it, at /usr/share/doc/devvm/README.md, and devvm-help in the VM prints it. It tells an agent what a devvm VM is, how its network tiers and secrets work, where its installs go, and which commands to ask you to run on this machine, such as devvm network allow for a blocked host or devvm agent login for a login. The guide is the same in every VM, so it says nothing about the VM’s own tier, ports or layers. Each launch installs it again whenever it differs from devvm’s, and it belongs to root and is read-only, so nothing that the VM’s user runs without sudo can change what the agents read, and a change made with sudo lasts only until the next launch. Ask your agent to read it, or to run devvm-help, when it doesn’t know where it’s running. devvm adds nothing about it to the agents’ instruction files.

Supported agents

A new VM gets an agent when you choose it as you customize the VM, or when you name it with --agents. A VM that exists gets one from devvm tools, which shows the same list with the VM’s agents already chosen, or from devvm tools add:

devvm # a new VM: customize it, then choose claude, codex or opencode
devvm --agents claude,codex # a new VM with Claude Code and Codex, without the list
devvm tools # the VM that exists: choose its agents in the list
devvm tools add opencode # the VM that exists: add opencode without the list

In the VM, you run the agent as claude, codex or opencode.

Name Agent What devvm adds Allowlist, on the allowlist and none tiers
claude Claude Code the newest release, with its auto-update off, since the shared copy is read-only, and its telemetry off Anthropic’s API, Claude’s login and Claude Code’s downloads: api.anthropic.com, claude.ai, downloads.claude.ai, platform.claude.com and mcp-proxy.anthropic.com
codex Codex the newest release, with its analytics and metrics off unless your config sets them the OpenAI API and the ChatGPT login: api.openai.com, chatgpt.com and auth.openai.com
opencode opencode the newest 2.x release, because opencode marks its 1.x releases as its latest on GitHub opencode’s own service and its model catalog: opencode.ai and models.opencode.ai

Claude Code’s telemetry hosts aren’t on its allowlist, because blocking them costs nothing. opencode talks to the model provider you choose, so on the allowlist tier you allow that provider’s API host yourself, such as devvm network allow api.anthropic.com (changing rules). Every VM sets OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE=1, as it sets DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1 for Claude Code, because the agents are read-only shared tools that can’t update themselves, and devvm keeps their versions.

Agents are shared tools, like the toolchains, so you can combine them with any layers and with each other, as in devvm --tools node --agents claude,codex. devvm follows each agent’s newest release, because agents release several times a week, and devvm update or devvm tools update moves a VM to newer versions (adding and removing tools).

Setup’s default agents

devvm setup chooses the agents that the list checks for every new VM, and that a new VM gets without a terminal. devvm asks for them on its first run in a terminal and again in devvm setup’s questions, and devvm setup --agents claude,codex or devvm setup --agents none sets them without asking. They’re a setting for new VMs only, so a VM that exists keeps its agents (devvm setup).

devvm’s agent store

devvm keeps the agents’ settings and logins on this machine in a store of its own, and every VM with an agent gets that agent’s settings and logins from there. devvm never reads the agents’ own files in your home folder for a VM, such as ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.config/opencode or ~/.local/share/opencode, so a VM gets the same settings and logins whether or not this machine has the agent. The one command that reads those files is devvm agent import, which copies them into the store when you run it, and devvm agent save copies the settings you changed in a VM into the store.

The store has two folders for each agent, and each one holds the agent’s files at the same paths below it as the agent keeps them in a home folder:

  • Settings go in ~/.config/devvm/agents/<agent>/, such as ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude/.claude/settings.json and ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude/.claude/skills. You can edit these files and make or delete these folders yourself, and a VM gets the change on its next launch, as mounts and copies describe.
  • Logins go in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/<agent>/, such as ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/codex/.codex/auth.json and ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude.json, and so does a login that you make inside a VM, such as Codex’s (Codex and opencode logins) or Claude Code’s in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude/.credentials.json (Claude Code login). Only you can read them, because devvm makes each agent’s logins folder yours alone (mode 700) and each login file mode 600. On macOS, devvm keeps each agent’s logins folder out of Time Machine’s backups.

Each VM gets its agents’ settings and logins from the store, but never your history. Transcripts, sessions and databases aren’t in the store, and each VM’s own stay in that VM. Before you leave an agent running unattended, read staying safe and rogue agents.

flowchart TD
home["the agents' files<br>in your home folder"]
subgraph store["devvm's agent store"]
folders["settings folders:<br>skills, plugins…"]
files["settings files<br>and logins"]
end
subgraph guest["The VM"]
links["linked into ~"]
copies["copies in ~"]
own["its own history"]
end
home -- "devvm agent import,<br>never your history" --> store
folders -- "mounted<br>read-only" --> links
files -- "copied on every<br>launch, without<br>your secrets" --> copies
copies -- "devvm agent save,<br>after a diff and a yes" --> store
own -- "devvm history export,<br>devvm rm" --> export["a .tar.gz<br>on this machine"]
export -. "devvm history import,<br>or yes when a new VM<br>offers it" .-> own

Each row lists the agent’s paths in the VM’s home, and the store keeps each one at the same path below the agent’s settings or logins folder:

Mounted read-only, linked into ~ Copied in on every launch
claude ~/.claude/{skills,agents,commands,output-styles,plugins} ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, and from the logins ~/.claude.json (merged, only its settings, account state and MCP servers)
codex ~/.codex/{prompts,skills} ~/.codex/{config.toml,AGENTS.md}, and from the logins ~/.codex/auth.json
opencode the subfolders of ~/.config/opencode (not node_modules) the files in ~/.config/opencode (not lock files), and from the logins ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json

Importing from this machine

When you already use an agent on this machine, devvm agent import copies its settings and logins from your home folder into the store, so your VMs get them. With no argument it imports every agent that your home folder has files of, and devvm agent import claude codex imports only the agents you name:

devvm agent import # copy every agent's settings and logins into the store
devvm agent import codex # copy only Codex's
devvm agent import --force # replace what the store has without asking

The import copies only the paths in the table above, from ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.config/opencode and ~/.local/share/opencode, so it never copies your history, such as ~/.claude/projects or ~/.codex’s sessions, and never ~/.claude/.credentials.json. From ~/.claude.json it keeps only the settings, account state and MCP servers, so your API key and your per-project entries stay out of the store. Claude Code’s plugin records name the plugins’ folders by their paths, so the store’s copies of the JSON files in ~/.claude/plugins name the plugins’ folders in the store, where the VMs mount them. devvm says which agents it imported and where, and an agent you named that your home folder has nothing of gets a warning.

devvm reads each agent’s settings inside the agent’s own folder, such as ~/.claude, and it never follows a link out of it. A link to a file inside the folder becomes a copy of that file, and a link that leads out of the folder, by a relative or an absolute path, or to a folder, is left out with a warning that names it. A login file that’s a link is left out with a warning too. So when your settings live elsewhere, such as in a dotfiles repo with links into ~/.claude, copy them into the store yourself.

When the store already has settings or a login of an agent you import, devvm asks in a terminal whether to replace them, with no as the default. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm refuses and names --force, which replaces them without asking. A replacement writes each file again and takes out what your home folder no longer has, but it keeps the store’s folders, so a running VM’s mounts still show them. An agent whose settings aren’t in your home folder keeps the store’s settings, and one without a login there keeps the store’s login.

On macOS, Claude Code keeps its own login in the Keychain, and devvm neither reads it nor copies it. You log Claude Code in from a VM instead, with devvm agent login claude, and every VM with Claude Code gets that login (Claude Code login).

opencode 2 keeps its logins in its own database rather than in ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json, so when this machine’s opencode is version 2 or later, devvm reads its logins with opencode auth export and saves them in the store in the format of auth.json, the file that devvm copies for opencode 1. It saves the API key of each provider, and your OpenAI login when you made it with one of opencode’s Codex logins, the browser or the headless one. Any other login is left out with a warning that names it, such as opencode’s Sign in with ChatGPT, whose tokens a VM can’t use, or another provider’s OAuth login, and you log in from a VM instead, with devvm agent login opencode (logging in with devvm agent login). When opencode auth export fails, the import fails too, and the store keeps the login it had.

Saving a VM’s settings

When you change an agent’s settings in a VM, for example by installing a plugin or writing a skill there, devvm agent save copies them into the store, so every VM with that agent gets them. With no argument it saves every agent that the folder’s VM has, and devvm agent save claude saves only the agents you name. devvm starts a stopped VM for it.

devvm agent save # show what changed in the VM's agents' settings, then save them
devvm agent save codex # save only Codex's

The save reads only the settings in the table above from the VM’s home, and never the logins, so it never reads your history, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json or opencode’s auth.json. From the VM’s ~/.claude.json it keeps only the settings, account state and MCP servers, as the import does, and the VM leaves out its per-project entries before it sends anything. devvm puts that part in the store’s logins folder, where the import keeps it too. A folder that the store already has is mounted read-only in the VM, so the agent there can’t change it, and the save leaves it as it is. A folder that the store doesn’t have yet is the VM’s own until you save it, and once the VM next starts with the store’s new folder mounted, its setup links that folder in place of its own (mounts).

Before it saves anything, devvm shows what would change. For each folder it lists the files it adds (A), changes (M) and removes (D), and then it shows a diff of each file it adds or changes against the store’s copy, with a line when a file’s mode changes. The diff shows the settings files and ~/.claude.json as a VM gets them, written out again with devvm-redacted in place of the values that look like secrets, so it never prints your secrets, and it says so when only those values or the file’s layout changed. Every character that a terminal wouldn’t show, such as a control character, a zero-width character or a character that reverses the text, appears in the diff as its code, such as \u{200b}, so a VM can’t hide a line from you. The diff names a binary file without showing it, and it shows a file of more than 1 MiB or 10,000 lines, and every line past the first 20,000 of the whole diff, only as a count. Then devvm says that every VM with these agents runs the hooks, the MCP servers’ commands and the plugins you save, and it asks whether to save them, with no as the default. Read the diff before you answer, because a hook or a plugin that a rogue agent added in one VM runs in every VM once you save it. devvm agent save always asks, and no flag answers for you, so without a terminal, or with --no-input, it shows what would change and then refuses.

devvm treats everything the VM sends as untrusted, because the agent in the VM could have changed any of it. It reads at most 128 MiB from the VM, in at most 20,000 files, folders and links, none of the files larger than 16 MiB, and when the VM sends more, or sends a path outside the agents’ settings or a name with a character that a terminal wouldn’t show, devvm saves nothing. Each file it saves is yours alone (mode 600), or mode 700 when it was executable in the VM, so it never keeps a set-user-ID or set-group-ID bit. A link in a settings folder that leads to a file in the same folder becomes a copy of that file. devvm leaves out any other link, any other kind of file, such as a socket, and a settings file that it can’t parse whole, such as a settings.json that isn’t JSON, and it warns you about each. When it leaves out a file in a folder, the store keeps its own copy of that file. A settings file that the VM doesn’t have stays in the store. A folder that the VM sends replaces the store’s folder whole, so devvm writes each of its files again and takes out the files that the VM’s folder doesn’t have, but it keeps the store’s folder itself, so a running VM’s mounts still show it.

The VM’s copies of the settings files and of ~/.claude.json hold placeholders, such as devvm-redacted, where the store has your secrets. devvm puts the store’s secret back in place of each placeholder, as long as the VM’s copy had that placeholder in that place and nothing around it changed, such as the URL of the MCP server that a header is for. When something around a placeholder changed, devvm leaves the whole file out and warns you, so a VM can’t send a secret it never saw to another host, and you can make that change in the store’s file yourself. devvm also leaves out any other file that holds a placeholder, such as a skill. No VM gets opencode’s files in ~/.config/opencode that are neither settings nor Markdown, such as a .env, so devvm leaves out the VM’s own file of that name and keeps the store’s.

Mounts

devvm mounts the store’s settings folders that exist when it creates the VM read-only, at the same path as in the store on this machine, and links them from the VM’s home. Absolute paths in them, such as Claude Code’s plugin paths, still work. This machine enforces read-only, so even root in the VM can’t write to them. devvm mounts each folder whole, whatever the VM’s network tier, so the VM reads every file in it, a .env or a key file in a plugin’s folder included, and the git config of a private plugin marketplace whose URL holds a password. devvm takes no secrets out of these folders, because they hold plugins, skills and their scripts that the agent runs as they are. So keep secrets out of these folders, as you keep them out of the project folder (why devvm mounts them whole). The VM follows a symlink in these folders among its own files, so a link to a file outside the folder, by a relative or an absolute path, doesn’t reach that file on this machine, on macOS’s virtiofs mounts and on Linux’s 9p mounts alike. devvm doesn’t mount a folder whose path has a comma, on any backend, and it warns you. Lima can’t mount such a path (Lima’s limits).

When you make or delete one of these folders in the store later, by hand or with devvm agent import, devvm notices on the VM’s next launch and names the folder. A VM’s mounts change only when it starts, so a stopped VM gets the new mounts as the launch starts it. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, in the one question that covers every change waiting for the VM’s next start, and because the mounts are among those changes, the default answer is yes (restarting). If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, the mounts change when the VM next starts, for example with devvm restart.

Copies

devvm copies the store’s files into the VM’s home on every launch, over the VM’s own. On every network tier, the copies of the logins and settings files have your secrets taken out, and the VM’s proxy puts them into requests instead (agents’ logins and settings).

devvm merges the settings and MCP servers from the store’s .claude.json into the VM’s own ~/.claude.json, so servers added in the VM stay (MCP servers). Your API key, your answers about API keys and your per-project entries never reach the VM. devvm also replaces the secrets in the agents’ settings files with devvm-redacted, and names what it replaced. Those are the values under keys that look like secrets, every env value and header, and the secrets in URLs and in arguments. In other text, such as a hook’s command, devvm replaces the secrets in its URLs, the keys that start like a known key, such as sk- or ghp_, and the credential after Bearer or Basic, and keeps the words around them (keys in settings files). From the env of Claude Code’s settings.json, the VM gets only Claude Code’s own settings, such as ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the CLAUDE_CODE_*, DISABLE_* and MAX_* variables and those ending in _TIMEOUT_MS, but none whose name marks it as a credential, such as ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN. It also gets the values that only name where a secret is, base URLs without their passwords, true, false and short numbers. Every other env value, and every env value of an MCP server, becomes devvm-redacted. When devvm can’t parse a settings file to take its secrets out, the VM doesn’t get a copy of it, and neither does it get opencode’s files in ~/.config/opencode that are neither settings nor Markdown, such as a .env. devvm names each file it doesn’t copy, and when it can’t make the copy of a login, it says why.

Claude Code login

You log Claude Code in once, from inside any VM that has it, and devvm keeps the login on this machine for every VM with Claude Code, so this machine never needs Claude Code:

devvm agent login claude # log Claude Code in to your Claude subscription
devvm agent login claude --setup-token # get a long-lived Claude Code token with claude setup-token instead

devvm starts the folder’s VM first if it’s stopped, as devvm host does, and then runs Claude Code’s own login in the VM, on your terminal: claude auth login --claudeai, or claude setup-token with --setup-token. Claude Code shows an address, which you open in a browser on any machine. When you approve the login there, the browser shows a code, which you paste back at Claude Code’s prompt, so devvm forwards no port. The VM’s proxy saves the login as it reaches Claude’s token endpoint, and Claude Code in the VM gets only placeholders. devvm then sets the VM up again, so it uses the login at once, and every other VM with Claude Code gets it from its next launch. When the login ends without a new login in the store, devvm says so and fails.

devvm keeps one Claude Code login, either your subscription’s login or a Claude Code token, and the newest replaces the other, so every VM uses the account you logged in to last:

  • Your subscription’s login, from devvm agent login claude or a claude /login that you run in a VM yourself, goes in devvm’s agent store, in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude/.credentials.json, only yours to read. The VM’s ~/.claude/.credentials.json holds placeholders, with no refresh token and an expiry in 2099, so Claude Code in the VM never refreshes the login itself. The VM’s proxy puts the login into the VM’s requests to api.anthropic.com, and refreshes it on this machine when it’s due, through the company proxy when config.toml names one. devvm keeps only a login that can use Claude’s models and can’t make API keys, so a login to an Anthropic Console account, which Claude Code uses to make an API key, fails in a VM, and no API key reaches it. Only a VM that has Claude Code can log it in.
  • A Claude Code token, from devvm agent login claude --setup-token or a claude setup-token that you run in a VM yourself, goes with the other secrets. You can also save one with devvm secret set claude and paste the token that claude setup-token printed on another machine (sk-ant-oat01-…), not the code the browser shows. devvm neither saves nor sends a Claude Code token that isn’t a setup token. Every VM with Claude Code gets the token in its environment as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, holding a placeholder of its own, and its proxy puts the token into its requests. When you set up a token in a VM, claude setup-token prints that VM’s placeholder, not the token, because devvm already saved it.

A VM gets either ~/.claude/.credentials.json or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from devvm, never both, because Claude Code would use the token in its environment over the login in its file. A VM that started with the login devvm replaced keeps working, because its proxy puts the login devvm keeps now in place of either placeholder. A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in devvm’s own environment on this machine wins over both, as it does in Claude Code, so VMs get that token, and devvm agent login claude warns you when it’s set. The VM gets placeholders whatever its network tier.

Anthropic doesn’t document the requests that Claude Code’s login sends, so devvm follows the ones Claude Code sends today, and a new Claude Code release can change them. When a login in a VM stops working, run devvm agent login claude again, or save a Claude Code token instead.

Codex and opencode logins

On every network tier, the VM’s auth.json holds placeholders, and its proxy holds the real API keys and logins. The proxy reads them from the login files in devvm’s store as it needs them and refreshes ChatGPT logins there, so when the agent in the VM stops getting answers, the proxy’s own log, proxy.log in ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/logs/, may say that refreshing a login failed or that you’re no longer logged in that way. To log in again, run devvm agent login codex or devvm agent login opencode in the VM’s folder, which also gives that VM the new login’s placeholders, and the other VMs get them on their next launch. The proxy puts in opencode’s API keys for Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenRouter, and its OpenAI and GitHub Copilot logins. The VM gets opencode’s API keys for other providers unchanged, and its well-known logins too, which an organization’s own opencode config sets up, because devvm doesn’t know which hosts those are for. devvm warns you about each. The VM gets opencode’s other OAuth logins, such as Copilot Enterprise’s, without their access and refresh tokens, so they don’t work in the VM, and devvm warns you about each. To use such a provider in the VM, log in to it with an API key on this machine and import the login again.

Logging in with devvm agent login

devvm agent login logs Codex or opencode in from inside this folder’s VM, so this machine never needs either agent, and devvm’s agent store keeps the login for every VM with that agent. Claude Code’s login is devvm agent login claude (Claude Code login):

devvm agent login codex # log Codex in to ChatGPT in a browser on this machine
devvm agent login opencode --device-code # log opencode in with a code, in a browser on any machine
devvm agent login codex --api-key # save Codex's OpenAI API key, asking for it
devvm agent login opencode --api-key --provider anthropic # save opencode's Anthropic API key

devvm starts the folder’s VM first if it’s stopped, as devvm host does, and the VM must have the agent, which devvm tools add codex gives it. Then devvm runs the agent’s own ChatGPT login in the VM, on your terminal: codex login for Codex, and opencode auth login openai --method chatgpt-browser, opencode’s Codex browser login, for opencode. The agent shows an address, which you open in a browser on this machine. When you approve the login there, the browser comes back to localhost:1455, where the agent’s own server in the VM waits, so devvm forwards this machine’s localhost:1455, and localhost:1457, which Codex uses when 1455 is taken in the VM, to the same ports in the VM. The forward lasts only while the login runs, and it ends when the login ends, fails or you press Ctrl+C, which ends the agent’s login in the VM too. When another program on this machine has port 1455, devvm refuses and names --device-code.

With --device-code, the agent shows a code instead, which you type into a browser on any machine, and devvm forwards nothing. Codex’s device code login is codex login --device-auth, which your ChatGPT account’s security settings must allow, and opencode’s is opencode auth login openai --method chatgpt-headless, its Codex device code login.

When the agent logs in, the VM’s proxy saves the login in the store, and the agent in the VM gets placeholders, as the next section describes. devvm then says what the store saved and the account’s email, and the VM uses the login at once. When the login ends without a new login in the store, for example because you chose another way to log in, devvm says so and fails, and devvm network log shows each login the proxy saved. Codex in a VM keeps its login in ~/.codex/auth.json, never in a keyring, because devvm sets cli_auth_credentials_store = "file" in the VM’s ~/.codex/config.toml on every launch.

With --api-key, devvm asks for the API key without showing it, or reads it from a line of input with --stdin, and saves it in the store itself, so the key never goes into the VM. Codex’s key is an OpenAI key, and it replaces Codex’s ChatGPT login in the store, as codex login --with-api-key does. opencode’s key is for the provider that --provider names, anthropic, openai or openrouter, the providers whose keys the proxy puts in, and the store keeps opencode’s other providers beside it. devvm then gives the running VM its copy of the login, with a placeholder in place of the key, and the VM’s proxy puts the key in at once. opencode keeps its logins in its own database in the VM, and it reads its auth.json only when it first makes that database, so when opencode has already run in the VM, devvm also gives it the key’s placeholder with opencode auth import. devvm reads at most 1 MiB of what that import prints in the VM, and when it prints more, devvm stops it and fails, so running devvm in the VM’s folder tries again. Every other VM with opencode gets the key’s placeholder at its next launch, the same way, and any credentials that you added to opencode in a VM yourself stay in its database.

opencode’s Anthropic login is an API key, because opencode itself has no other way to log in to Anthropic. opencode’s Claude Agent provider uses Claude Code’s own login instead, so it works in a VM that has Claude Code too, with the login that devvm agent login claude saves.

Logins made in a VM

When Codex or opencode in a VM logs in to OpenAI, whether devvm agent login runs it or you run it yourself, the VM’s proxy saves the login in devvm’s store, in the agent’s own auth.json, and the agent in the VM gets only placeholders, so the VM never holds the login’s tokens. The VM you logged in from uses the login at once, and every VM with that agent gets it from its next launch. opencode reads its auth.json only when it first makes its database, so in a VM where opencode has already run, devvm adds the store’s logins to opencode’s database at each launch when they changed since the VM last got them, and makes them the ones opencode uses. Credentials that you added to opencode in the VM yourself stay in its database, labeled with your names rather than devvm, and opencode auth switch changes back to one of them. A login that shows a code to type into a browser on any machine works in a VM as it is, such as codex login --device-auth and opencode’s Codex device code login. opencode’s Sign in with ChatGPT doesn’t work in a VM, because it gets its tokens from another endpoint, whose replies the VM’s proxy refuses so that they never reach the VM, so choose one of opencode’s Codex logins instead, as devvm agent login opencode does. A new login replaces the one in the store, together with Codex’s API key, so every VM with the agent uses the account you logged in to last. In a VM with both Codex and opencode, devvm tells their logins apart by the program that sends them. devvm network log shows a login line for each login it saved. On the open tier, a program that goes around the VM’s proxy gets the login’s tokens itself, and devvm saves nothing (logins made in a VM). Claude Code’s logins in a VM are saved in the same way (Claude Code login).

History

Each VM’s transcripts and sessions stay in that VM. devvm history export [FILE] saves them, and devvm rm saves them before it deletes a VM that has an agent. The export is a .tar.gz of ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.local/share/opencode and ~/.local/state/opencode in the VM, written to FILE or to ~/.local/share/devvm/exports/<vm>-<date>-<time>.tar.gz. An export in that folder gets a <vm>-<date>-<time>.folder file beside it, which names the VM’s project folder and the VM’s network tier when devvm wrote the export.

devvm history lists the exports in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports, oldest first, in a table with a header. It shows each export’s file, the VM it’s of, that VM’s folder, the date and time devvm wrote it, and its size, with - for a folder devvm has no record of. Exports you wrote to a FILE of your own aren’t listed, and devvm history changes nothing and starts no VM.

devvm history –json

devvm history --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the exports has its file, its vm, the VM’s folder, which is "" when devvm has no record of it, the date devvm wrote it in RFC 3339 with this machine’s time zone, and its size in bytes.

{
 "version": 1,
 "exports": [
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/exports/devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c-20261001-120000.tar.gz",
 "vm": "devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c",
 "folder": "/Users/you/code/website",
 "date": "2026-10-01T12:00:00+02:00",
 "size": 1048576
 }
 ]
}

After devvm rm, an export is the only copy of that VM’s history, so devvm keeps the exports until you ask it to delete them. devvm gc --history deletes the exports in that folder, and devvm gc --history --older-than 30d deletes only those written 30 days ago or more. An export’s age counts from the date and time in its name, which is this machine’s local time when devvm wrote it, so across a change to or from daylight saving time an export reaches an age such as 30d an hour earlier or later, for --older-than and for the history.age retention setting alike. gc lists each one by its VM and date first, and in a terminal it asks. Exports you wrote to a FILE of your own stay where they are.

The agents’ logins aren’t in the export, which leaves out ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, and opencode’s auth.json, account.json, mcp-auth.json and bin. opencode keeps its sessions and its logins together in one database, ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db, so the export holds a copy of that database without its logins. The VM makes the copy with sqlite3, which every base image has, and the copy has no logins, API keys or opencode account in any part of the file, not even a key you typed into opencode in the VM, while the VM’s own database keeps them (how). The export never holds the database’s -wal, -shm or -journal files, which can hold logins that opencode saved last. When the VM has no sqlite3, such as a VM made from an image built without it, the export leaves the database out, so opencode’s sessions aren’t in it, and the run log says so. devvm starts a stopped VM for the export as a launch does, so it locks the folder’s .git again and checks the VM’s confinement first, and the VM stays running. devvm writes the file only once the export is complete, so a failed export leaves no file and leaves an existing FILE as it was. An export holds at most 2 GiB, because a VM could otherwise write until this machine’s disk is full. When the VM sends more, devvm stops the export and keeps nothing of it, so devvm history export fails, while devvm rm and the commands that make a VM again warn that they kept no export and go on without one. Only you can read the file, and devvm makes the exports folder yours alone each time it writes one there, whatever its mode was before. When FILE is in a folder of your own, that folder keeps its mode. If the export fails, devvm rm keeps the VM, and devvm rm --no-export deletes it without exporting. devvm rm VM, for a VM whose folder is gone, exports in the same way, but only from a running VM or a --clone VM, because starting any other would make its folder again (a VM whose folder is gone).

Importing history

devvm history import [FILE] puts an export back into this folder’s VM, so the agents’ transcripts and sessions carry over when you delete a VM and make it again. Without FILE, it imports the newest export in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports that devvm saved for this folder, going by the .folder file beside each one, and it never picks an export made for another folder. With FILE, it imports that .tar.gz, such as one you saved with devvm history export FILE. devvm starts a stopped VM for the import, as it does for an export. The import works on every VM, whether its base is Ubuntu’s image or a Debian-, Ubuntu- or Alpine-based container image (starting from a container image), because it unpacks the export with GNU tar, which Debian and Ubuntu always have and which devvm installs in every base made --from alpine.

When devvm makes a new VM that has an agent, and it saved an export for the same folder before, it offers that export. In a terminal it asks whether to import it into the new VM, with no as the default. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, it doesn’t ask, and it says which export it found and that devvm history import in the folder puts it into the VM. devvm imports the export once the VM has started and before its setup, and if the import fails, devvm warns and makes the VM anyway, so you can run devvm history import later.

An export holds what a VM wrote, so devvm treats it as untrusted. Its transcripts can hold what the old VM’s agents read, and a VM on a less strict tier reaches more, such as your local network on the open tier. So when the export comes from a VM on a less strict tier than the VM you import it into, going from open to internet, allowlist and none, devvm warns you before it imports. devvm knows an export’s tier only from the .folder file beside it in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports, so it warns about an export with no tier recorded, or any FILE elsewhere, such as in the project folder that a VM can write, as if it came from an open VM. devvm never unpacks an export on this machine. It streams the file into the VM as it is, and the VM’s own tar unpacks it there as the VM’s user, so it can only write what that user can write. Before unpacking anything, the VM lists the paths in the export, and when one of them is outside ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.local/share/opencode and ~/.local/state/opencode, starts with / or has a .. part, devvm imports nothing and says so. The import keeps no owner or mode from the export, so the VM user’s umask applies and no file is set-user-ID. It also takes out every symbolic link that points outside the folder it’s in, which is any link to an absolute path or one with a .. part, so an agent writing to a session file can’t follow a link out of its history. An export that devvm didn’t write, such as a .tar.gz you made yourself, can hold opencode’s database with its logins, so the import takes out the database’s -wal, -shm and -journal files and puts in a copy of the database without its logins, as the export makes it, or leaves the database out when the VM has no sqlite3. opencode in the new VM then reads the logins that devvm gave the VM, as it does when it first makes its database. When the VM already has an opencode database, it keeps its own, and opencode’s sessions from the export aren’t imported.

The import leaves out what devvm puts in the VM itself. That’s the agents’ logins, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, and opencode’s auth.json, account.json, mcp-auth.json and bin. It’s also ~/.claude.json, whose copy in the old VM held that VM’s own placeholders, and every agent’s mounted folders and copied files, which the new VM’s setup links and copies from devvm’s agent store. A file or folder the VM already has stays as it is, so importing into a VM that has history of its own adds the export’s files without replacing any of its own.

The VM’s setup

Besides the agents’ config, every launch sets the VM up from this machine’s settings:

  • its hostname, which is the folder’s part of the VM’s name;
  • the timezone (TZ, else this machine’s) and, when it’s UTF-8, the locale (LC_ALL, else LANG);
  • git’s user.name and user.email, as git has them in the project folder;
  • telemetry off where an environment variable can’t turn it off, which is Go’s, and Codex’s analytics and metrics;
  • (devvm) at the start of the prompt.

On every network tier, the launch also installs the VM’s own CA and the next one, points apt, sudo, ssh, the docker layer’s Docker and the nix layer’s Nix at the proxy, and adds devvm-why, which shows what the proxy blocked lately. It also tells the agents, in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, why a request may fail (inside the VM). The VM’s secrets go in ~/.config/devvm/env in the VM, which login shells read, and that file holds their placeholders.

item.title: devvm
item.description:
Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first

Synopsis

Open a shell in this folder’s VM, at the same path, and create the VM first when the folder has none. devvm shows what a new VM gets, and in a terminal you can customize its toolchains, coding agents, layers, tier, ports and size, which –tools, –agents, –layers, –network, –ports, –cpus, –memory and –disk choose without asking. The VM mounts only this folder read-write, and with –clone it gets its own clone of the repo instead.

devvm [flags]

Examples 

 devvm # open this folder's VM, choosing what a new one gets
 devvm --agents claude # create the VM with Claude Code and the toolchains the folder needs
 devvm --tools node --agents none --layers docker # create the VM with node and the docker layer alone
 devvm --clone # create the VM with its own clone of this repo
 devvm ls # list every VM

Options 

 --agents LIST the LIST of coding agents a new VM gets, such as claude,codex, or none (default: devvm setup's)
 --clone create the VM with its own clone of this repo instead of mounting the folder
 --cpus N the N CPUs the VM gets (default: devvm size -g, else the image's)
 --disk GiB the VM's disk in GiB, at least the image's (default: devvm size -g, else the image's)
 --from IMAGE the container IMAGE base starts from, such as node:24, instead of Ubuntu's cloud image (default: $DEVVM_FROM)
 -h, --help help for devvm
 --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside
 --layers LIST the LIST of layers a new VM's image gets, bottom first, such as docker,mine, or none (default: devvm setup's)
 --memory GiB the VM's memory in GiB, such as 16 or 16G (default: devvm size -g, else the image's)
 --network TIER the network TIER a new VM gets: open, internet, allowlist or none (default: devvm network -g's, else allowlist)
 --no-devcontainer create the VM without reading the folder's devcontainer.json
 --no-git-protect create the VM without .git protection
 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own
 --ports PORTS the PORTS the VM forwards: all, none or a list like 5173,8000-8010 (default: devvm ports -g, else all)
 --ssh-agent create the VM with your SSH agent forwarded, so anything in it can use your keys while you're connected
 --ssh-config add devvm's Include line to ~/.ssh/config without asking
 --tools LIST the LIST of toolchains a new VM gets, such as node,python, or none (default: those the folder's files call for)
 --unsafe-folder mount a folder devvm refuses, such as your home folder
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line
 --version print devvm's version

Docs

The docs page for devvm explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm adopt: Give this folder the VM made for an earlier folder or path
  • devvm agent: Fill devvm’s store of the agents’ settings and logins that every VM gets
  • devvm build: Build an image and the images under it, unless they’re built
  • devvm clone: Show or change whether this folder’s VM has its own clone of the repo
  • devvm code: Open this folder’s VM in VS Code over Remote-SSH
  • devvm completion: Print the shell completion script for bash, zsh or fish
  • devvm desktop: Open this folder’s VM’s desktop in a VNC viewer
  • devvm doctor: Check what devvm needs on this machine
  • devvm gc: Delete stale images, unused tools, old files and the Nix cache over its cap
  • devvm git-protect: Show or change .git protection for this folder’s VM
  • devvm group: Show the group this folder’s VM is in
  • devvm history: List the saved exports of agents’ history
  • devvm host: Get this folder’s VM ready for ssh and editors, and show its host name
  • devvm images: List the images and the shared tools
  • devvm layer: Make image layers of your own, or change this folder’s VM’s layers
  • devvm limactl: Run Lima’s limactl for debugging, which starts VMs unconfined, whatever their tier
  • devvm link: List this folder’s VM’s links to your other VMs
  • devvm ls: List the project VMs
  • devvm network: Show or change the network tier of this folder’s VM
  • devvm ports: Show or change which ports this folder’s VM forwards
  • devvm rebuild: Build an image again, and delete the old one
  • devvm restart: Restart this folder’s VM and open a shell in it
  • devvm retention: Show or change what devvm deletes on its own
  • devvm rm: Delete this folder’s VM, or a VM whose folder is gone
  • devvm secret: List the secrets kept on this machine, for VMs to use
  • devvm setup: Choose base’s features, and new VMs’ size, network tier, coding agents and layers
  • devvm size: Show or change this folder’s VM’s size
  • devvm space: Show what devvm keeps on this machine and the space it takes
  • devvm ssh-agent: Show or change SSH agent forwarding for this folder’s VM
  • devvm stop: Stop this folder’s VM
  • devvm tools: Show or choose this folder’s VM’s shared tools
  • devvm update: Bring this folder’s VM up to date, then open a shell in it
  • devvm upgrade: Install devvm’s newest release

item.title: Installing
item.description:
This page gets devvm installed and checked on your machine. Upgrading and uninstalling covers what comes later.

Installing devvm

Run the command for your system:

# Install devvm, and Lima with it
brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm
brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm

The install script in the Linux tab also works on macOS.

# Install devvm and what it needs
curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash

The script asks before it installs Lima, QEMU or access to /dev/kvm.

Install devvm one way, with Homebrew or with the install script, but not both (one devvm). The install script needs curl, tar, and sha256sum or shasum, it never needs sudo for devvm itself, and it checks the download’s checksum and signature before it installs anything (Installing and updating). To check the script itself against devvm’s release key before you run it, follow checking the install script. It takes options after bash -s --, as in curl -fsSL … | bash -s -- --yes:

Option What it does
--yes answer yes to every question
--version 0.1.0, or DEVVM_VERSION=0.1.0 install that release
--no-deps install devvm only
--force install even when Homebrew installed devvm, which leaves you with two copies
DEVVM_PREFIX=/some/dir install under that folder instead of ~/.local

Requirements

devvm runs its VMs on Lima, its default backend. It’s tested on Apple silicon Macs and on Linux on both arm64 and x86_64, but not yet on Intel Macs (Known limits). The last column says whether the install script offers to install a requirement for you.

You need To check To get it The install script
macOS at Lima’s minimum, on arm64 or x86_64 sw_vers and uname -m doesn’t
8 GiB of memory and 4 CPUs, recommended sysctl hw.memsize hw.ncpu doesn’t
Lima at its minimum limactl --version brew install lima, or Lima’s install guide offers it: Homebrew’s when you have Homebrew, otherwise Lima’s latest release into ~/.local
OpenSSH 8.7 or newer, for ssh and editors by name (details) ssh -V macOS 13’s has it doesn’t
Docker Desktop, only for --from with an image only Docker has docker version Docker Desktop doesn’t
You need To check To get it The install script
Linux on arm64 or x86_64 uname -m doesn’t
8 GiB of memory and 4 CPUs, recommended free -g and nproc doesn’t
Lima at its minimum limactl --version brew install lima, or Lima’s install guide offers it: Homebrew’s when you have Homebrew, otherwise Lima’s latest release into ~/.local
QEMU qemu-img --version your package manager: apt, dnf, pacman or zypper offers it, with sudo
Access to /dev/kvm ls -l /dev/kvm sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER, then log out and back in offers it, with sudo
OpenSSH 8.7 or newer, for ssh and editors by name (details) ssh -V Ubuntu 22.04’s has it doesn’t
Docker’s engine, only for --from with an image only Docker has docker version Docker’s engine doesn’t
  • A smaller machine works too. devvm gives base fewer CPUs and less memory there (size and ports).
  • Your first VM needs 8 GiB of free disk space, for the base image, the VM’s own image and the shared tools (free space).
  • Everything else goes inside the VMs, including the toolchains, the coding agents and Docker for your projects (docker layer), so you don’t install Claude Code, Codex or opencode on this machine (devvm’s agent store).
  • Linux hosts have a few limits, such as no .git protection (Known limits).

Checking what devvm needs

Run devvm doctor:

devvm doctor

It lists everything that devvm’s backend, Lima, needs and doesn’t have, each with what to do, then its warnings, such as a machine with less than the recommended memory, and it fails only when something is missing. devvm never installs anything on this machine itself, and every command that needs the backend checks it first and stops at the first thing that’s missing. What devvm doctor checks lists each check and warning.

When devvm doctor finds nothing missing, you’re ready for your first VM. Before you make it, read staying safe, which lists the habits that close most of what devvm leaves open.

item.title: Lima
item.description:
Lima is devvm’s backend, so every new VM runs on it (a VM’s backend). Each project gets a full VM with a kernel of its own, which runs on Apple’s Virtualization framework (vz) on macOS and on QEMU on Linux. How it works › Lima explains how devvm sets up, confines and clones Lima’s VMs.

Requirements

  • macOS 13 or newer, on arm64 or x86_64.
  • Lima 2.2 or newer, with limactl on your PATH. Install it with Homebrew, brew install lima, or see Lima’s install guide.
  • Linux on arm64 or x86_64.
  • Lima 2.2 or newer, with limactl on your PATH. Install it with Homebrew, brew install lima, or see Lima’s install guide.
  • QEMU from your package manager: qemu-system-aarch64 (or qemu-system-x86_64) and qemu-img.
  • Read and write access to /dev/kvm. That means virtualization is turned on in the firmware (or nested virtualization, in a VM), and your user is in the kvm group.

Every command that needs Lima checks these first and stops at the first one that’s missing. devvm doctor lists them all, each with the command that installs it where there’s one to run. That’s Homebrew’s command for Lima when you have Homebrew, your package manager’s for QEMU (apt, dnf, pacman or zypper), and sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER for /dev/kvm, after which you log in again. devvm never runs them itself (details).

devvm’s Lima home

devvm keeps its VMs and images in a Lima home of its own, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima (under $XDG_DATA_HOME when that’s set), whatever LIMA_HOME says. Your own Lima VMs stay where they are, and Lima settings you made for them don’t reach devvm’s VMs. Because of this, a plain limactl list doesn’t show devvm’s VMs, so run devvm limactl list instead (below). To keep devvm’s VMs somewhere else, such as a sandbox or a shorter path, set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to that folder.

Lima adds _config/default.yaml and _config/override.yaml from its home to every VM it starts, so devvm refuses to start a VM while devvm’s Lima home holds either file, and you move them out of it to go on. devvm also refuses a VM that has a network devvm didn’t give it, because a second network would get around the VM’s proxy, so remove the networks: entries from the file that devvm names (why).

Running limactl

devvm limactl ARGS... runs limactl with ARGS on devvm’s Lima home, in devvm’s place. Its input, output, terminal and exit code are limactl’s, and devvm passes every option on to it, --help included. devvm help limactl shows devvm’s own help for the command.

devvm limactl list
devvm limactl shell --start devvm-img-<key>
  • It runs from devvm’s data folder, as devvm’s own limactl commands do, so give files by their absolute path.
  • It runs without your SSH agent, so a VM never gets your agent through it, whatever its SSH agent choice says (why).
  • A VM you start this way, with devvm limactl start or shell --start, runs unconfined, whatever its tier, and devvm ls shows it as unenforced (confinement). Start project VMs with devvm.

File watchers

A dev server or a watcher that runs in the VM, such as Vite, webpack, tsc --watch or nodemon, learns about changed files from the VM’s kernel. The kernel sees every change made in the VM, so a file that a coding agent or a command in the VM’s shell writes reaches the watcher at once. Lima’s mounts don’t pass on the changes you make on this machine, though, so a watcher in the VM misses a file you save in your editor here, and the dev server doesn’t reload. On Linux the project folder is a 9p mount, and there a watcher also misses the VM’s own changes in the folder’s subfolders, and sees only those to files at the top of the folder.

To have a watcher see your edits, set it to poll the project folder, which costs some CPU in a large project:

Tool Setting
chokidar, and tools built on it CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING=1
Vite server.watch.usePolling: true in vite.config
webpack watchOptions.poll in webpack.config.js, or WATCHPACK_POLLING=true
nodemon nodemon --legacy-watch
tsc --watch "watchOptions": { "watchFile": "fixedPollingInterval" } in tsconfig.json
cargo watch cargo watch --poll

Set the variables in the VM’s shell or in your project’s scripts, before the tool starts. Leave Lima’s own file event setting, mountInotify, off, because with it on, commands in the VM that write to the project folder, such as git init, fail at random (details).

Cleaning up

devvm gc deletes devvm’s stale and unfinished Lima images and the shared tools that no VM has and that aren’t current, and it leaves your VMs as they are. devvm images rm deletes an image that’s current, except on Linux hosts one whose disk VMs use (cleaning up). Lima also keeps a download cache of its own, which holds Ubuntu’s cloud images that devvm’s builds downloaded, and which your own Lima VMs share. devvm gc --caches deletes the cloud images that devvm downloads and that no image of devvm’s names, after listing them and asking, and devvm never runs limactl prune, which empties the whole cache (what devvm keeps).

Limits

  • Folder names in VM names are cut short. Lima keeps each VM’s ssh socket in the VM’s folder in its home, and a socket path has at most 104 characters. A long Lima home leaves less room for the name, so set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to a shorter folder if devvm says the home is too long, or that a VM’s name leaves no room for the folder’s name (VM names).
  • Paths can’t contain commas. Lima and QEMU split mount options on commas, so devvm refuses to mount a project folder whose path has one, and it leaves out an agent’s folder whose path has one, with a warning.
  • Disks can grow but not shrink.
  • Mounts on Linux are 9p. A 9p share mounts once per guest, and file watchers in the VM miss changes in its subfolders (file watchers).
  • A VM that Lima reports as failed to start still starts, with a warning, when it’s running but degraded because one of Lima’s boot scripts failed. A VM that doesn’t answer over ssh within a minute is stopped instead, and its console log is in its Lima folder (serial*.log).

item.title: Network tiers
item.description:
Every VM goes through a proxy that devvm runs for it on this machine, and the VM’s network tier decides what the proxy lets it reach. New VMs get the allowlist tier by default, so they reach only the hosts on their allowlist. No VM holds your secrets, whatever its tier, because its proxy puts them into its requests. A secret is a credential devvm keeps on this machine for VMs to use: your GitHub token, Claude Code’s token, an agent’s login or an API key. An open VM, the one tier that isn’t confined to its proxy, reaches anything this machine can, including this machine’s own services on localhost and your LAN.

sequenceDiagram
participant P as The VM
participant X as Its proxy,<br>on this machine
participant H as api.github.com
P->>X: GET /user, with<br>a placeholder
Note over X: on the allowlist
X->>H: GET /user, with<br>your GitHub token
H-->>X: the response
X-->>P: the response
P->>X: CONNECT<br>example.com:443
X-->>P: 403: not on<br>the allowlist

This page covers what you do with a VM’s tier and what you see. How it works › Network tiers explains how devvm confines a VM to its proxy and how the proxy handles each connection.

Network tiers

A VM is on one of four tiers, from the lowest to the highest:

Tier What the VM reaches Confined to its proxy
open whatever this machine reaches, its localhost and the LAN included; the proxy applies no rules no
internet every public host, on any port, apart from your denies; never this machine’s addresses or its networks' yes
allowlist only the hosts its allowlists allow, apart from your denies yes
none only its agents’ hosts, the hosts of its secrets and logins, and its links, apart from your denies yes

--network TIER chooses a new VM’s tier, and devvm network with a tier changes an existing VM’s, such as devvm network internet (choosing a tier). A higher tier is stricter, and a VM on any tier but open is confined: it reaches nothing but its proxy, and a direct connection from it fails.

An open VM runs on its backend’s own network, so it reaches this machine and your LAN directly, as a VM without a proxy would. Its environment names its proxy all the same (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and their lowercase forms), and the proxy reaches every host and address for it, this machine’s localhost and your LAN included, so a tool behaves the same through the proxy as it does directly. Its NO_PROXY names the VM itself and this machine as the VM reaches it, host.lima.internal, so requests to those go directly. Every launch checks that an open VM’s proxy is set in the VM and answers it, and when it doesn’t, devvm warns you and opens the VM all the same. An open VM gets a placeholder for each secret it may use, as every VM does, and only its proxy puts the real value in. So a request that goes around the proxy, directly from the VM, carries only the placeholder, and the secret’s host refuses it.

On the internet and none tiers, devvm reads only the denies of your policy files: the internet tier allows every public host itself, and the none tier allows only what the VM’s agents, secrets and links need. devvm network marks each such file (denies only), and when you add an allow to a VM on either tier, devvm says that the allow changes nothing until the VM is on the allowlist tier. On the open tier no rule applies at all.

Changing a VM from one confined tier to another applies at once, because the VM’s proxy starts again with the new tier’s rules and the VM keeps running. A change into or out of the open tier applies from the VM’s next start, as below describes. devvm ls and devvm network show a VM’s tier, or unenforced when a confined tier isn’t in force (when it isn’t enforced).

Choosing a tier

A new VM gets the allowlist tier unless you choose another, and the summary devvm shows before it makes the VM names its tier. When you customize the VM in a terminal, devvm lists the four tiers, each with what it reaches, and the tier the summary showed is chosen (what a new VM gets):

Network tier for devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c (up/down to choose, enter to confirm):
 ( ) open reaches anything this machine can
 ( ) internet reaches any public host
> (*) allowlist reaches only the hosts you allow (recommended)
 ( ) none reaches only its agents' and secrets' hosts and its links

Up and down move the choice, and enter gives the VM the chosen tier, so pressing enter at once keeps the tier the summary showed. --network TIER answers the question up front, such as devvm --network internet, and when there’s no terminal to ask in, or you give --no-input, the VM gets the tier the summary showed. A VM keeps its tier. On an existing VM devvm ignores --network and warns you, naming the devvm network command that changes the tier.

To give every new VM another tier, save it with devvm network -g, such as devvm network -g none, or choose it in devvm setup. Each new VM’s summary then shows that tier, and customizing the VM still asks, with Enter keeping the saved tier. devvm network -g shows what new VMs get, allowlist until you save another tier, followed by where it came from after a #, and devvm network -g --json prints it as policy, with source. devvm reads the saved tier only when it creates a VM, so the VMs you already have keep their own tier, and --network still chooses for one new VM. You can also set it with network in config.toml, which wins over the saved tier, and then devvm network -g refuses to change it and names the file (where a default comes from).

Lima confines every VM to its proxy, so every VM can be on any tier, the docker layer’s included. devvm never starts a VM on a confined tier with an open network, so if a VM’s backend couldn’t confine it, the VM could only be open: devvm would refuse to make it on any other tier unless you give --network open, and it would refuse to give it any other tier with devvm network (when a backend lacks something).
devvm network print this folder’s VM’s tier as devvm ls shows it, open, internet, allowlist, none or unenforced, and then its allowlist
devvm network open|internet|allowlist|none change it: between confined tiers at once, and into or out of open from the VM’s next start, which devvm restart gives you, and for a running VM, ask in a terminal whether to restart it now
devvm network -g [open|internet|allowlist|none] show or change what new VMs get

When a change into or out of open finds the VM running, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, and if you answer yes, it restarts the VM as devvm restart does, so the change applies at once. If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, the change waits until the VM starts again. If you give a running open VM a confined tier, the VM isn’t confined yet, so devvm ls shows it as unenforced, and its next launch offers to restart it confined, as it does for a VM started outside devvm. If you make a VM open while it runs confined, its launches keep it confined to its proxy, which now applies an open VM’s rules, until it next starts, and they warn you that the VM leaves its proxy’s confinement when it next starts. In a terminal, each of those launches first asks whether to restart the VM now, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too (restarting).

When it isn’t enforced

On every launch devvm checks on this machine that the VM still runs on the process devvm started confined, and that a direct connection from the VM to the internet fails. A VM that fails either check shows as unenforced, and devvm offers to restart it confined or stops it, as the self-check describes.

Allowlists

The VM’s proxy reads devvm’s built-in policies first and then your policy files, in order, as one list:

  • devvm’s own rules for every VM, which allow OS packages, mise’s version lists, the Sigstore and GitHub trust roots that mise checks a download’s attestations against, Node’s downloads for a project’s own node, and GitHub;
  • devvm’s rules for each shared tool in the VM’s image (node, claude and the others), which allow its registries, downloads and APIs;
  • devvm’s rules for each built-in layer in the VM’s image, so the docker layer allows Docker’s packages and the container registries Docker Hub and ghcr.io, and the nix layer allows Nix’s binary cache, channels and flake registry;
  • ~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.policy, for each of your own layers in the VM’s image;
  • ~/.config/devvm/policy, your own rules for every VM, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change with -g;
  • ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/policy, the rules for that VM only, in the VM’s own folder, which is named by the hash that the VM’s name ends with, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change;
  • the hosts of the VM’s secrets and logins, and the host its agents log in at, such as Codex’s and opencode’s auth.openai.com and Claude Code’s platform.claude.com and console.anthropic.com, on port 443, which devvm adds.

The first three are built in: they come with devvm, inside its binary, so you can’t edit them, and an upgrade of devvm is what changes them. To change what a VM reaches, add your own rules, and to keep a VM from a host that devvm’s rules allow, add a deny, which beats any allow. devvm leaves storage and paste sites out of its defaults on purpose, because they’re easy ways to send data out. Rules never come from the project folder, because the VM can write it. The proxy reads each of your files again when it changes, so an edit applies at once, from the next connection. How it works lists where each policy comes from.

Rules

A policy file holds one rule per line. # starts a comment, and matching ignores case.

Rule Matches
example.com that host only
*.example.com any subdomain, at any depth, not example.com itself
** any host, and any address, though an internal address still needs its own rule
10.0.0.5, 10.0.0.0/8, fd00::/8 addresses, IPv4 or IPv6 (also what lets a connection past the internal-address refusal)
RULE:22, [fd00::1]:22, 10.0.0.0/8:8080 only that port; without a port, 443 and 80
RULE:*, **:* any port
!RULE deny: a deny beats any allow

A rule is plain ASCII with no spaces in it, and a port is a number from 1 to 65535, or * for any port. A host’s one trailing dot is dropped, so example.com. matches example.com. Brackets hold only an IPv6 address, and an address can’t follow *.. A line that holds anything else, such as example.com:x, a*.example.com or ! example.com with a space after the !, isn’t a rule.

When a line that isn’t a rule starts with !, it reads as a deny, but the proxy can’t tell what it would deny. So while the line is there, the proxy of every VM that reads the file denies every new connection apart from the VM’s links, whatever the other rules allow. Connections that are already open stay open. Each refusal names the file and the line, and it suggests no devvm network allow command, because no rule would help. Any other line that isn’t a rule is skipped, and the file’s other lines still apply. The proxy names each such line in its own log.

devvm warns about each line that isn’t a rule, with the file and the line’s number, and the warning for a broken deny says that the proxies deny everything until it’s fixed. It warns when you open a confined VM whose proxy reads the file, when devvm network allow, deny or rm changes the file, and in devvm doctor. devvm network also marks the line. Fix the line or remove it, and the change applies from the next connection.

The proxy never dials a denied address, even for an allowed name that resolves to it or to its NAT64 form. A missing file has no rules. A file that changed but can’t be read keeps its last rules, so a deny never lapses.

Changing rules

devvm network shows this folder’s VM’s allowlist after its tier. It prints each of the VM’s policies that holds more than comments, and then its rules without their comments. A built-in policy has its name after # devvm:, because it has no file you could edit, and one of your files has its path after #, followed by (denies only) on the internet and none tiers, where it shows only the file’s denies. An open VM has no policies, so devvm network prints its tier alone. A line that isn’t a rule is marked # not a rule, skipped, with its line number:

allowlist
# devvm: layers/base.policy
 ports.ubuntu.com
 github.com
# /Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy
 example.com
 example.com:x # not a rule, skipped (line 2)
devvm network allow RULE... add the rules to the VM’s own file
devvm network deny RULE... add them as denies, adding ! when it’s missing
devvm network rm RULE... remove the lines with these rules, a deny with its !, and warn about one that isn’t there
-g, --global with allow, deny or rm, change ~/.config/devvm/policy, for every VM, instead, which needs no VM

A rule is what Rules lists, without spaces or a comment. devvm refuses anything else before it adds any rule, and it also refuses allow !RULE. A rule that’s already in the file, in any case, isn’t added again. Each change applies at once, from the next connection. For an open VM, devvm notes that no rule applies to it, and for an allow on the internet or none tier, that only denies apply there. When devvm network log --blocked or a blocked request in the VM suggests a devvm network allow command, its rule is one that devvm network allow takes.

If a VM was deleted outside devvm, devvm deletes what it kept for that VM when it makes a new VM for the same project folder, so the new VM never gets the old one’s rules.

devvm network –json

devvm network --json prints the VM’s tier and its allowlist as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. policy is open, internet, allowlist, none or unenforced, and allowlist has each policy that holds more than comments, in the order the proxy reads them. Each has builtin, a built-in policy’s name, or file, the path of one of your files, then its rules and, in not_rules, each line that isn’t a rule, with its line number and its text. On the internet and none tiers, a file whose denies alone apply also has denies_only set to true, and its rules are its denies, as devvm network lists them under (denies only). Without denies_only, a file’s rules are all of its rules. With -g, the object has only policy, which is the tier new VMs get, and source, which says where it came from: config.toml, settings.json for what devvm network -g or devvm setup saved, or built-in (where a default comes from). With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses a tier with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "allowlist",
 "source": "config.toml"
}
{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "allowlist",
 "allowlist": [
 {
 "builtin": "layers/base.policy",
 "rules": [
 "ports.ubuntu.com",
 "github.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 },
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy",
 "rules": [
 "example.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": [
 {
 "line": 2,
 "text": "example.com:x"
 }
 ]
 }
 ]
}

On the none tier, a VM with Claude Code gets Claude Code’s built-in policy whole, and its own file shows only its denies:

{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "none",
 "allowlist": [
 {
 "builtin": "shared-tools/claude.policy",
 "rules": [
 "api.anthropic.com",
 "claude.ai"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 },
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy",
 "denies_only": true,
 "rules": [
 "!tracker.example.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 }
 ]
}

Inside the VM

Every login in the VM has the proxy settings in its environment (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and their lowercase forms, NO_PROXY for the VM itself, and NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY), and the CA variables that every VM has point the tools that don’t read the system’s store at the VM’s own CAs. devvm also points apt, sudo, ssh and Docker at the proxy (how), on every tier. On a confined tier, a direct connection fails at once, even as root, and so does DNS, because names resolve in the proxy. A tool that skips the proxy, even for a host the rules allow, fails with a DNS or connection error rather than the proxy’s 403, and nothing reaches the log (what to do).

A blocked request gets 403, and the response names the host, the reason and the rule that would allow it. The proxy also answers at http://devvm.proxy/:

  • /blocked lists the last 50 blocks.
  • /blocked/new?after=N gives the number of blocks so far, then those after the Nth, with each rule once, so a shell prompt can show what a command hit.
  • /ca.pem is the VM’s own CA certificate and the next one’s, never their keys.
  • /nix/ is the shared Nix cache, in a VM with the nix layer (below).

In the VM, devvm-why prints what the proxy blocked lately, and a note before each prompt tells you when something new was blocked. When the proxy blocked nothing lately, devvm-why says so, and it adds that a DNS or connection error for a host the tier allows means the tool skipped the proxy, so you turn on the tool’s own proxy setting or give it the address in $HTTPS_PROXY (a host on the allowlist doesn’t resolve). devvm also tells Claude Code and Codex, in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, why a request may fail and to run devvm-why, and that such an error while devvm-why shows nothing means the tool skipped the proxy.

Nix

In a VM with the nix layer, Nix’s daemon makes most of Nix’s downloads, and devvm also points it at the proxy, so its downloads go through the same allowlists. The layer’s allowlist has cache.nixos.org for Nix’s binary cache, and channels.nixos.org and releases.nixos.org for its channels and flake registry, and GitHub, where most flakes’ inputs come from, is in devvm’s rules for every VM.

Nix asks the proxy’s shared cache, http://devvm.proxy/nix, before cache.nixos.org, so every VM with the layer shares the packages that any of them downloaded (shared downloads). The proxy fetches what the cache doesn’t have from cache.nixos.org alone, and only while the VM’s tier and rules let it reach cache.nixos.org. It keeps a package only when cache.nixos.org’s signature on it checks, and the VM’s Nix checks that signature again. A VM can only make the proxy fetch from cache.nixos.org: the proxy refuses anything a VM sends to store, and every request that isn’t for one of Nix’s cache files. Each request shows in devvm network log as cache, with whether it was a hit, fetched, or why it wasn’t found. What one VM can learn of another through the cache is under Attack vectors. An open VM has its proxy too, so it shares the cache as well, and its proxy fetches from cache.nixos.org for it.

When a package isn’t in the binary cache, Nix builds it from source, and the build downloads its sources from their own hosts, such as ftpmirror.gnu.org. The proxy blocks those hosts until you allow them, so the build fails, and the error, devvm-why and devvm network log --blocked name the host and the devvm network allow command that allows it.

Behind a company proxy

When this machine reaches the internet only through a company proxy, the VM’s proxy sends the requests it allows through that proxy. devvm reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY, or their lowercase forms, from the shell you run it in. When that shell sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, devvm reads the [proxy] table of config.toml instead, so the proxy works from every shell, including an editor’s terminal that didn’t load your profile. The shell’s settings win whole: devvm never mixes them with config.toml’s, so a NO_PROXY alone in the shell still leaves config.toml’s proxy in effect, with its own no-proxy.

[proxy]
https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com"

devvm passes the settings to the VM’s proxy when the proxy starts, and when you run devvm again with different settings, devvm starts the VM’s proxy again with the new ones. So after you change them, run devvm again in the folder or devvm restart. When a VM’s proxy went through a company proxy the last time it started and devvm finds none this time, devvm warns you and names config.toml, because a VM’s proxy that a shell without the settings starts sends the VM’s requests directly.

The VM’s proxy still decides each request by the host name the VM asked for, against the same allowlists, and only then passes it on. It sends tunnels, which carry HTTPS and the requests it puts your secrets into, through HTTPS_PROXY’s proxy, and plain HTTP requests through HTTP_PROXY’s. It reaches the hosts that NO_PROXY names directly, and also localhost and loopback addresses. In NO_PROXY, example.com matches that host and its subdomains, .example.com matches only its subdomains, an address or a CIDR matches addresses, any entry can end in a port, and * matches every host. devvm network log adds through host:port to each request that went through the company proxy.

The company proxy needs an http:// address, such as http://user:password@proxy.example.com:8080 in HTTPS_PROXY, and a proxy without a port is on port 80. devvm doesn’t start a VM’s proxy while HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY or a [proxy] key names an https:// or socks5:// proxy, and it tells you which setting to change. The company proxy’s password stays on this machine. The VM never gets it, and devvm writes it into no log, no image and no process’s arguments.

config.toml never holds the password, because it’s a file you might copy to other machines or keep with your dotfiles, and devvm refuses a [proxy] URL that has one. Put only the user in the URL, as http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080, and save the password with devvm secret set proxy, which keeps it as it keeps the other secrets. devvm’s proxies look it up themselves when they start, so no file of devvm’s holds it in the clear. devvm doesn’t make a new VM, start a VM’s proxy, or build an image or the shared tools while config.toml’s proxy names a user and no password is saved, and it checks before anything starts. A VM’s proxy reads the password only when it starts, so after you change it, run devvm restart in each VM’s folder. No VM ever gets the proxy secret, and devvm secret use proxy refuses.

The company proxy sees the name and port of every host the VM reaches, and if it inspects TLS, the CA you add for it also lets it read the traffic. The company proxy also looks up each name itself, so the VM’s proxy can’t check every address a name leads to. It still refuses an address that’s this machine’s own or internal, unless a rule names it, and it refuses a name when this machine’s lookup gives an internal or denied address for it. A name that this machine can’t look up goes to the company proxy unchecked only when an allowlist names it, as example.com or *.example.com. When only ** allows a name that this machine can’t look up, the VM’s proxy refuses it, so ** never lets a VM send the company proxy a name of its own making. What a VM can still reach through the company proxy, such as hosts on your company’s network, is under Attack vectors.

Open VMs and builds

An open VM goes through its proxy as every VM does, and its proxy sends its requests through the company proxy, from the shell’s settings or config.toml’s, so the company proxy’s password stays on this machine for it too. The VM never gets the shell’s proxy settings, and Lima gets none to pass on to it. What an open VM reaches directly, past its proxy, such as the hosts its NO_PROXY names, doesn’t go through the company proxy.

Lima prints each proxy setting it gives a VM, password and all, as it starts the VM. devvm keeps the password out of its run log, and once the VM has started, it replaces the password with as many * in the log Lima keeps for the VM.

Builds never get your company proxy’s settings, and images never keep them. A build goes through the shell’s company proxy, or else config.toml’s, as a VM’s proxy does. When devvm builds an image, builds the shared tools or converts a --from container image on Lima behind a company proxy, the build goes through a proxy of devvm’s on this machine, made for that build alone, which goes through your company proxy. The build’s commands get only that proxy’s address, with a password devvm makes for the build, while they run, and devvm stops the proxy when the build ends. So the code a build runs, which includes a container image’s own, never sees your company proxy’s address or password. That proxy also runs on this machine, so a company proxy on localhost, such as one a VPN client runs, works for builds too.

A build’s proxy allows any host, as ** does. It sends a name that this machine can’t look up on to the company proxy, so builds work where only the company proxy looks up outside names.

devvm’s own downloads on this machine go through the company proxy too. They are devvm’s copy of mise and the versions it looks up for the shared tools, the list of Ubuntu’s cloud images, and a container registry’s answers for --from. With the shell’s settings, each of them uses the shell’s. With config.toml’s, devvm’s own requests send the password only to the company proxy. The mise it runs on this machine gets the proxy’s URL with the password in it, in its environment, because mise takes a proxy’s password nowhere else. devvm percent-encodes the password in that URL and mise decodes it before it sends it, so a password with characters such as @, :, /, #, % or a space works too. devvm never puts that URL in mise’s arguments or in a file. When a VM’s proxy refreshes a Codex or opencode login on this machine, the refresh goes through the same company proxy as the VM’s requests, with the password kept on this machine.

Tools that ignore the proxy

On the open tier, a tool that ignores the proxy settings in the VM’s environment connects directly, past its proxy.
