For a folder with flake.nix, shell.nix or devenv.nix at its top level, or with a default.nix that makes a shell with mkShell, the list devvm shows when you customize a new VM names that file in the nix row, and you choose it there. A layer isn’t chosen by default, so a VM made as its summary shows, or without a terminal, gets it only with --layers nix, as in devvm --layers nix in a folder with package.json and flake.nix, which gives node on the nix layer.

  • Dev shells. Put use flake (or use nix for a shell.nix) in the project’s .envrc and run direnv allow in the VM once. From then on, each shell that changes into the folder loads the dev shell, and leaving the folder unloads it. This works in your terminal and in the terminals of editors connected over SSH.
  • The flake’s tools come first. While the dev shell is loaded, its tools are ahead of the shared tools on the PATH, so a flake’s node wins over the shared node, and the shared tools come back when you leave the folder.
  • Files in the project. nix-direnv keeps its cache of the dev shell in your home in the VM, so the project gets no .direnv folder. Nix itself writes a flake.lock next to a flake.nix that has none, and in a git repository it marks that file to be added, as it does on any machine.
  • One store per VM. Each VM has its own Nix store, so a package one VM builds isn’t in another’s. nix run nixpkgs#hello works in any VM with the layer.
  • Shared downloads. VMs share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache, on every network tier, an open VM’s included, because every VM’s Nix goes through its proxy. The first VM that needs a package gets it from cache.nixos.org through devvm, which keeps a copy on this machine, and the other VMs get that copy, so each package downloads once per machine instead of once per VM. Only devvm adds to this shared cache, and only what cache.nixos.org signed, so no VM can change what another VM gets. When the cache doesn’t have a package or can’t get it, Nix goes to cache.nixos.org itself. The cache keeps to 10 GiB, deleting the packages used least recently first, unless you set another size with devvm retention nix-cache.size=20G (retention). devvm space shows what it takes, and devvm gc --nix-cache empties it (how it works).
  • Trust. Only root is a trusted Nix user, so the VM’s user can’t add caches or signing keys of their own, and Nix ignores --option substituters from them. sudo nix works. Nix builds every package in its sandbox, and a build fails rather than run without it.
  • Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach Nix’s binary cache and its channels and flake registry, which are cache.nixos.org, channels.nixos.org and releases.nixos.org, and GitHub, where most flakes’ inputs come from. A package that isn’t in Nix’s binary cache builds from source, which downloads its sources from their own hosts, and those are blocked until you allow them (Nix through the proxy).

Sharing a team’s packages

When your team’s projects use one flake for their dev shell, you can put that dev shell’s packages into an image, so every VM made from the image starts with them in its store and downloads none of them. VMs made from one image share its disk, because on macOS each VM’s disk is a copy-on-write clone of the image’s, and on Linux hosts it’s an overlay of the image’s, so the packages take their space once. This works with the stable Nix that the nix layer installs, on every network tier.

To do it, make a layer of your own that builds the dev shell while the image builds, and give it after nix, so that it runs on top of the nix layer:

devvm layer new myteam
$EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/myteam.sh
devvm --layers nix,myteam # a new VM of the image nix+myteam

Put these lines in ~/.config/devvm/layers/myteam.sh, below the starter’s set -euo pipefail, with your team’s flake at the commit you want:

# The team's flake at a commit, so the image holds exactly that dev shell.
flake=github:myorg/devshell/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
bin=/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/bin
"$bin/nix" develop "$flake" --profile /tmp/myteam-shell --command true
# A garbage collector root in the VM's home keeps the dev shell's packages in the store.
mkdir -p ~/.cache/myteam
"$bin/nix-store" --add-root ~/.cache/myteam/dev-shell --realise "$(readlink -f /tmp/myteam-shell)"
rm -f /tmp/myteam-shell /tmp/myteam-shell-*-link

nix develop builds or downloads every package of the flake’s dev shell into the image’s store and records the dev shell in a profile. nix-store --add-root then makes ~/.cache/myteam/dev-shell a garbage collector root, so nix-collect-garbage in a VM never deletes those packages. A project that loads the same dev shell, with use flake github:myorg/devshell/<commit> in its .envrc, finds every package already in its VM’s store, and so does most of a project whose own flake pins the same nixpkgs revision. The image is built without your credentials, because credentials never go into images, so the flake has to be one that anyone can fetch, such as a public repository.

What this doesn’t cover:

  • Packages a VM gets after it’s made stay on that VM’s own disk. The shared downloads at least save downloading them again.
  • A new version of the flake needs a new image. Moving flake to another commit edits the script, so devvm builds the image again the next time it’s used, while VMs made earlier keep the packages they have. When the script names a branch instead of a commit, a changed flake.lock upstream doesn’t change the script, so run devvm rebuild myteam to build the image again.
  • A flake that pins another nixpkgs revision shares few packages with the image, and its VM downloads the rest.
  • Nix’s local overlay store, which would let VMs share one store as it changes, is left out until Nix makes it stable.

How toolchains are shared and updated

The toolchains are shared tools, like the coding agents, so they aren’t part of any image. devvm builds each version once and mounts it read-only into every VM that has it, and mise runs it, so node, python, cargo, go and dotnet work from any shell in the VM, including bash -c from agents and from editors over SSH. Because the shared copy is read-only, a toolchain can’t update itself, and anything you install globally goes into your home in the VM, as each section above says.

devvm follows each toolchain’s newest release, and Node 24 for node. Which bases they run on says what each one needs from a VM’s base. Adding and removing tools explains how devvm update and devvm tools update move a VM to newer versions, how devvm tools add adds a toolchain to an existing VM, and how devvm tools rm takes one out. What a new VM gets explains what happens when a folder calls for more than one toolchain.

Which bases they run on

Every toolchain runs on base from Ubuntu’s own image, and on an Alpine-based image with --from, which gets musl builds of the tools. dotnet also needs ICU, the Unicode library that .NET’s globalization uses, so devvm installs ICU in base, whether it’s made from Ubuntu’s image or --from a container image. On a Debian- or Ubuntu-based image, each tool needs at least the glibc version that its prebuilt release was built against. devvm measures that version from the tool’s files whenever it builds a new version, and it refuses a tool whose version is newer than the image’s glibc (shared tools and glibc). Today the shared tools need these glibc versions, so Debian 10 and Ubuntu 20.04 and newer images run all of them:

Shared tool arm64 amd64
node 2.28 2.28
pnpm and bun, with node 2.18 and 2.17 2.18 and 2.17
python 2.17 2.17
uv, with python 2.28 2.17
rust, with rustup 2.17 2.17
go none, because its programs need no glibc none
dotnet 2.27 2.27
claude and opencode 2.17 2.17
codex 2.28, for its voice helper 2.28

Adding and removing tools

A new VM gets the shared tools chosen when devvm makes it, the toolchains and the coding agents, and keeps those versions. On each launch, devvm warns when there are newer ones and names devvm update, which moves the VM to them, and also makes the VM again when its image has changed, after asking (outdated VMs).

In a terminal, devvm tools shows the same list as for a new VM, with this folder’s VM’s toolchains and agents already chosen and its layers greyed out, because they’re built into the VM’s image, which keeps them until devvm layer add or devvm layer rm makes it again. The Layers heading names devvm layer add and devvm layer rm, which change a VM’s layers by making it again (adding layers to a VM). Choose the tools and confirm, and devvm adds and takes out what changed, as devvm tools add and devvm tools rm do, then opens a shell in the VM. When a new agent’s config folders need the running VM to start again, devvm asks first. When nothing changed, devvm says so and opens nothing.

Without a terminal, or with --no-input or --json, devvm tools shows the tools of this folder’s VM in a table, one row per tool, with node’s pnpm and bun and python’s uv in rows of their own:

Column
TOOL the tool’s name, such as node or pnpm
VERSION the version the VM has
NEWER the version in devvm’s tools lock when the VM has another build, which is usually a newer version, or - when the VM has the lock’s build
BUILT yes when that newer version is built, no when devvm tools update builds it first, or -

The table changes nothing and starts no VM. devvm reads the tools lock as it is, without going online, so a release that came out since devvm last checked isn’t in it yet.

devvm tools –json

devvm tools --json prints the same table as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the tools has the tool’s name and the VM’s version. A tool that the lock has another build of also has newer, which is the lock’s version, and newer_built, which says whether that version is built.

{
 "version": 1,
 "tools": [
 {
 "tool": "node",
 "version": "24.10.0",
 "newer": "24.11.0",
 "newer_built": false
 },
 {
 "tool": "pnpm",
 "version": "10.18.0"
 }
 ]
}

The commands below change the VM’s tools from a script or the command line. They don’t change the VM’s disk, because its tools are mounted, so a change takes effect when devvm then opens a shell in the VM. Each takes the tools’ names as separate words, as in devvm tools add python claude, and devvm refuses names joined with + or a comma.

  • devvm tools add TOOL... builds the tools that the share lacks, and they join the VM’s list at once. It says which of the tools the VM has already and leaves those as they are. A new agent’s config folders are mounted too, which needs the VM to start again. A stopped VM gets them as it starts, and for a running VM devvm asks before restarting it, because anything running in it stops (restarting). If you answer no, there’s no terminal or you pass --no-input, the VM gets them at its next start.
  • devvm tools rm TOOL... takes tools out. What the VM installed itself, such as other versions or global packages, stays.
  • devvm tools update checks upstream for newer versions, builds what’s missing, and moves the VM to them. When the VM already has the newest versions, it builds any of them that are missing. It changes only the shared tools, and never makes the VM again.
  • devvm update does the same first, without asking, and then asks to make the VM again only when the VM’s image has changed (outdated VMs), or its devcontainer.json has (updating a VM from the file).

--tools, --agents and --layers choose only what a new VM gets, so on a VM that exists they change nothing, and devvm warns and names devvm tools. Layers aren’t shared tools, so devvm tools can’t add or take out a layer such as docker or nix. A VM gets its layers when devvm makes it, so devvm layer add and devvm layer rm change them by making the VM again, after asking (adding layers to a VM).

item.title: Your first VM
item.description:
This page assumes you’ve installed devvm and that devvm doctor finds nothing missing.

Making the VM

  1. Run devvm in a project folder.

    cd ~/some-project
devvm

  2. Answer the first-run questions. The first time, devvm asks for the CPUs and memory new VMs get, the coding agents they get, and the optional extras the base image gets, such as oh-my-bash and fzf. These set devvm’s defaults for every new VM, and devvm setup changes them later (devvm setup).

  3. Check the summary. devvm shows what this folder’s new VM gets: the toolchains your folder’s files call for, the agents and layers you chose for new VMs, its size, its network tier and its ports.

    ==> This folder's new VM, devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c, gets:
 toolchain node, for package.json
 agent claude, from devvm setup
 layers: none
 size: 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk
 network tier: allowlist
 ports: all
Customize it? [y/N]

  4. Confirm, or customize it. Confirm to make the VM as shown, or customize it to choose its toolchains, coding agents, layers, network tier, ports and size first (what a new VM gets). Flags such as --agents claude choose a part beforehand, and devvm asks nothing when the flags choose everything.

    Tip

    Keep allowlist, the default, unless the VM needs more. The allowlist network tier limits the VM to the hosts you allow, and every tier keeps your secrets on your machine.

  5. Wait for the base image. The first time, devvm builds it with the extras you chose, which takes a few minutes once, and later VMs start in seconds (images).

    ==> building image base (e9f517dddef1)
 a few minutes, and Ubuntu's cloud image to download the first time
 (details: ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/20261024-090616-83541.log)
==> image base ready
==> creating devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c from base
==> starting devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c

Then devvm opens a shell in the VM at the same path, ~/some-project, with (devvm) at the start of the prompt.

Claude Code’s login

If the VM has Claude Code, log it in to your Claude account once. Run this in a terminal on this machine, not the VM’s shell, in the project folder:

devvm agent login claude

Open the address it shows in a browser, approve the login, and paste the code the browser shows. devvm keeps the login on this machine for every VM with Claude Code, and the VMs get only a placeholder (Claude Code login). If you already use an agent on this machine, devvm agent import copies its settings and logins into devvm’s agent store instead (devvm’s agent store).

Starting the agent

Start the agent in the VM’s shell, so it runs in the VM:

~/some-project $ devvm
(devvm) ~/some-project $ claude

Run claude, codex or opencode, whichever the VM has (running an agent).

What’s in the VM

  • Your project folder, read-write, so your editor and the VM share the same files. It’s the only folder of yours the VM sees, and its .git hooks and config are locked (.git protection).
  • The toolchains, ready at once (toolchains).
  • Your git name and email, so commits made in the VM are yours.
  • Ports: a dev server on :5173 in the VM opens at localhost:5173 on your machine (ports).
  • sudo without a password, so apt install works as on any Ubuntu machine.

Working on a clone instead

To keep the VM out of your working tree and .git entirely, make it with its own clone of the repo:

devvm --clone # a VM with its own clone of your branches
git fetch devvm # later, on this machine: the VM's work as devvm/<branch>
git log -p main..devvm/main # review it before you merge it

Use it for an agent working unattended, a repo you don’t trust, or on Linux hosts, which have no .git protection (working on a clone).

Coming back to it

The VM belongs to its folder, and its subfolders use it too (a subfolder):

devvm # a shell in this folder's VM, started if it's stopped
devvm tools # choose its toolchains and agents
devvm tools add claude # add Claude Code to this folder's VM
devvm code # open it in VS Code
devvm stop # stop it
devvm ls # list every VM
devvm rm # delete it after asking, saving its agents' history first

Everyday commands lists the rest, and managing VMs covers restarting, deleting and moving VMs. Before you let an agent loose in the VM, read staying safe.

item.title: Attack vectors
item.description:
This page lists the common ways that code you didn’t write gets to run on a developer’s machine or gets data off it, and what devvm does about each one. devvm stops most of them on its own, and the habits close most of what’s left. Narrowed, not closed and Left to you are the one list of what devvm leaves open, and each entry links to the page that explains its mechanism.

How devvm handles each attack

The rest of this page sorts the attacks by how much of each one devvm stops:
Blocked The attack can’t work, because what it’s after isn’t in the VM or the VM can’t reach it.
Kept inside the VM The attacker’s code runs, but it runs in the VM, where it reaches only the project folder and what you gave the VM.
Narrowed, not closed devvm closes part of the attack, and the entry says what’s still open.
Left to you devvm doesn’t stop the attack, and the entry says what to do instead.

Some protections hold only on some network tiers or only on macOS, and each entry names its conditions. Everything here rests on the VM’s boundary. How devvm does each of these is in the security model.

Blocked

Credentials on this machine

  • SSH keys. Malware on a developer’s machine looks in ~/.ssh first, because a private key opens every server and repo that trusts it. A VM never mounts ~/.ssh or anything else from your home folder, so there’s no key in it to copy. Agent forwarding, which you turn on yourself, lets the VM use your keys but never copy them.
  • Cloud, cluster and registry logins. Worms that steal credentials collect ~/.aws, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.azure, ~/.kube/config, ~/.docker/config.json and the npm publish token in ~/.npmrc. A VM mounts none of them, so a package that goes looking finds nothing. Secrets you keep in the project folder are a different case, which Left to you covers.
  • The Keychain, browsers and password managers. Stealers read saved passwords, cookies and login sessions from browser profiles and the Keychain. The VM has no browser profile of yours, and it can’t reach this machine’s Keychain.
  • Your coding agents’ history. Agent transcripts hold what you pasted into them, such as secrets and code from other projects. Your history never goes into a VM, and each VM’s own history stays in that VM (coding agents).
  • Secrets, on every tier. Every VM, an open one included, gets a placeholder instead of each secret, such as your GitHub token or Claude Code’s token, and the proxy on this machine puts the real value only into requests for that secret’s own hosts (secrets). A placeholder copied out of the VM is worthless elsewhere, because it ends in a random value of that VM’s own, and an open VM that sends a request around its proxy sends only the placeholder. Another VM or a program on this machine can’t spend the secret through the proxy either, because the proxy needs the VM’s own password. Codex and opencode logins and Claude Code’s MCP secrets work the same way, and devvm refreshes OAuth logins on this machine, so a VM never holds a refresh token.

Git running code on this machine

  • Git hooks and config, on macOS. A VM can write the project folder, so without protection it could add a hook such as .git/hooks/post-checkout, or set a command in .git/config: core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, core.editor, a filter.* or diff.*.textconv driver, a credential.helper or a ! alias. Your next git command on this machine would run it. devvm locks hooks and config with a flag that even root in the VM can’t clear (.git protection). Linux hosts have no such flag, which Left to you covers.
  • The shell prompt. Many shell prompts and editors run git status as soon as you cd into a folder or open it, and git status runs core.fsmonitor. The lock covers that as well, so opening the folder runs nothing that the VM wrote into .git.
  • devvm’s own git commands. devvm runs git on this machine itself, for example to read your name and email for the VM, to check a --clone VM’s repo for uncommitted changes, and to fetch from the VM. A VM can write a repo that git on this machine reads, such as the project folder’s on Linux or a repo inside a folder it mounts, so devvm’s git runs none of the programs a repo’s config can name. It turns off the repo’s fsmonitor, its hooks, including those its config defines, and its filters, it never enters a submodule for git status, and it uses no transport but ssh, so git status, a fetch or a push of devvm’s runs nothing that the VM wrote into the repo. It ignores the git variables of the shell you run devvm in, such as GIT_DIR and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, so it never works on another repo or config by mistake, and it never asks you anything (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0). Its fetches and pushes reach the VM with ssh in batch mode (-o BatchMode=yes), so the VM’s ssh server can’t ask you for a password. They always connect to that VM itself, whatever host the repo’s config sends them to, accept only the host key devvm pinned for it, and forward neither your agent nor any port.

Getting out over the network, on the allowlist and none tiers

  • Sending data to the attacker’s server. Most attacks end by sending what they stole to a server the attacker runs. A confined VM reaches only its proxy, and on the allowlist tier the proxy allows only the hosts on the VM’s allowlist, and on the none tier only its agents’ and secrets’ hosts. On the internet tier the proxy allows every public host, the attacker’s included, so this holds only for this machine and your networks. devvm leaves storage and paste sites out of the default allowlist on purpose, because they’re easy ways to send data out (allowlists).
  • DNS tunnelling. An attacker can encode data into names and look them up at a DNS server of their own. A VM sends no DNS queries of its own, because names resolve in the proxy on this machine.
  • Services on this machine and your network. Code in a VM could attack what developers leave open on localhost, such as databases, dev servers, Docker’s API and other VMs’ ports. It could also attack your router, a NAS, or a cloud provider’s metadata service at 169.254.169.254. The proxy refuses this machine’s own addresses and internal ones, such as loopback, private, link-local and CGNAT ranges, unless a rule names the address (the proxy).
  • DNS rebinding and address tricks. A name can resolve to a public address when it’s checked and to an internal one when it’s dialed, and an internal address can hide in an IPv6 or NAT64 form. The proxy dials only the address it checked, and it sees through NAT64 forms (the proxy).
  • Going around the proxy. Root in a VM can change its routes and firewall, but devvm confines the VM from outside it, so nothing in the VM reaches anything but the proxy (confinement). devvm catches a VM started outside devvm, or one given a second network, with the self-check. It stops a VM that gets out through a second network, and it offers to restart one started outside devvm confined, or stops it when there’s no terminal to ask in.

Spreading beyond the VM

  • Your agents’ config. A rogue agent could add a hook to ~/.claude/settings.json or a skill to ~/.claude/skills, so that it runs the next time you use the agent on this machine. devvm mounts the agents’ config folders read-only, which this machine enforces, and copies their files in on every launch, so nothing the VM changes goes back (mounts). Only devvm agent save copies a VM’s settings into devvm’s agent store, for every VM, and it shows what changed and asks first, so read its diff for hooks, MCP servers and plugins you didn’t add (saving a VM’s settings).
  • Other projects and other VMs. Each project folder gets its own VM with its own disk, and a VM mounts only its own project folder. Each VM’s proxy has its own password, so one VM can’t use another’s secrets. A VM reaches a service in another VM only through a link between VMs that you add in its folder, to a port that the other VM’s folder publishes. A link joins the two VMs’ trust, because code in one can often run code in the other through its service, so a VM links only to a VM on its own tier or a stricter one, and nothing in a VM can add a link (links between VMs).
  • Images, layers and devvm itself. Malware could try to make itself permanent by editing an image, a layer script or devvm’s own files. devvm builds images with nothing from this machine mounted, and the shared tools are read-only in every VM. devvm also refuses a project folder that holds its own folders or sits inside them, so a VM can’t reach the layer scripts that every build runs or the files devvm runs on this machine (only the project folder).
  • A folder made again. If you delete a repo and clone another at the same path, the new folder never gets the old VM’s disk or anything left in it. devvm knows a folder by its inode as well as its path, so it refuses and offers devvm rm or devvm adopt (a folder made again).
  • A devcontainer.json that reaches this machine. Other tools run a devcontainer’s initializeCommand on the host. devvm never runs it, refuses ${localEnv:…}, adds no mounts from the file and doesn’t follow a link out of the folder (devcontainer.json). devvm uses the file’s image only when the image’s registry gives it to anyone who asks, and it refuses a registry on this machine or its network. Behind a company proxy, devvm looks the image up through the company proxy and checks only the registry’s name, so a company proxy that reaches this machine or its network for a name that looks public takes the lookup there (the design note).
  • Impersonating a VM. ssh checks a VM against host keys that devvm reads through the VM’s backend instead of over the network, so a program that answers on the VM’s port in its place is refused (ssh access by name).

Kept inside the VM

The attacks in this section run the attacker’s code, and devvm doesn’t stop that code from running. It runs in the VM, as the VM’s user, who has passwordless sudo. From there it reaches the project folder, or with --clone the VM’s own clone of it, and the secrets the VM uses, which are placeholders on every tier. It reaches what the VM’s tier allows: the hosts on the allowlist on the allowlist tier, every public host on the internet tier, and the whole network on the open tier. Everything in Blocked still holds. What the code writes into the project folder can still reach you when a program on this machine runs it, which Left to you covers.

Install and build scripts

  • npm, yarn, pnpm and bun lifecycle scripts. A package’s preinstall, install, postinstall and prepare scripts run any command when the package is installed, and most npm attacks use them. pnpm’s build approvals (pnpm approve-builds) and --ignore-scripts narrow which packages run scripts, and they’re still worth using, but a package you approved runs its scripts all the same, even one compromised after you approved it. In a VM, those scripts reach only what this section’s introduction lists.
  • Python packages. Installing a source distribution runs its setup.py or its build backend, and a .pth file in site-packages runs code every time Python starts.
  • Ruby gems. A gem with a native extension runs its extconf.rb when it’s installed, and Bundler can install gems straight from a git repo.
  • Rust build scripts and procedural macros. build.rs and procedural macros run on cargo build and cargo check, and also when rust-analyzer opens the project, so opening the folder in an editor is enough to run them. With devvm code, VS Code’s extensions, rust-analyzer among them, run in the VM (devvm host and devvm code).
  • Go modules. Go has no install scripts, but cgo passes flags to the C compiler, go generate runs commands, a toolchain line in go.mod makes Go download another toolchain, and a module’s init functions run in every test and program that imports it.
  • Makefiles, task runners and curl | sh. A Makefile, a justfile or a project’s install line from its README runs whatever its author wrote.

Bad packages and images

  • Typosquatting, dependency confusion and made-up names. Attackers publish packages under names one typo away from popular ones, under a company’s internal package names with a higher version, and under names that AI coding agents invent and that attackers then register. Their code runs as the scripts above do.
  • Compromised maintainers. A trusted package can turn malicious when its maintainer’s account is taken over or a new maintainer joins with bad intent, as event-stream (2018) and xz (2024) did. Updating such a package runs its new code in the VM.
  • Malicious images. An image from --from or from a devcontainer’s image runs its own code as root in the build VM (the image is untrusted). devvm uses only images that the registry gives to anyone who asks anonymously, never one that only your Docker or your registry login reaches, and it confines builds so they reach the internet but not this machine’s services (read-only and confined builds).
  • A devcontainer.json’s commands and features. A project’s postCreateCommand and its other commands run in the VM as the VM’s user, as soon as devvm makes the VM. Its image and features decide what’s in the VM, and devvm adds its ports to the ones it forwards to this machine’s localhost, even beyond a list you narrowed, so the VM is the project’s from the start. Its features can only be devvm’s own layers, so devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script. devvm --no-devcontainer skips the file for a project you don’t trust that far (devcontainer.json).

Rogue agents

  • Prompt injection. Instructions hidden in a README, an issue, a code comment, a web page, a dependency’s docs or an MCP tool’s output can turn a coding agent against you. devvm can’t tell an agent’s own work from injected work, so it limits what the agent reaches instead. An attack like this needs private data, untrusted input and a way to send the data out. On the allowlist tier, the only way out is the hosts on the allowlist, which Left to you covers.
  • Agents with their checks off. An agent run with claude --dangerously-skip-permissions or codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox acts without asking, and a mistaken rm -rf ~ or sudo command reaches only the VM. The project folder is still the agent’s to change, so commit often, or use --clone to keep the agent’s work apart until you fetch it.
  • Malware that stays. Anything the attacker leaves in the VM, such as a cron job, a changed shell startup file or a backdoored program, stays in that VM and goes into no other, unless you save an agent’s settings that it changed with devvm agent save. devvm never deletes a VM on its own, because it may hold unsaved work, so save what you need and run devvm rm, then make the VM again.
  • Mining and resource abuse. A VM’s CPUs, memory and disk are capped by its size, which devvm size shows and changes (size). The VM’s proxy on this machine carries at most 1024 tunnels for it at once, but it doesn’t count the VM’s plain HTTP requests in absolute form or its idle kept-alive connections (the proxy).

Narrowed, not closed

Secrets and keys the VM may use

  • Worms that use your GitHub token. Shai-Hulud (2025) spread through npm install scripts. It collected npm, GitHub and cloud credentials, then used them to publish repos and new versions of packages. A VM holds no npm or cloud credentials, and its GitHub token is a placeholder. The proxy still puts the real GitHub token into every request to GitHub’s hosts, so a worm in the VM can push, make repos and do whatever else the GitHub token’s scope allows. Use a fine-grained GitHub token scoped to the repos the VM needs, or bind none (saving and binding secrets).
  • Minting credentials with a secret. A VM that can use a secret can use it to make another credential that outlasts it. The proxy refuses GitHub REST calls that add an SSH key, a deploy key, a self-hosted runner or a webhook with 403, but it can’t refuse everything, such as GitHub’s GraphQL API, an OAuth app grant or other services. If a VM may have done this, rotate the secret and check the service’s keys, access tokens and runners.
  • Keys devvm can’t tell apart. devvm takes the keys out of the VM’s copies of your agents’ settings and logins only where it can tell a key from the rest. A key in other text, such as a hook’s command, stays when it neither starts like a known key nor follows Bearer or Basic. Logins that devvm can’t bind go in as they are, such as the entries of Codex’s login that devvm doesn’t know, opencode’s API keys for providers other than Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenRouter, and opencode’s well-known logins, and devvm names each one. The agents’ folders that the VM mounts whole, such as ~/.claude/skills or ~/.config/opencode/plugin, reach the VM with every file in them, so a .env in one is in the VM, and so is a private plugin marketplace’s git config with a password or an access token in its URL. Keep secrets out of those folders (what stays in the VM’s copies).
  • Your SSH agent. While agent forwarding is on, anything in the VM can use the agent’s keys to push or log in to servers, though it can’t copy them. The VM has the agent while you’re connected. devvm ssh-agent devvm limits it to the keys you add to devvm’s own agent, and an agent that asks you to approve each use, such as 1Password’s or Secretive, narrows it further.

Git

  • Submodules with their own config. The VM writes .git/index to commit, so it can add a submodule whose config sets core.fsmonitor. Host git status reads that config before devvm’s next launch finds the submodule and locks it. devvm git-protect strict stops git status and git diff from looking inside submodules, but git submodule commands still enter them, so use --clone for a repo with submodules you don’t trust.
  • Replacing .git. The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, or add a commondir that points git at another config. devvm reports these on each launch but doesn’t prevent them, so check what it names before you run git in the folder (what a lock can’t stop).

Network

  • Domain fronting. The proxy checks the host name that a TLS connection asks for, its SNI, but not the Host inside the encrypted traffic, so a CDN that serves many sites on one address can route an allowed connection to a site that isn’t allowed. The proxy reads the connections to hosts with a bound secret, and it refuses a request in them that names another host.
  • Ports the VM listens on. devvm forwards the VM’s TCP ports from 1024 up to this machine’s localhost, unless you list the ports with --ports, so a VM could take a port that a program on this machine trusts while that port is free, and what the VM serves there reaches whatever connects to it. devvm’s forwarder never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, or one that devvm records for a VM, but a program that binds a port on all addresses after devvm forwarded it gets its localhost connections sent to the VM. devvm ports limits what a VM forwards, and devvm ports none forwards nothing, though a project’s devcontainer.json adds its forwardPorts to that list when devvm makes the VM or devvm update reads the file (devcontainer.json, ports, port forwarding).
  • VS Code’s relays. Over Remote-SSH, which devvm code opens, VS Code forwards the ports that programs in the VM listen on, and it answers git’s prompts with your GitHub sign-in. devvm turns both off in the VM’s VS Code settings each time it sets the VM up, but the VM can turn them back on, so turn them off in your own VS Code settings as well (VS Code).
  • What a VM does through a link. A link between VMs joins the two VMs’ trust. Code in the client can often run code in the target through the service it reaches, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM, and it then has the target’s network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. devvm limits a link to the ports the target publishes, on the target’s loopback, and a client to targets on its own tier or a stricter one, but it doesn’t limit what the service does. In a group, every VM trusts every other in the same way, and a VM that joins later gets the same reach (links between VMs).
  • History imported from a less strict tier. An export of agents’ history carries what the old VM’s agents read, so importing one from an open VM into a VM on the allowlist tier can bring in credentials and data that the new VM couldn’t reach itself, along with any instructions planted in them. devvm warns before such an import, and before importing an export whose tier it has no record of, but it imports all the same. Import history only from a VM you trusted as much as the new one (importing history).
  • What one VM learns of another through the shared Nix cache. VMs with the nix layer share one cache of Nix’s packages on this machine. A VM can tell by how fast the cache answers whether some VM fetched a public package. The packages are public, and a project’s flake.lock names the ones it needs, so this tells a VM only that another project on this machine uses a package. A VM that fetches many packages can also fill the cache up to its cap and push other VMs’ packages out, so they download them again, but it can’t fill the disk past the cap or keep anything that cache.nixos.org didn’t sign (the shared Nix cache).
  • Through a company proxy. The company proxy looks up the names it’s sent itself, and it may get another answer than this machine did, or a later one, so the VM’s proxy can’t check every address a name leads to there. Under a name that an allowlist names, a VM reaches whatever the company proxy reaches, such as your company’s internal hosts and the company proxy’s own host, which is this machine’s loopback when the company proxy runs on this machine, as a VPN client’s does. A name that the VM’s allowlist doesn’t allow never reaches the company proxy (the design note).
  • Which names resolve to internal addresses. When the proxy refuses a name because this machine’s lookup gives it an internal address, its refusal says so, so a VM can learn which names this machine’s DNS resolves to internal addresses. The refusal never names the address, this machine’s DNS server or the company proxy, which stay in the proxy’s own log (log files).

This machine

  • A nested project replaced through its parent folder’s VM. A project with a VM of its own inside a folder with another VM is in both VMs, so code in the parent folder’s VM can replace the nested project folder with a link, such as one to your home folder, which the nested VM would mount at its next start. devvm warns each time it makes or opens such a nested VM, naming the parent folder’s VM. It checks the nested folder, by its path and by the folder itself, just before it starts the nested VM and again once the VM runs, and it refuses the start or stops the VM again when the folder was replaced. On macOS the VM mounts the folder itself rather than its path, so it never mounts what a link points to, even when the folder is put back before devvm checks again. On Linux the VM mounts the folder by its path, so code that replaces the folder for the moment the VM’s backend mounts it and puts it back before devvm checks again stays unseen, and the VM keeps what the link pointed to until its next start. Keep a nested project that you don’t want the parent folder’s VM to reach out of the parent folder (a nested project replaced).
  • Set-id files on Linux hosts. Root in a VM can set the set-user-id bit on a file in the project folder, and on Linux hosts that bit reaches the host, so the file runs as its owner for whoever runs it. devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, but not at a launch into a running VM, and Troubleshooting says how to clear them. Don’t run programs from the project folder outside the VM (set-id files).
  • The proxy’s CA keys. Inside a VM, its CA vouches for any site, so someone with a copy of its key and a place on your network could impersonate sites to that VM. Each VM has CAs of its own, so a copy reaches one VM and no other. Only you can read the keys, they never leave this machine, and devvm keeps them out of Time Machine. Each CA lasts 30 days, so a copy goes stale, but the next CA’s key is on disk for up to 23 days before that CA starts, so a copy of it taken then works until that CA ends, up to 53 days later. Keep ~/.local/share/devvm/vms out of other backup and sync tools as well, and on Linux, which has no Time Machine, out of your backups (the VM’s CA).
  • Your company proxy’s password. No VM gets the company proxy’s settings: an open VM goes through its own proxy, which goes through the company proxy for it. devvm keeps the password out of its run logs only where it can tell it’s a password, so one in an address with neither a scheme nor a port, one with a raw /, ?, # or @ in it, or one in a run of more than 4 KiB without a space that a command writes in pieces can stay. Lima’s own log for the VM holds the password until the VM has started, when devvm replaces it with as many *, so the log still shows its length. If devvm is killed before then, or you run limactl start outside devvm, the log keeps it. With config.toml’s proxy, the mise that devvm runs on this machine gets the password in its environment, where programs that run as you can read it (open VMs and builds, the run log).

Left to you

Files the VM writes

The VM can write anything in the project folder, and devvm locks only .git. Any other file there that a program on this machine runs, or reads as its config, is the VM’s to change. --clone keeps all of these away from this machine until you fetch the VM’s work and review it.

  • Hooks in the working tree. Hooks kept in the project, such as husky’s .husky/ with core.hooksPath pointing there, run on this machine, and so do an include.path or a hook symlink that leads into the folder. devvm warns about them when it makes the VM (not covered).
  • Agent config in the project. Claude Code reads a project’s .claude/settings.json, whose hooks run commands, and .mcp.json, which starts MCP servers, and agents follow a project’s CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. Running an agent on this machine in the folder after the VM has worked in it runs what the VM wrote, so run your agents in the VM.
  • Editor and tool config. VS Code runs .vscode/tasks.json tasks set to runOn: folderOpen and starts the interpreters and formatters that .vscode/settings.json names. direnv loads .envrc, and mise reads mise.toml’s environment, hooks and tasks. Keep VS Code’s workspace trust on, and use direnv’s and mise’s own approval prompts.
  • Project code and binaries. npm install, make, a test run or ./bin/tool on this machine runs whatever the VM wrote. Run them in the VM instead.
  • Symlinks out of the folder. The VM can create a link in the project folder that points at a file of yours, such as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. A program on this machine that follows it, such as an upload, an archive or an agent reading files, reads your file instead. devvm itself never follows a link out of the folder.
  • Backdoors in code you merge. Treat the VM’s commits as an untrusted contributor’s, and review them before you merge, deploy or publish them.
  • Secrets in the project folder. A .env file, a project .npmrc or a cloud key in the folder is in the VM. On the allowlist tier it can reach only the hosts on the allowlist, on the internet tier any public host, and on the open tier anywhere. Keep secrets out of the project folder, or use --clone, which copies no untracked files into the VM. The same goes for your agents’ config folders, which keys devvm can’t tell apart covers (mounts).

The network

  • Allowed hosts. Anything an allowed host accepts can carry data out. github.com accepts a push from anyone with an account, including an attacker with an account of their own, and the npm registry accepts packages the same way. Keep allowlists short, and check what a VM reached with devvm network log.
  • What your secrets allow. A VM can push with a GitHub token it may use and spend Claude quota. Use a fine-grained GitHub token, and bind only the secrets a VM needs.
  • Open VMs. An open VM, because you chose open or passed --network open, reaches everything this machine can, including its services on localhost, such as other VMs’ ports, dev servers and databases, and your local network, directly and through its proxy, which applies no rules for it. Its proxy still puts its secrets in, so it can spend them on their hosts as any VM can, but it holds only their placeholders, as every VM does. A VM started outside devvm, such as with limactl start, or one running since before devvm network gave it a confined tier, runs unconfined in the same way until devvm restarts it confined (the self-check).
  • Your browser. Programs in a VM can open URLs in this machine’s browser, and a page that a VM serves on a forwarded port runs in your browser like any other. From there it can reach the internet past the VM’s tier, and your services on localhost.
  • Remote forwards you add. A RemoteForward in your ssh config, or an ssh -R you type, makes this machine connect to whatever it names for the VM. devvm’s ssh entries can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours without also refusing an ssh -R you type. The VM’s ssh server refuses a remote forward on any address outside 127.77.0.0/16, the range devvm keeps for links between VMs, so one on the VM’s localhost, which ssh -R asks for by default, is refused. Root in the VM can change that setting, though, and the server allows a forward on an address in 127.77.0.0/16 for anyone it lets in. A forward you ask for by a host name that begins with 127.77. binds whatever address that name resolves to in the VM. So keep remote forwards out of Host *, and don’t forward into a VM you don’t trust (ssh into VMs).
  • A company CA you add. A company CA that you put in ~/.config/devvm/ca can read the TLS traffic of every VM, whatever its tier, as it can this machine’s, and the proxy trusts it for its own connections. Only that folder adds CAs to the proxy, and nothing a VM sends can.

The platform

  • .git on Linux hosts. Linux has no flag a user can set to lock a file, so VMs on Linux hosts have no .git protection, and the VM can change hooks and config that run on the host. Use --clone there (Linux hosts).
  • Escaping the VM. A bug in Lima, Apple’s Virtualization framework or QEMU could let code out of the VM.

Found a way out of a VM? See SECURITY.md.

item.title: devvm agent
item.description:
Fill devvm’s store of the agents’ settings and logins that every VM gets

Synopsis

devvm keeps the coding agents’ settings in ~/.config/devvm/agents and their logins in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins, and every VM with an agent gets them from there, never from the agents’ own files in your home folder. devvm agent login saves a login made in this folder’s VM, devvm agent import copies those files into the store once, and devvm agent save copies a VM’s settings into it.

devvm agent [flags]

Examples 

 devvm agent login codex # log Codex in, in this folder's VM, for every VM
 devvm agent import # copy every agent's settings and logins from this machine
 devvm agent import codex # copy only Codex's
 devvm agent save # copy the settings of this folder's VM's agents, after showing what changed

Options 

 -h, --help help for agent

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm agent explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm: Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first
  • devvm agent import: Copy the agents’ settings and logins from this machine into devvm’s store
  • devvm agent login: Log an agent in, in this folder’s VM, and save the login in devvm’s store
  • devvm agent save: Copy the agents’ settings from this folder’s VM into devvm’s store

item.title: Everyday commands
item.description:
This page lists devvm’s commands in the groups that devvm --help shows them in, and each row links to the page with the details. devvm COMMAND --help shows a command’s examples and flags, the command line covers what works the same in every command, and the CLI reference has every command with all its flags.

Your VM

devvm open a shell in this folder’s VM, at the same path, making the VM first with the toolchains, agents and layers you choose, or that --tools, --agents and --layers name (details)
devvm restart stop this folder’s VM, start it again and open a shell in it, for changes that apply only when it starts (details)
devvm stop stop this folder’s VM (details)
devvm update [--force] [--no-export] [--clean-home] move this folder’s VM to the newest shared tools, and when its image or its devcontainer.json has changed, make it again from the image’s new build and the file as it is now, keeping its home folder and settings, after asking, then open a shell in it (details)
devvm rm [--force] [--no-export] [--no-clone-check] delete this folder’s VM after asking, exporting its agents’ history first unless --no-export (details)
devvm rm VM [--force] [--no-export] [--no-clone-check] delete a VM whose folder is gone, by its name or ssh alias, after asking (details), or one whose folder is on a disk that isn’t connected, only after asking in a terminal (details)
devvm adopt use the VM made for an earlier folder at this path here (details), or the VM made for this folder before you moved or renamed it (details)
devvm adopt VM move a VM whose folder is gone to this folder, such as a copy of that folder on another disk, after asking (details)
devvm ls list the project VMs (details)
devvm code get this folder’s VM ready as devvm host does, then open its folder in VS Code over Remote-SSH (VS Code)
devvm desktop [--clipboard] [--no-open] serve this folder’s VM’s desktop on 127.0.0.1 with its password until Ctrl+C, and open it in Screen Sharing on macOS (details)
devvm host get this folder’s VM ready for ssh and editors, and show the host name they reach it by, such as devvm-website (details)
devvm history list the exports of agents’ history that devvm saved in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports (details)
devvm history export [FILE] save the history of this folder’s VM’s agents to FILE, or to a new .tar.gz in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports (details)
devvm history import [FILE] put the agents’ history in FILE, or in the newest export devvm saved for this folder, into this folder’s VM (details)

In a folder without a VM of its own, each of these commands but devvm adopt uses the VM of the nearest folder with one that it’s inside, and says which VM that is. --here and --parent choose which VM a command uses (a subfolder).

These options are for a new VM, and only devvm takes them. A VM that exists ignores them with a warning (what a new VM gets).
--tools LIST|none the toolchains the VM gets, such as --tools node,python, in place of those the folder’s files call for (details)
--agents LIST|none the coding agents the VM gets, such as --agents claude,codex, in place of those devvm setup chose (details)
--layers LIST|none the layers the VM’s image gets, bottom first, such as --layers docker, in place of those devvm setup chose (details)
--network TIER create the VM on a network tier: open reaches anything this machine can, internet any public host, allowlist, the default, only the hosts you allow, and none only its agents’ and secrets’ hosts and its links
--clone create the VM with its own clone of the repo instead of mounting the folder (details)
--no-git-protect create the VM without .git protection
--ssh-agent create the VM forwarding your SSH agent, so while you’re connected, anything in it can use your keys (details)
--unsafe-folder mount a folder that devvm refuses, such as one that is or holds your home folder (details)
--cpus N, --memory GiB, --disk GiB the VM’s size (details)
--ports all|none|LIST which ports the VM forwards (details)
--from IMAGE start its base from a container image, such as node:24, instead of Ubuntu’s cloud image (details)
--no-devcontainer create the VM without reading the folder’s devcontainer.json, which otherwise describes the VM as far as devvm supports it, with the options you give taking priority (details)

Working on a clone

devvm --clone make this folder’s VM with its own clone of the repo, copy your branches into it and open a shell in the clone (details)
git fetch devvm on this machine, fetch the VM’s work as devvm/<branch>, to review before you merge it (details)
devvm rm delete the VM, first offering to keep the work you haven’t fetched as saved/devvm/<branch> branches (details)
devvm clone on|off make an existing VM again with its own clone of the repo, or with the folder mounted once devvm has offered to keep the clone’s work as devvm rm does (details)

Change your VM

devvm tools in a terminal, choose this folder’s VM’s toolchains and agents in a list, then open a shell in it, and otherwise show its shared tools, each with its version and any newer one (details)
devvm tools add TOOL... add shared tools to this folder’s VM, such as devvm tools add python claude, then open a shell in it (details)
devvm tools rm TOOL... take shared tools out of this folder’s VM, such as devvm tools rm python claude, then open a shell in it
devvm tools update move this folder’s VM to the newest shared tools, and only those, then open a shell in it (details)
devvm size [--cpus N] [--memory GiB] [--disk GiB] show or change this folder’s VM’s CPUs, memory and disk (details)
devvm size -g ... show or change the size new VMs get (details)
devvm ports [all|none|LIST] show or change which ports this folder’s VM forwards to this machine’s localhost, even while it runs (details)
devvm ports add|rm LIST forward more ports, or stop forwarding some (details)
devvm ports -g ... show or change what new VMs forward (details)
devvm network [open|internet|allowlist|none] show this folder’s VM’s tier, open, internet, allowlist, none or unenforced, and then its allowlist, file by file, or give it a tier: between the confined tiers at once, and into or out of open from its next start, offering to restart a running VM now (details)
devvm network -g [open|internet|allowlist|none] show or change new VMs’ tier, which is allowlist until you change it (details)
devvm network allow|deny|rm RULE... [-g] add allow or deny rules to this folder’s VM’s own, or remove them, at once, and with -g, change yours for every VM (details)
devvm network log [--follow] [-n N] [--blocked] show what this folder’s VM connected to and what its proxy blocked (details)
devvm ssh-agent [on|devvm|off] show this folder’s VM’s SSH agent forwarding, which is off, on for yours or devvm for devvm’s own, then the keys devvm’s own agent holds and those added to it, or change the forwarding from the VM’s next start (details)
devvm ssh-agent add KEY_FILE [--confirm] [--lifetime DURATION] load a key into devvm’s own agent, and load it again whenever a VM needs it (details)
devvm ssh-agent rm KEY_FILE take a key out of devvm’s own agent, so devvm doesn’t load it again (details)
devvm git-protect [on|strict|off] show or change this folder’s VM’s .git protection, while it’s stopped (details)
devvm clone [on|off] [--force] [--no-export] [--clean-home] [--no-clone-check] show whether this folder’s VM has its own clone of the repo, or make it again with one, or with the folder mounted, keeping its home folder and settings, after asking, then open a shell in it (details)
devvm secret, devvm secret rm NAME list the secrets, whether each is saved and the VMs using it, or delete a saved one (details)
devvm secret set claude|github [--stdin] save your Claude Code token or GitHub token on this machine, so that VMs get a placeholder and their proxy puts the secret in (details)
devvm secret use|unuse NAME let this folder’s VM use a secret, or stop it, though a VM with Claude Code always uses claude (details)
devvm layer add LAYER... [--force] [--no-export] [--clean-home] make this folder’s VM again with more layers on top, keeping its home folder and settings, after asking, then open a shell in it (details)
devvm layer rm LAYER... [--force] [--no-export] [--clean-home] make this folder’s VM again without some of its layers, keeping its home folder and settings, after asking, then open a shell in it (details)

Links between VMs

devvm link list this folder’s VM’s links, each with its name, port, target VM and folder, the target’s status, and whether the link applies (details)
devvm link add TARGET PORT [--as NAME] link this folder’s VM to PORT of the VM that TARGET names, so programs in it reach the port as NAME:PORT and NAME.devvm.internal:PORT (details)
devvm link rm TARGET PORT remove one of this folder’s VM’s links (details)
devvm link publish [PORTS] show the ports this folder’s VM publishes, or offer PORTS to links from any of your other VMs (details)
devvm link unpublish PORTS stop offering ports to links (details)
devvm group show the group this folder’s VM is in, with each of its VMs, the name the others reach it by, its folder and the ports it publishes (details)
devvm group join NAME [--as NAME] put this folder’s VM in the group NAME, which its first VM makes, so each VM in the group reaches the ports the others publish (details)
devvm group leave take this folder’s VM out of its group, removing the links the group made (details)

Images

devvm images list the images, then the shared tool images (details)
devvm images rm IMAGE|KEY... delete images, by name or by the key devvm images shows (details)
devvm build IMAGE build an image and the images under it, unless they’re built, such as devvm build docker or devvm build foo+bar, where IMAGE is base or layers and never a shared tool (details)
devvm rebuild IMAGE build an image of base or layers again from its parent as it is, and delete the stale images no VM uses, while shared tools follow the tools lock instead (details)
devvm layer new NAME start a layer of your own, ~/.config/devvm/layers/NAME.sh, with its allowlist, NAME.policy (details)

devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm take --from IMAGE to work on a base made from that container image (details).

Disk space

devvm space show what devvm keeps on this machine, the disk each kind takes, and what frees it (details)
devvm gc delete the stale and unfinished images and the tool images no VM uses, after listing them, and never a VM (details)
devvm retention [KEY=VALUE...] show the retention settings, which say what devvm deletes on its own, or change them, with KEY=off turning one off (details)

This machine

devvm setup [--features LIST|none] [--agents LIST|none] [--layers LIST|none] choose base’s features and the coding agents and layers new VMs get, and in a terminal also new VMs’ size and network tier (details)
devvm agent import [AGENT...] copy the agents’ settings and logins from your home folder into devvm’s agent store, which every VM gets them from, never their history, asking before it replaces the store’s (details)
devvm agent login AGENT [--setup-token] [--device-code] [--api-key] log Claude Code in to your Claude subscription inside this folder’s VM, or get a Claude Code token with --setup-token (details), or log Codex or opencode in to ChatGPT there, in a browser on this machine or with a code, or save an API key, and keep the login in devvm’s agent store for every VM (details)
devvm agent save [AGENT...] copy the agents’ settings from this folder’s VM into devvm’s agent store, never their logins or history, after showing what changed and asking (details)
devvm doctor check what devvm needs on this machine and say how to get what’s missing (details)
devvm upgrade [--check] [--to VERSION] install devvm’s newest release the way you installed devvm, after asking, or with --check only say whether a newer one is out (details)
devvm completion SHELL print the shell completion script for bash, zsh or fish (details)
devvm limactl ARGS... run Lima’s limactl on the VMs and images in devvm’s own Lima home, not ~/.lima, for debugging, which starts VMs unconfined, whatever their tier (details)

devvm itself

devvm help [COMMAND] print the help for devvm or a command, as --help and -h do (details)
devvm --version print devvm’s version alone, as devvm version also does

The folders devvm keeps its state in and the environment variables it reads are in Settings and files.

item.title: Images and caching
item.description:
This page explains how devvm builds images and shared tools, how it keys and caches them, and how it checks what they start from: Ubuntu’s cloud image, a container image from --from, and each tool’s downloads. Images and tools covers choosing, rebuilding and cleaning up images, and Starting from a container image covers --from.

Building

devvm builds each image in a VM of its own, and that VM then is the image:

  1. For base, devvm makes a new VM from Ubuntu’s cloud image with base.yaml’s settings, or, with --from, from a container image converted into a disk. A layer’s VM is a copy of its parent image.
  2. The VM starts confined, so it reaches the internet but not the host’s own services on loopback, and it forwards no ports. How that’s enforced depends on the backend, as Lima describes.
  3. The script runs. For base, that’s assets/layers/base.sh and then the features you chose, and for a layer, it’s the layer’s script.
  4. The VM stops. devvm writes the image’s record last, ~/.local/share/devvm/images/<key>/record.json, with its name, its chain, what base started from and its digest, its C library, the glibc version of a --from base with glibc, when the build finished and the version of the devvm that built it (made_by). The record is JSON that only devvm writes, and devvm ignores fields it doesn’t know, so a newer devvm’s record still reads.

While the VM is being built, it already has the image’s final name, so devvm holds a lock for each image it builds, ~/.local/share/devvm/images/locks/<key>, from before it looks for the image until the record is written. Another devvm that builds the same image waits for that lock and says so (image_build_waiting) after 3 seconds, and once it gets the lock, it finds the image built. An image without a record is unfinished only when its lock is free, so devvm then deletes it and builds it again (image_leftover). While the lock is held, the image is building, and devvm gc, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm leave it alone (image_building). The lock is an OS lock on an open file, which the system releases when its devvm ends, however it ends, so a crash never leaves an image looking like it’s still being built. devvm deletes the lock file together with the image’s folder.

Nothing from the host is mounted into a build, because layer scripts run third-party installers, which mustn’t see your files. Behind a company proxy, a build on Lima goes through a proxy of devvm’s on this machine for that build alone, which goes through the company proxy. The scripts’ commands get only that proxy’s address, with a password devvm makes for the build, so neither the build nor its image ever has the company proxy’s password (a company proxy). A build gets base’s size fitted to the host, which the images built on base, and their VMs, keep (base’s size).

Keys and caching

devvm builds images in layers and caches them, as Docker does. base comes first, and each layer is built on its parent, so foo+bar is bar on foo on base. A layer starts from its parent and runs its script inside it, and devvm stores it under a key, which is a hash of everything that goes into it. When an image with that key already exists, devvm uses it, and otherwise it builds one.

Image Its key hashes
base the backend, assets/base.yaml, assets/prelude.sh, assets/layers/apt.sh, assets/layers/base.sh, the chosen features that devvm has, in order (each name and its script, assets/features/<name>.sh), its rebuild counter, and with --from, the image, its digest and the scripts that convert it; on Lima, the Ubuntu cloud image pinned on this machine (its release, file and SHA-256), base’s disk size, and the user that a --from conversion puts in the image (its name, uid and home folder) with the converted disk’s size
a built-in layer its parent’s key, its name, assets/prelude.sh, assets/layers/apt.sh, its script (assets/layers/<name>.sh) and its rebuild counter
a custom layer its parent’s key, its name, assets/prelude.sh, assets/layers/apt.sh, its script (~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.sh) and its rebuild counter

devvm puts together each image’s recipe once, as the ordered list of steps its build runs. A step is a script with its name, its arguments and whether it runs as root. Each of devvm’s own scripts in a recipe starts with devvm’s prelude, assets/prelude.sh, which the scripts’ prelude describes, so the recipe holds the prelude and the script together, and a custom layer’s script, which is yours, runs as you wrote it. The recipe of base starts with the backend’s own steps, which say what the backend makes base’s disk from. On Lima, those are the Ubuntu cloud image pinned on this machine, base’s disk size and base.yaml, and with --from, the conversion’s scripts too, build.sh with its arguments. Then come apt.sh begin, base.sh, the chosen features’ scripts and apt.sh end, while a layer’s recipe is apt.sh lists and then its own script. The key hashes that recipe, and the backend is given the same recipe and runs it as it is, so nothing reaches a build that its key doesn’t hold, apart from base’s packages: those are the ones its key recorded at its first build, or the mirror to record them from, which base’s packages describes. A chosen feature without a script isn’t in the recipe, and devvm warns about it (unknown_feature) when it builds base. The user’s CAs and a company proxy’s variables are added to each step while it runs and taken out again, so they aren’t in the recipe, and the image keeps none of them. A build’s CPUs and memory aren’t in it either, because the host’s size doesn’t change what an image holds, but base’s disk size is, because the disk is part of the image (base’s size).

A key is the first 12 hex digits of a SHA-256. Each input goes into the hash with its length, so different inputs never hash the same bytes. An image’s record keeps its chain, which is the key of each image it’s built on, from base up.

Each key hashes its parent’s, so a new key anywhere in the chain changes the key of every image above it:

flowchart TD
subgraph next["after foo.sh is edited,<br>or devvm rebuild foo"]
b2["base<br>key 1a2b3c4d5e6f<br>reused"] -- "its key" --> f2["foo<br>key 9a0b1c2d3e4f<br>built again"]
f2 -- "its key" --> fb2["foo+bar<br>key 5a6b7c8d9e0f<br>built again"]
end
subgraph built["built"]
b1["base<br>key 1a2b3c4d5e6f"] -- "its key" --> f1["foo<br>key 7a8b9c0d1e2f"]
f1 -- "its key" --> fb1["foo+bar<br>key 3a4b5c6d7e8f"]
end

This means:

  • When you edit a script, its layer and every layer above it rebuild the next time they’re used, and the layers below are reused.
  • Each backend builds its own images and never uses another backend’s.
  • With --from, base’s key has the image’s digest, so when the tag moves to a new image, base and everything on it rebuild.
  • A layer whose script is gone hashes as missing, so its images don’t match any more.
  • Nothing else counts. Features you haven’t chosen change no key, and neither do policy files (*.policy), which the proxy reads at run time and which never go into an image.

An image whose key doesn’t match its inputs any more is stale. It stays until it’s deleted (cleaning up), and the next use builds a new one.

Rebuilding

devvm rebuild works through the rebuild counter, which each image’s key hashes. The counters are in ~/.local/share/devvm/images/rebuilds.json, one for each backend, each image that base starts from, as --from gives it, and each image, so a rebuild on one backend leaves the other backends’ images and their VMs as they are, and so does a rebuild from another container image. A rebuild writes a new value into its counter, made of the time and a random part, so the image gets a new key, and so does every image built on it. A rebuild of base on Lima also pins the newest Ubuntu cloud image first, while a rebuild of a --from base looks up its container image’s digest again and keeps the cloud image pinned. The counters can’t be in an image’s folder, because a counter is an input to the key that names that folder. A devvm changing a counter holds a lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/images/locks/rebuilds, while it reads the file and writes it whole, so two rebuilds at once both keep their new values. devvm lists those images first (rebuild_replaces). After the build, it deletes every stale image that no VM uses, which includes the old image and those built on it, and they’re built again, on the new image, the next time they’re needed. On Linux hosts, an image whose disk VMs are overlays of stays, and devvm says which VMs use it.

A VM keeps the image it was made from, and its state keeps that image’s chain. When a key in the chain changes, after an edited script or a rebuild, devvm warns on each launch that the VM is outdated (vm_outdated) and leaves the VM as it is (outdated VMs). devvm update makes the same check, comparing each image’s key in the recorded chain with its key as it is now, and when one differs, it makes the VM again from the same image name (making a VM again). Otherwise, when the VM also had the newest shared tools, it says the VM is current (vm_current). Shared tool images have keys of their own, which building tools describes, and they’re never in the chain, so newer shared tools alone don’t lead devvm update to make the VM again.

Ubuntu’s cloud image

On Lima, base starts from a dated release of Ubuntu 26.04’s cloud image (release-YYYYMMDD on cloud-images.ubuntu.com), which devvm pins on this machine the first time it builds base. devvm’s own files hold only the release, 26.04, and Ubuntu’s cloud image key, assets/layers/ubuntu-cloud.gpg (fingerprint D2EB44626FDDC30B513D5BB71A5D6C4C7DB87C81), so nothing in devvm needs moving when Ubuntu publishes a new image.

To pin an image, devvm reads the list of dated releases at cloud-images.ubuntu.com and takes the newest one whose checksums list an image for the host:

  • The release’s SHA256SUMS must carry a valid signature from Ubuntu’s cloud image key, in its SHA256SUMS.gpg. No other key counts. devvm checks the signature itself, with the standard library’s RSA and SHA-2, so it needs no gpgv or other program. When the signature is missing or doesn’t check out, devvm refuses the release (ubuntu_bad_signature), and it never falls back to an older release for that reason.
  • The host’s image, ubuntu-26.04-server-cloudimg-arm64.img or -amd64.img, must be listed with a SHA-256 of 64 hex digits. A release that lists none is passed over for the next older one, and when no release has one, devvm stops (no_ubuntu_release).
  • When devvm can’t read the list, it stops (ubuntu_unreachable), and nothing is pinned.

devvm records the pin in ~/.local/share/devvm/images/ubuntu.json: the release, the image’s file name, its SHA-256 and when it was pinned. One devvm pins at a time, holding ~/.local/share/devvm/images/locks/ubuntu, so two first builds pin the same image. Every later build of base on this machine uses the pinned image without looking anything up, so it needs no network for the image once Lima has it cached, and Lima checks the download against the pinned SHA-256. A pin for another architecture, such as in a data folder copied from another machine, counts as none, and the next build pins one for this host. A --from base’s conversion boots the pinned image too, and pins one only when none is.

An image devvm pinned in the same run that doesn’t boot, so that the backend fails to start base’s build VM, gets one second chance. devvm says so (origin_no_boot), pins the newest release older than it, which it checks the same way, and builds base on that, so a broken new release of Ubuntu’s doesn’t stop new machines’ first builds. The older release is what stays pinned. devvm tries this once a run, and never for an image that was pinned before the run, because that one booted then. The build VM that didn’t boot stays, stopped, as a failed build does.

The pin is part of base’s recipe, so base’s key hashes the release, the file and its SHA-256, and a new pin makes a new base. base’s record keeps the address and SHA-256 of the image it was built from. Ubuntu removes its dated releases after a few months, so a base built from one that’s gone can still be used, but building it again needs Lima’s cached copy of the image.

Base’s settings and pins

Base’s size is 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk, which devvm sets in its own code, and it fits the CPUs and memory to the host (base’s size). On Lima, assets/base.yaml holds base’s other VM settings. assets/layers/base.sh installs base, and the optional features you chose follow it.

Each download in assets/layers/base.sh is pinned to a version and a SHA-256 at the top of the script, and the build fails if a checksum doesn’t match. Each feature pins its downloads in the same way, at the top of its script, assets/features/<name>.sh in the repo, which is built into devvm. apt’s packages are pinned per image key, as base’s packages describes.

The scripts’ prelude

assets/prelude.sh comes first in each of devvm’s scripts that a build runs with bash: assets/layers/base.sh and apt.sh, the built-in layers and features, assets/shared-tools/build.sh, and a --from conversion’s assets/oci/build.sh. devvm puts it before the script on the script’s standard input, and for the conversion, in the copy of build.sh that it writes into the conversion’s own temporary folder, so no copy of either is kept anywhere else. The prelude sets no shell options and runs only uname and command -v. It gives the script three things:

  • $devvm_arch is the VM’s architecture as the pins name it, arm64 or amd64. On any other architecture, the prelude stops the script.
  • $devvm_libc is the VM’s C library, musl on Alpine, where apk is, and gnu everywhere else.
  • devvm_sha TOOL prints TOOL’s pinned SHA-256 for this VM, which is the script’s own TOOL_sha256_<arch>_musl on musl when the script pins one, and its TOOL_sha256_<arch> otherwise. A script that pins none for this VM gets an error that names the pin.

A script that uses the prelude checks that it came first, with : "${devvm_arch:?}" for each variable it reads, so it stops at once when run without it. The key of each image and tool image whose build runs one of these scripts hashes the prelude with the script, so a change to the prelude rebuilds every image and every shared tool image. bootify.sh, which runs with the container image’s own sh, and kernel.sh don’t get it, and neither do your own layers and features.

Base’s packages

base’s recipe runs assets/layers/apt.sh begin as root before base.sh, and apt.sh end after the last feature. Both are steps of the recipe, so base’s key hashes the script. What the build gives the script in /var/cache/devvm/packages/in decides where apt’s packages come from:

  • A first build of a key records them. devvm sends in/mirrors, which holds the mirror that ubuntu-mirror sets, or nothing. apt.sh begin points each of the image’s sources at an apt mirror+file: list of that mirror and then the source’s own archive (archive.ubuntu.com, or ports.ubuntu.com on arm64), so apt tries them in that order, and it keeps every package it downloads. apt also installs phased updates (APT::Get::Always-Include-Phased-Updates), which Ubuntu otherwise rolls out to only some machines at first, so it always takes the newest version that the lists have. apt checks the archive’s signature with Ubuntu’s archive key, which the image has, whichever mirror answers. At the end, apt.sh end moves each downloaded package to out/<sha256>.deb and writes its entry from apt’s package lists, which apt checked against that signature, to out/Packages. The script fails the build when the lists have no entry with the file’s SHA-256. It also copies each InRelease file and package list that apt used to out/<n>.InRelease or out/<n>.Packages, so devvm can check them on this machine. apt keeps those lists uncompressed while base builds (Acquire::GzipIndexes "false"), as they’re signed.
  • Every later build of the key replays them. devvm sends the files the key recorded, from its cache, and in/Packages, their entries, each naming its file. apt.sh begin moves the image’s sources aside and gives apt only that folder, so base.sh and the features install exactly what the first build did, with no network for them.
  • A --from base gets neither. Its packages come from the container image’s own sources as they are when it builds, and they aren’t pinned.

Both ends put the image’s own sources back, remove devvm’s apt settings, empty apt’s cache and delete the package lists, so a first build and a replay make the same image. A VM made from it fetches lists when you run sudo apt update, and each layer’s recipe starts with apt.sh lists, as root, which fetches them from the image’s own sources when there are none, so a layer’s script installs as it would on any Ubuntu. apt.sh turns apt’s retries off and makes a source that sends nothing for 30 seconds fail, and when no source answers, it exits 75, which the backend reports as build_sources_unreachable, not as a script that failed.

The backend sends the build’s input into the VM as a tar stream before the first step, and after the last step it hands devvm a tar stream of out/ and deletes the folder (backend.Packages). On Lima, both run as root over limactl shell. What comes back is the build VM’s, so devvm checks it before it keeps anything (packages_refused). It takes only regular files named Packages, <64 hex digits>.deb, <n>.InRelease or <n>.Packages, each package’s content must hash to its name, and each entry must name a file that came back with the size and SHA-256 the entry gives, with no file left over. Each InRelease file is at most 4 MiB and all of them 32 MiB, and each package list is at most 512 MiB, with lines of at most 1 MiB and entries of at most 4 MiB, and all the lists 2 GiB. A name that comes back twice is refused.

devvm doesn’t take the build VM’s word for the entries, because anything with root in that VM could write them. It checks each InRelease file’s clearsigned signature itself, in Go, against Ubuntu’s archive key, which devvm’s own files hold (assets/layers/ubuntu-archive.gpg, fingerprint F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C), and refuses one that doesn’t check out or isn’t one of the suites an Ubuntu 26.04 image’s sources name: resolute, resolute-updates, resolute-security and resolute-backports, never resolute-proposed. It tries at most 4 signatures in each file, because each one hashes the whole file. It also refuses an InRelease whose Date: is older than the archive state the pinned cloud image was built from, because Ubuntu’s InRelease files carry no Valid-Until, so a mirror that stopped updating still serves validly signed ones. The release pocket, resolute, which Ubuntu stopped changing at release, must be dated no earlier than that day, 2026-04-23 (ubuntu.Released). Every other pocket (resolute-updates, resolute-security, resolute-backports) must be dated no more than a day before the pinned release’s date (release-YYYYMMDD). devvm names the mirror that ubuntu-mirror sets (packages_stale_mirror), or Ubuntu’s archive when none is set (packages_stale).
