Each package list must have the SHA-256 and size that a verified InRelease gives for one of its Packages lists, which devvm checks before it reads the list, and each package’s SHA-256 must be in one of those lists, as the same package, version, architecture and size that apt’s entry says. devvm then keeps the archive’s own entry for the package, not apt’s.

devvm also checks that each package is the newest version that apt would install, because whatever has root in the build VM could hand back only the lists it chooses, such as the release pocket’s, and record an older version than resolute-updates or resolute-security has. A recording must give back the InRelease files of resolute-updates and resolute-security with lists for the architectures whose lists have the recorded packages, such as binary-arm64, so another archive’s InRelease, such as archive.ubuntu.com’s on arm64, where ports.ubuntu.com has the lists, doesn’t count. For each InRelease it gives back, it must also give back every package list that the file gives for those architectures, in every component (main, restricted, universe and multiverse). An empty list is the one exception, because it lists nothing. When one is missing, devvm names the suite and keeps nothing (packages_lists_missing). devvm then refuses a recorded package when the release pocket’s list, resolute-updates’ or resolute-security’s has a newer version of it for that architecture, and it names the package, both versions and the suite (packages_not_newest). resolute-backports doesn’t count, because apt installs its packages only when you ask for them (its InRelease says NotAutomatic). devvm orders versions as dpkg --compare-versions does, in Go (ubuntu.CompareVersions): the epoch first, then the upstream version, then the Debian revision, with letters before other characters and ~ before everything, even the end, so 1.0~rc1 is older than 1.0.

A recording that gives back no packages needs no lists. devvm writes the files into a folder of the build’s own in the cache while it checks them, and once the image is built, it moves each into the cache, ~/.local/share/devvm/packages/<sha256>.deb, and writes the key’s set, ~/.local/share/devvm/packages/sets/<key>.json: each package’s name, version, architecture, SHA-256, size and entry. A file the cache already has under that name is kept only when its checksum still matches it; devvm replaces a changed one with the build’s copy and notes that in the run log. That happens before the image’s record, under a lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/images/locks/packages, and a build that fails keeps nothing.

A key’s set is written once, and the cache holds each file under its own SHA-256, so a build can’t change what another key installs. Before a replay, devvm reads each of the set’s files and checks its SHA-256 and size, and it refuses to build when one is gone or changed (packages_missing), so it never records the key’s packages again. devvm rebuild base gives base a new key, which records anew. devvm gc deletes the sets of keys that are neither base’s key as it is now nor an image the backend has, and then, holding the lock, the package files that no set names then, so a set recorded meanwhile keeps its files. It also deletes a build’s own folder of what it gave back that’s over a day old, which a build that was killed leaves.

Base’s size

devvm fits base’s CPUs and memory to the host with one rule that every backend uses. Base gets its 4 CPUs, or the host’s count when the host has fewer, because a Lima vz VM given more CPUs than the Mac has can start so slowly that its ssh never comes up, as Lima’s issue reports. Base gets its 8 GiB of memory, or half the host’s whole GiB when 8 GiB would leave the host less than 2 GiB, because a VM asking for all of the host’s memory doesn’t start.

  • Lima passes the fitted size to limactl create as --cpus and --memory, and base’s 100 GiB disk as --disk, for base and for the VM that converts a --from image. The images built on base are clones of it, so they and their VMs keep that size. A new VM’s disk is never smaller than base’s, because disks can’t shrink.

A size you set with --cpus, --memory or devvm size -g replaces the fitted one. devvm checks that size against the same rule, so it refuses more memory than the host’s whole GiB less 2, or half of them on a host of 4 GiB or less, and the fitted memory always passes (size). The fitted size isn’t in image keys, because the host’s size doesn’t change what an image holds.

The desktop layer

The built-in desktop layer’s script is assets/layers/desktop.sh, and its allowlist is assets/layers/desktop.policy, which has no rules, because the layer downloads nothing of its own and its packages come from the distribution’s archive, which base’s allowlist has. base’s image has no package lists, so the layer’s apt.sh lists step fetches them first, and its packages are the archive’s as they are when the layer builds, which aren’t pinned. On --from alpine, the script installs Alpine’s own packages, which aren’t pinned either. Besides Xfce and TigerVNC, the script writes /usr/local/bin/devvm-desktop, which devvm desktop runs in the VM. The layer needs no backend feature of its own, because it runs on any VM that can build an image and reach its ssh.

The docker layer

The built-in docker layer’s script is assets/layers/docker.sh, embedded in devvm, and its allowlist is assets/layers/docker.policy. The script pins the checksum of the signing key of Docker’s apt repository and each package’s version at the top. On --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s own packages, which aren’t pinned. Running Docker’s engine in a VM is a backend feature of its own, docker-layer (features).

The nix layer

The built-in nix layer’s script is assets/layers/nix.sh, and its allowlist is assets/layers/nix.policy. The script pins Nix’s release tarball, the direnv binary and nix-direnv’s direnvrc at the top, each with its version and SHA-256, which are per architecture for Nix and direnv, and fetches them with devvm-fetch. scripts/bump.sh nix direnv nix-direnv moves them. Nix’s version is the one nixos.org’s installer fetches, at least 2.35.3, which fixes the scripted installer’s store ownership (GHSA-hf6w-2rg9-v84g) and the daemon’s store corruption through repair (CVE-2026-110450). Nix’s newer releases come with another installer, from artifacts.nixos.org, so the layer’s pins change shape when it moves to one of them.

The script runs the tarball’s own installer as install --daemon --yes --no-channel-add, which copies the tarball’s store into /nix, downloading nothing, makes the nixbld build users and, under systemd, starts nix-daemon. On OpenRC, which a base --from alpine runs, the script adds a service of devvm’s, /etc/init.d/nix-daemon, to the default runlevel and starts it, and before the install it adds Alpine’s xz, unpinned, which GNU tar needs for the tarball. Nix’s own binaries are static or linked against the C library in its store, so they run on musl. Its extra settings turn on flakes and the nix command and keep trusted-users = root, so only root can choose caches and signing keys. They also set sandbox = true and sandbox-fallback = false, so a build fails where the kernel can’t sandbox it, rather than run outside the sandbox without a word. The installer writes any proxy variables it finds into a systemd drop-in for the daemon, which would put a build’s proxy into the image, so the script runs it without them. It points Nix at the system’s CAs, which hold devvm’s and yours. After the install, the script checks that every path in the store is root’s, and it fails otherwise.

It also adds Nix’s default profile to the end of sudo’s secure_path, through /etc/sudoers.d/devvm-nix, so sudo nix works, and appends Nix’s profiles to the PATH that BASH_ENV gives shells that read no profile. direnv goes into /usr/local/bin and nix-direnv into /usr/local/share/nix-direnv. A file in ~/.config/direnv/lib loads nix-direnv and puts each project’s direnv layout under ~/.cache/direnv/layouts, named by a hash of the project’s path, so its cached dev shell and garbage collector roots stay in the VM’s home and out of the project folder. direnv’s shell hook is in ~/.bashrc.d/direnv.sh, which bash loads before mise.sh, and since each hook puts itself first in PROMPT_COMMAND, direnv’s runs after mise’s, and a dev shell’s PATH comes before the shared tools'.

The daemon doesn’t read /etc/environment, so the VM’s setup gives it the VM’s proxy on every tier, in a drop-in of its own under systemd, or else in /etc/conf.d/nix-daemon, which OpenRC reads for the service. The setup also puts the shared Nix cache first in Nix’s substituters, in /etc/nix/devvm-cache.conf. It removes both files from a VM whose environment names no proxy. Running the layer is a backend feature, nix-layer (features), and building it also needs the feature, so a backend without it refuses devvm build nix. With sandbox-fallback = false, every Nix build fails in a VM that can’t make the kernel namespaces that Nix’s sandbox needs.

How it’s converted

With --from, devvm turns the container image into a disk in a throwaway VM, devvm-oci-build, which it makes from Ubuntu’s cloud image with base.yaml’s settings and base’s size. No Docker is needed:

  1. crane downloads exactly the digest in base’s key, for this machine’s architecture, and flattens its layers. crane is pinned like every download: its version and SHA-256 are at the top of assets/oci/build.sh, checked with sha256sum.
  2. assets/oci/bootify.sh, in a chroot of the image, adds what a container lacks to boot as a VM: a kernel and initramfs, an init system (systemd, or OpenRC on Alpine), cloud-init, sshd and sudo, and your user in the VM. Your user has your uid, so bootify.sh first removes a user of the image’s that has it, such as Ubuntu’s own ubuntu (uid 1000, the uid a Linux host’s first user usually has).
  3. mke2fs writes the image’s files into a raw ext4 disk, and base grows it to base’s 100 GiB disk.

build.sh also writes down the image’s C library, from its /etc/os-release, and for a glibc image, its glibc version, which getconf GNU_LIBC_VERSION prints in a chroot of the image. devvm checks both, keeps them in the record of base and of every image on it (libc and glibc), and checks each shared tool against that glibc version (building tools).

devvm then deletes the build VM and creates base from the disk, booting its kernel and initrd directly. One conversion runs at a time, because each holds a lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/oci-build.lock, so another devvm’s conversion waits for it and says so (oci_waiting) after 3 seconds. The lock is an OS lock on an open file, which the system releases when its devvm ends, however it ends, so a devvm that crashed never keeps another from converting.

Digests

base is keyed by the container image’s digest, not its tag. When devvm builds, it asks the image’s registry for the digest anonymously, with a HEAD request for the image’s manifest, which doesn’t count against Docker Hub’s pull limit. When the registry asks for a token, devvm gets one from the registry’s token service, at an https address only. The digest goes into base’s key, and devvm records it for each container image in its cache, ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/from-digests.json, and in the record of each image it builds on that base. An existing VM’s state records what its base was made from (from).

The cache may be deleted at any time. Without it, devvm takes the digest from the record of the newest base built from the same container image, so every key stays as it was, and images stay current until a lookup finds that the tag has moved. The next lookup writes the cache again.

devvm refuses a reference it can’t read (bad_from). When it can’t reach the registry, it uses the digest it recorded last, with a warning (from_cached_unreachable), and with none recorded, it fails (from_unreachable). Tags and digests covers when a moved tag rebuilds base, how @sha256: pins an image, and how devvm reads a reference.

The image is untrusted

The container image’s own code runs as root in the build VM, so devvm treats what it writes as hostile:

  • The build VM is confined like any build, so it reaches the internet, for crane, but not this machine’s own services. It mounts three folders of the conversion’s own temporary folder, devvm-oci.<random>, and nothing else. oci/ holds the conversion’s scripts, which devvm writes there from its own files for this build alone, and the VM mounts it read-only. guest/, also read-only, holds only ca.sh, and devvm writes and mounts it only when there are company CAs. vm/ is the one writable folder, and devvm writes nothing there itself except an image only Docker has, before the VM starts. The scripts sit beside vm/, never inside it, so what the image writes can’t replace them on this machine.
  • devvm checks what comes out once the build VM is gone. Each file must be a regular file, because a link could point Lima at a file on this machine. The kernel command line can hold only letters, digits, spaces and =,./:_-, because it goes into Lima’s config. The C library must be gnu or musl. The disk must be raw ext4 as mke2fs writes it into a new file, its first 1024 bytes zero and an ext4 superblock after them, because another format, such as qcow2, can name a file on this machine as its backing file, and its header would sit in those first bytes. A glibc file must be a regular file before devvm reads it, because a link could name a FIFO on this machine, and the read would wait. devvm refuses anything else (convert_bad_output), and it doesn’t create base.
  • devvm deletes the build VM and the temporary folder, with the scripts it wrote there, however the run ends, Ctrl+C included.

Images only Docker has

When the registry doesn’t give devvm the image (images only Docker has), devvm keys base by Docker’s image ID instead of a digest. devvm exports the image with docker save into the build VM’s folder, where crane reads it, and it checks that the export is the image it looked up. The image is saved by name, so if the tag has moved since, for example after a rebuild, devvm stops and asks you to run it again. devvm only asks Docker about images, with docker image inspect, docker info and docker save.

Versions

devvm doesn’t pin the shared tools’ versions (shared tools). Instead, assets/shared-tools/mise.toml says which releases to follow, which is the latest of each tool, and Node 24. The first time a tool is needed, devvm resolves it to upstream’s newest release and writes that into the tools lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/mise.lock, with each download’s checksum for every platform that VMs run (Linux, with glibc and with musl). Builds install exactly the lock’s versions and check them against those checksums. Resolving needs this machine to be online once, and until it has been, devvm says so (tools_need_resolve).

mise’s registry decides where a tool comes from, and a mise release can change its choice, so assets/shared-tools/mise.toml names the backend of every tool that isn’t one of mise’s own core: tools in its [tool_alias] table. Claude Code, Codex, pnpm and uv come from their GitHub releases through aqua, and opencode comes from its GitHub releases directly (github:anomalyco/opencode), because only that gives musl VMs opencode’s own musl build. Without the alias, mise’s registry would take opencode 2 from npm, which has no download for each platform. The step back locks the older versions from the backend that the newest came from, and every project VM’s mise config gets the same [tool_alias] table, so the VM’s mise finds each tool where its image came from.

The resolving runs on this machine with a mise of devvm’s own. That mise is a pinned release, which devvm downloads once into ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/mise/<version> and checks against its SHA-256 before it runs it (mise_checksum). A download that gets no answer, loses it partway or gets a 408, 429 or server error is tried again up to three times, after one second and then twice as long each time, and any other answer fails it at once (mise_download_failed). devvm never uses the mise you have installed, and nothing it does reaches your own mise config. Each run of that mise gets temporary folders for its data, cache, state and config, which devvm deletes afterwards, so cache/mise/<version> holds only the binary. devvm gc deletes the folders of other versions (Versions.StaleMise), unless one changed in the last hour.

Sometimes a tool’s newest version isn’t published for every platform yet, for example when a release is still uploading, when a tag has no release, or for a few days after a Node release until its musl builds appear. A version counts as published only where its lock entry has a download with a checksum, since mise checks the download against it. devvm then takes the newest of the next five older versions that is published everywhere, and says so (tool_stepped_back). When none of them is, devvm says that too (tool_no_download). The next check tries the newest version again.

A new VM gets the lock’s versions, and devvm checks the lock again first when the last check was more than a day ago. When a check fails, devvm uses the versions it found last (tools_check_failed). When assets/shared-tools/mise.toml changes, as it can in a devvm upgrade, devvm resolves the tools again. A VM lists its tool images in its state, so a newer version never changes a VM that has an older one. Older versions that no VM has are unused, and devvm gc deletes them.

Building tools

devvm builds the tool images that a VM’s shared tools need when it makes the VM, after its image, and when devvm tools add, devvm tools update or devvm update gives a VM new ones, unless the share already has them (Launch.buildTools). devvm build builds images alone, never tool images. Each tool image builds in a throwaway VM of its own, one after another, which devvm makes from a base image and confines like an image build. Which base it makes the VM from depends on the C library the images are for, because any VM whose tools need an image’s key mounts it:

  • glibc: devvm’s own base from Ubuntu’s cloud image, on the VM’s backend, whatever base the VM has. A VM on a --from Debian or Ubuntu image gets images built there too, so the container image’s code never runs in the build of images that other VMs mount. When that base isn’t built yet, devvm says so (tools_need_own_base) and builds it first, pinning the cloud image on its first build as usual (Ubuntu’s cloud image).
  • musl: the VM’s own --from base, as it is now, because musl builds need Alpine. Its key hashes that base’s digest, so the images are only ever another VM’s on the same container image. devvm tools add, devvm tools update and devvm update build that base first, looking up its digest, so the keys they work out are those of the base that the images build in.

Before a build, devvm reads the record of the base it’s about to clone and refuses to build in it unless it’s the base the images are for (tools_wrong_base): base from Ubuntu’s cloud image for glibc, and for musl a --from base with the digest that the images’ keys hash. A tool’s installer can run anything in its VM, as root too, so a VM and a folder for each tool are what keep one tool from writing into another tool’s image, whose key doesn’t hash it. A build VM gets its one tool and version, and it never sees the share. It writes into a folder of its own, ~/.local/share/devvm/tools-build.<random>, which devvm deletes once that tool is done. Lima mounts that folder at boot and goes on when the mount fails, so the build script waits up to 60 seconds for the tools lock that devvm put in the folder, mounting the folder again while it isn’t mounted. If the lock never appears, the build fails, naming the folder and the mount’s last error. devvm then checks that each image is a plain file and not a link (tool_bad_output), moves it into the share and writes its record beside it, never through a name the VM could have planted.

A glibc build also measures the newest glibc version that each tool needs, because each upstream download is built against a glibc of its own and doesn’t run on an older one. After installing the tool, the build script reads the version needs of every ELF program and library in it with readelf, which base’s build-essential installs, and writes the newest GLIBC_ version they name into <image>.glibc, or nothing when none needs one. It leaves out folders named testdata, because Go’s has ELF files from other systems that nothing runs. devvm takes that file only as a plain file holding one version (tool_bad_output) and keeps the version in the image’s record (glibc). Before it gives a VM its tools, devvm compares each image’s version with the glibc of the VM’s --from base, and an older base refuses the tool, naming it and both versions (tool_needs_glibc). It checks the same way when devvm tools add, devvm tools update or devvm update gives an existing VM tools, against the glibc its state recorded when it was made. A base from Ubuntu’s cloud image has no glibc version in its record, so its tools aren’t checked, and a musl base gets musl builds, which need no glibc. Only one build at a time writes to the share, because each holds the share’s lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/tools.lock, outside the share that VMs mount. Another devvm waits for it, saying so (share_waiting) after 3 seconds, until the build ends or you press Ctrl+C. The lock is an OS lock on an open file, so the system releases it when its devvm ends, however it ends, and a devvm that crashed or that you killed never leaves another one waiting.

Each tool image is named <tool>-<version>-<key>.erofs. Its key hashes the tool’s entry in the tools lock (its version, its downloads and their checksums), assets/shared-tools/build.sh with the prelude before it, the [settings] table of assets/shared-tools/mise.toml, the version of mise that assets/layers/base.sh pins, the C library the image is built for, the base it builds in (devvm’s own for glibc, and for musl the digest of the --from base), and the backend’s format. The build VM is made from base, so base’s mise is the one that installs the tool, and a new mise builds every tool image it installs again. A tool that build.sh installs itself, without mise, doesn’t have mise’s version in its key, because mise doesn’t install it: rustup installs rust, and dotnet comes from Microsoft’s own archive (dotnet’s download). The tests check that base.sh pins the same mise as the one devvm runs on the host, with the same Linux checksums. devvm reads the lock as TOML and hashes what the tool’s entry says, the entry of the version the image installs, so a mise that writes the same lock in another order, with other spacing or quoting, leaves every key as it is. The settings are in the key because they change what mise installs, such as python.compile, and the key reads what they say in the same way, so a comment or another way of writing the same settings leaves it as it is. Lima’s format is build.sh’s own, compressed EROFS, which adds nothing to the key. A new version, a new download, an edited build script or a changed setting builds the image again, and a base with a different C library, such as Alpine’s musl, gets an image of its own, and so would a VM on another backend. Every glibc image’s key names devvm’s own base, because glibc images build only there, so a VM on Ubuntu’s base and one on a --from Debian image share them. A musl image’s key has its base’s digest, so when the container image’s tag moves to a new image, its VMs’ next tools build again in the new base. When the lock has no download of a tool for the VM’s platform, devvm doesn’t build it and says to try again later (tool_unbuilt).

An image is base and its layers alone, and a VM’s shared tools are a list in its state (the tools section’s names) beside its image. build.Names refuses a shared tool’s name in an image name (tool_not_layer), so devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm refuse one, because shared tools aren’t images and their versions come from the lock.

dotnet’s download

mise resolves dotnet’s version like any tool’s, but it locks the version alone, without a download, because its installer runs Microsoft’s install script, which nothing pins. So devvm adds each platform’s SDK archive to the lock itself (withSDKDownloads in internal/tools/dotnet.go). For each dotnet entry that lacks a platform’s download, it fetches the channel’s list of releases, https://builds.dotnet.microsoft.com/dotnet/release-metadata/<channel>/releases.json, over HTTPS and capped at 32 MB, and it records that platform’s dotnet-sdk-<rid>.tar.gz with its SHA-512. It keeps a file only when its URL is under https://builds.dotnet.microsoft.com/dotnet/ and its hash is 128 hex digits, and a version that Microsoft doesn’t list gets no download, so devvm doesn’t build it. The image’s key hashes that lock entry, its URLs and checksums included, as it does every tool’s.

build.sh gets the URL and the SHA-512 from devvm and downloads the archive with devvm-fetch, which checks a 128-character checksum as a SHA-512 and any other as a SHA-256, and which deletes the file and fails when the sum differs. The script unpacks the archive and checks that dotnet --list-sdks names the locked version. The SDK’s folder is read-only in VMs, so the script puts a userlocal marker in its metadata/workloads/<band> folder, for its feature band (10.0.400 for 10.0.403), which makes dotnet workload install install into ~/.dotnet in the VM. In the VM, sync.sh writes the shared SDK’s folder into /etc/dotnet/install_location, where .NET’s programs look for an installed runtime, so global tools find it in every shell and not only those that mise activates, and it sets mise’s dotnet.isolated, which gives each SDK a folder of its own, so the shared one runs from its image.

The trust root is Microsoft’s releases.json, read over HTTPS, which is the same model as the upstream checksums that mise locks for the other tools. An SDK that a project’s global.json asks for is different: mise installs it in the VM with Microsoft’s install script, which checks only HTTPS and the download’s size, and it stays in that VM’s home, so no image or other VM gets it.

A company’s CA in builds

Build VMs trust the CA certificates in ~/.config/devvm/ca (a company’s CA) while they build, and images never keep them. Network tiers describes how devvm reads them and how assets/guest/ca.sh installs them.

A build’s ImageSpec.Trust holds two scripts made from ca.sh, which run as root: Add, which writes the certificates from heredocs to a temporary folder and installs them, and Remove, which is ca.sh without a folder. Each script of the build, build.sh of a tools build too, also gets the Trust’s Env at its start, which exports trust.Env, so its tools find the CAs, and nothing of that is written in the VM. The backend puts it there, as it does the build’s proxy variables. Each backend runs Add before anything in the build VM downloads, and Remove once the scripts are done, before the VM stops:

  • Lima: Add runs right after the start, through sudo sh, then base’s or the layer’s scripts, then Remove, before the final sync and the stop.
  • Lima with --from: the conversion’s build VM, which is deleted afterwards, also runs Add. oci/build.sh gets ca.sh, from devvm’s guest/ folder mounted read-only, and runs it in the image’s chroot with the CAs before bootify.sh and without them after it, so that Alpine’s apk reaches its HTTPS mirrors. The converted base then builds as Lima’s does.
  • Shared tools: ToolsSpec.Trust.Add runs before build.sh. devvm deletes the build VM and keeps only its output folder, so it needs no Remove.

An image is therefore the same with or without CAs, which is why its key holds none of them, and a tool image’s key stays its lock entry, build.sh, mise’s settings, the C library and the base it builds in. When there are CAs, the build’s numbered steps include the two scripts. A layer script that copies the system’s bundle elsewhere keeps that copy.

End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, images): a layer built with a test CA in the folder trusts it while its script runs, keeps its key once the folder is emptied, and a copy of its image booted without devvm has none of devvm’s CA files.

The share

devvm builds each tool version once for each backend and C library into a read-only image (EROFS) in ~/.local/share/devvm/tools, with its record next to it in <image>.json. The record is JSON that only devvm writes, with the image’s SHA-256 (sha256), its C library (libc), for glibc the newest glibc version it needs (glibc), for musl the digest of the base it was built in (base), its backend’s format (format), the backend that built it (backend), when it was moved in (built), the version of the devvm that built it (made_by) and, once retention finds that no VM has it, since when (idle_since). The share holds only the images and their records, and Lima’s images are compressed. That folder is mounted read-only in every VM at /mnt/devvm-tools, and each VM mounts the images its tools need at /opt/devvm/tools/<tool>/<version>, at boot and on every launch. A VM can’t change the shared images, even as root.

A tool that doesn’t mount fails the launch (tools_unmounted). mise’s auto_install stays on for a project’s own version files, so without this check a tool that isn’t mounted would download into the VM on first use without a word. The VM’s mount script, devvm-tools, tries every image in the VM’s list. It leaves out the empty mount point of one that fails, lists each failed image in /run/devvm/tools-unmounted and exits non-zero, which fails the launch’s setup. The setup removes that list before anything else it runs, so a list left from the VM’s boot isn’t read after a failure that has nothing to do with the tools. devvm then reads the first 16 KiB of that list from the VM, and it gives up after 10 seconds, because root in the VM could make the read hang. It counts only a whole line that is one of the VM’s own tool images from its state, so the error shows devvm’s own names, never the VM’s text. devvm reads the list with a command of its own because the setup’s output goes straight to the run log, and a pipe for reading it would keep devvm waiting on any process that the setup left running.

At boot the same failure fails only the devvm-tools service, and the boot goes on. Either way, the launch’s setup runs the mount script again and stops on the failure.

Listing and cleaning up

Listing images describes the columns of devvm images. An unfinished image is a build that didn’t finish, so it has no record, and a building image has no record yet because another devvm holds its lock. A tool image’s STATE compares it with the tools lock and with the VMs’ state:

  • current is the tools lock’s version, for the C library of the base that new VMs get, which --from changes, and for musl, for that base’s digest.
  • in use is another version, which a VM has in its state.
  • unused is neither.
  • not built is the lock’s version of a tool that the share has other versions of.
  • not installed means the share has nothing of that name’s.

Listing never resolves the tools lock. Before there is a lock, no tool image is current, and the tool images that no VM has show no state.

A tool image’s name doesn’t say which backend and C library it’s built for, so LIBC comes from its record, which also names the backend that built it, as devvm images --json shows in backend. An image without a record shows -, and has no backend or libc.

devvm images rm deletes images with their records. devvm gc deletes stale and unfinished images with their records, and unused tool images with theirs. With --tool-images, it also deletes the current tool images that no VM’s state lists and that have a record (Share.NoVM), however recently they were built.

A VM’s launch builds its tools before it records them in its state, and a new VM can also pick a tool that was built long before and that no VM has, so deleting current tools needs a reliable sign that no VM is being made. That sign is the making lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/making.lock (Dirs.MakingLock, held through tools.Making). Each devvm that makes a VM holds it shared from before it picks the VM’s tools, and devvm tools add, devvm tools update and devvm update hold it until the VM’s state lists the new tools. A new VM’s devvm keeps it until just before the VM’s first shell. Any number of devvms hold it at once, on every backend, because it’s taken before the backend does anything. devvm gc --tool-images and retention’s tools.unused-age (retainTools) take it exclusively without waiting (flock with LOCK_NB), after the share’s lock, and hold it until they’re done, so no VM picks its tools between their list and their deletions. A devvm that starts to make a VM meanwhile waits, and says so (making_waiting) after 200 ms. In a terminal, gc holds it while it asks. Every tool image build (Share.Build) runs for one of those devvms, under the making lock, and holds the share’s lock while it builds and moves the images in, so gc, which takes the share’s lock first, waits for a build in progress and then finds the making lock held until the VM’s state lists what it built.

When a VM is being made, devvm gc --tool-images keeps every current tool image that no VM’s state lists and names them (gc_tools_making), after the same filters, and deletes the rest of its list. Retention deletes no tool images in that run and leaves their records’ idle_since as it is, then applies its other settings. The lock is an OS lock on an open file, which the system releases when the last descriptor closes, so a devvm that crashes or is killed lets go of it. Its descriptor is close-on-exec, so neither the processes devvm starts (a Lima host agent, a proxy) nor the shell that takes devvm’s place inherit it. gc and retention never wait for it, so they can’t block, and the order the two locks are taken in can’t deadlock: a devvm making a VM takes the making lock and then the share’s, and gc and retention take the share’s and only try the making lock. Retention at a command’s start doesn’t wait for the share’s lock either: while another devvm holds it, as a tool build does, that run deletes no tool images (ShareBusy), and they wait for the next day’s run.

When a tool image that a new VM’s state lists is gone by the VM’s setup, devvm-tools can’t mount it, the setup fails with tools_unmounted, and the VM and its state stay, because only an interrupt undoes a new VM. Every launch of the VM fails the same way until devvm tools update builds the missing images, as Launch.buildTools builds whatever the share lacks.

gc holds the share’s lock throughout, so no tool build or devvm tools update changes the share meanwhile. A tool image is unused only when compared with the tools lock, so before there is a lock, gc deletes none. Because current is for the C library of the base that new VMs get, the musl tool images of an Alpine VM are unused once it’s gone, unless you give gc that --from.

gc also trims the shared Nix cache to its cap, deleting its least recently used files under the lock that the VMs’ proxies take, and with --nix-cache, it deletes all of the cache’s files. devvm images ends with what the cache takes of its cap when it holds anything.

item.title: SSH and editors
item.description:
You can reach each running VM by name from ssh and from editors such as VS Code, and you choose for each VM whether it can use your SSH keys. ssh into VMs explains how devvm’s ssh entries keep a VM away from the rest of this machine.

SSH access by name

Each running project VM can be reached as devvm-<folder>, as in ssh devvm-website or VS Code’s Remote-SSH: Connect to Host. devvm chooses this alias once, when it makes the VM, and records it, so it never changes. A VM gets devvm-<folder> unless another VM already has that alias, and then its alias is its full name. So when two folders share a name, the first VM made keeps devvm-website, and the second one’s alias is its full name, whichever of them you delete first. The VM’s full name (devvm-website-<hash>) always works as well.

devvm writes these entries to ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config each time it launches or stops a VM, because a VM’s SSH port can change each time it starts. To use them, add this line to the top of ~/.ssh/config, before any Host block:

Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config

You can also point ssh at the file, as in ssh -F ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config devvm-website. devvm host, devvm code and a new --clone VM offer to add the line in a terminal, and without one, they show it.

  • Only running VMs are listed. A stopped VM’s port is free for any program on this machine to take, so an entry for it could hand your connection, and your agent, to that program. Start the VM with devvm host or devvm before you connect from an editor.
  • Each entry checks the VM’s own host keys, which devvm reads from the VM once each time it starts and keeps in the VM’s folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/known_hosts. ssh refuses a host key that doesn’t match, and a VM whose keys devvm can’t read gets no entry.
  • Each entry reaches the VM on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, as the VM’s user with the VM’s own key. A VM whose backend names any other address, or no user or key, gets no entry, so ssh never takes your connection somewhere else.
  • The entries need OpenSSH 8.7 or newer (ssh -V), and an older ssh refuses them.
  • Keep remote forwards out of Host *. The entries turn off what else your ssh config could share with a VM, but they can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours.

devvm host and devvm code

devvm host gets this folder’s VM ready for ssh and editors, then shows its host name (devvm-website) and its folder in the VM. It does what a launch of an existing VM does, without opening a shell. It checks .git, applies the size, ports and agent forwarding that a stopped VM’s state asks for, starts the VM if it’s stopped, runs the self-check, sets the VM up and writes the ssh config. A VM whose tier isn’t enforced is stopped, and it gets no name.

devvm code does the same, then opens the folder in VS Code over Remote-SSH with VS Code’s code command, as in code --remote ssh-remote+devvm-website ~/website. VS Code gets the SSH agent that devvm was started with, not the one that devvm’s own connections to the VM carry. Without code on PATH, devvm names the host to connect to with Remote-SSH: Connect to Host.

VS Code

Over Remote-SSH, VS Code reaches further than ssh:

  • Ports. It forwards the ports that programs it starts in the VM listen on to this machine’s localhost, whatever devvm ports says. Those programs include its terminals, its tasks and an agent.
  • Git sign-in. It answers git’s credential prompts in the VM with your GitHub sign-in in VS Code.

devvm turns both off in VS Code’s settings for the VM, ~/.vscode-server/data/Machine/settings.json in the VM. Each time devvm sets the VM up, it sets remote.autoForwardPorts, git.terminalAuthentication and github.gitAuthentication to false and keeps the file’s other settings. A file with comments isn’t plain JSON, so devvm leaves it as it is and says so in the run log.

The VM can change that file back, so for a VM you don’t trust, also set the three in your own VS Code settings on this machine. Programs in the VM can also open URLs in this machine’s browser ($BROWSER).

Agent forwarding

SSH agent forwarding is off by default. While it’s on and you’re connected, anything in the VM, coding agents included, can use the agent’s keys, for example to push or to log in to servers. It can’t copy them. Turn it on for one VM when you need git over SSH there.

flowchart TD
choice{{"devvm ssh-agent"}}
choice -- "off, the default" --> off["no agent:<br>git over SSH fails"]
choice -- "on" --> on["your agent, while<br>you're connected"]
choice -- "devvm" --> own["devvm's own agent,<br>with only the keys<br>you added"]
  • devvm --ssh-agent creates the VM forwarding your agent. devvm ssh-agent on, devvm or off changes it for an existing VM from its next start, and devvm ssh-agent shows it. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, as devvm restart does, and otherwise, or without a terminal or with --no-input, the change waits for devvm restart or the VM’s next start. Until then, each time devvm opens the running VM it asks in a terminal whether to restart it with the change, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too (restarting).
  • The choice applies to devvm’s shells and to the ssh entries alike, both as the VM’s current start was made with, so a change reaches neither until the VM next starts, whichever folder devvm runs from. For a VM started outside devvm, such as with limactl start, they follow the current choice. When forwarding is off, an entry says ForwardAgent no, whatever your own Host * settings say, and none of devvm’s own connections to the VM carry your agent.
  • With forwarding off, git over SSH in the VM fails. devvm says so when it creates a VM for a repo whose origin is an SSH URL. Use an HTTPS remote with a GitHub token instead, or turn forwarding on.
  • No keys loaded. When a VM forwards your agent, the agent has no keys and ~/.ssh has one, devvm offers to load it (ssh-add --apple-use-keychain on macOS). To keep it loaded across reboots, add AddKeysToAgent yes, and UseKeychain yes on macOS, under Host * in ~/.ssh/config.
  • You can also use an agent that asks you to approve each use, such as 1Password’s or Secretive.

GitHub’s host keys are preinstalled in every VM, so a first connection to GitHub doesn’t prompt.

devvm’s own agent

devvm’s own agent keeps your other keys out of reach, because it holds only the keys you add to it, such as a deploy key or a key with access to fewer repos.

  • devvm ssh-agent add ~/.ssh/deploy_key starts the agent and loads the key. The agent’s socket is ~/.local/share/devvm/agent.sock. devvm ssh-agent devvm makes this folder’s VM forward that agent instead of yours, in devvm’s shells and in the ssh entries alike. The entries name it as the agent, so an editor forwards it however the editor was started.
  • devvm ssh-agent shows this folder’s VM’s choice, and once you’ve added a key, it then lists the keys devvm’s agent holds, as ssh-add -l does, and each key you added, with its file, its fingerprint and how it’s loaded. It loads the keys the agent lacks before it lists them.
  • devvm ssh-agent rm ~/.ssh/deploy_key takes the key out of devvm’s agent and out of ~/.local/share/devvm/agent-keys.json, so devvm doesn’t load it again. devvm finds the key in the agent by the fingerprint it recorded, so the key file can have changed or be gone, and devvm leaves the file itself as it is. devvm refuses a key you didn’t add, and devvm ssh-agent lists the ones you did.
  • devvm loads a key again when a VM that uses the agent launches without it, such as after a reboot or once the key’s lifetime ran out, and it asks for the key’s passphrase if it has one. It does so only while the file holds the key you added. add records the key’s fingerprint, so devvm doesn’t load a file that was replaced since, or a link that was swapped to another key. A key you replaced in place needs devvm ssh-agent add again.
  • devvm refuses a key inside a folder a VM mounts, and doesn’t load it, because that VM could read it. That’s every folder that a VM’s state says it mounts, whether the VM is running or stopped: its project folder, its agents’ config folders and the shared tools. Keep the keys for devvm’s agent outside project folders.
  • An encrypted key in the old PEM format needs converting first, with ssh-keygen -p -f KEY, because devvm can’t read its fingerprint without the passphrase.

The agent drops each key 12 hours after it loads it, so a VM can’t keep using the key indefinitely. --lifetime 30m changes that for one key, and it takes a duration in minutes, hours, days or weeks, such as 30m, 8h or 1d, or forever. --confirm makes the agent ask you before each use, such as each push or each login, through an ssh-askpass program. macOS doesn’t include one, so install one and put it on your PATH, or set SSH_ASKPASS to it. devvm keeps the keys and their options in ~/.local/share/devvm/agent-keys.json, and running devvm ssh-agent add on the same key again replaces its options.

devvm ssh-agent –json

devvm ssh-agent --json prints what devvm ssh-agent shows as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. mode is this folder’s VM’s choice, off, on or devvm. Each of the keys is a key you added to devvm’s agent, with its file, the fingerprint devvm recorded, confirm, its lifetime and loaded, which says whether the agent holds it. As without --json, devvm loads the keys the agent lacks first, and with no key added, keys is [] and devvm doesn’t start its agent. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses on, devvm or off with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "mode": "devvm",
 "keys": [
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.ssh/deploy_key",
 "fingerprint": "SHA256:mVPwvezndPv/ARoIadVY98vAC0g+P/5633yTC4d/wXE",
 "confirm": false,
 "lifetime": "12h",
 "loaded": true
 }
 ]
}

item.title: devvm agent import
item.description:
Copy the agents’ settings and logins from this machine into devvm’s store

Synopsis

Copy the settings and logins of AGENT, claude, codex or opencode, or of every agent, from your home folder into devvm’s store, never their history. It follows no link out of an agent’s folder, and it asks before replacing what the store has.

devvm agent import [AGENT...] [flags]

Examples 

 devvm agent import # copy every agent's settings and logins, asking before replacing the store's
 devvm agent import claude codex # copy only Claude Code's and Codex's
 devvm agent import --force # replace the store's without asking, as a script must

Options 

 -f, --force don't ask to confirm, which devvm needs without a terminal or with --no-input
 -h, --help help for import

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm agent import explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm agent: Fill devvm’s store of the agents’ settings and logins that every VM gets

item.title: Port forwarding
item.description:
This page explains how devvm’s forwarder forwards a VM’s ports to this machine, which ports it never takes, and how it runs. Ports and size covers choosing a VM’s ports with --ports and devvm ports.

devvm forwards a VM’s ports with its own forwarder, never with Lima’s own forwards. Lima explains why, and what devvm sets on Lima instead.

What it forwards

Ports lists which ports the forwarder forwards, for --ports all, the default, and for a list such as --ports 5173,8000-8010, and how soon. A listed port also carries a server on the VM’s loopback (127.0.0.1 or ::1) to this machine. You can list port 22, which forwards the VM’s sshd to port 22 on this machine, while ssh by name keeps using the VM’s own ssh port.

The forwarder never forwards a server on an address in 127.77.0.0/16, on any VM, because that’s where a VM listens for its links to other VMs, so a link never appears on this machine’s localhost. A server of the VM’s own on 127.0.0.1 with the same port is forwarded as usual. It also never forwards a server on 127.0.77.1, where the desktop’s local proxy listens, because the local proxy adds the VM’s password to what it sends to the VM’s proxy, and on this machine’s localhost other users and programs could use it.

What it never takes

The forwarder never takes a port that a program on this machine has on any address. That program keeps the port and its localhost connections, and the forward waits until the VM’s server stops and starts again.

The forwarder also never takes a port that devvm records for a VM, even while that port is free. Those are the ssh, proxy and desktop ports that devvm chooses for VMs, the VM’s own ssh port, and the ports other VMs list. devvm chooses and records every VM’s ssh port, whatever its tier, so no forwarder takes it in the seconds before Lima binds it (the threat check).

When a start, or a change of a running VM’s ports, finds that a program on this machine has a listed port, devvm doesn’t forward that port and warns you (ports_taken). The VM starts or runs on all the same, and the next start or change that finds the port free forwards it again. Ports says what happens to a program that binds a port on all addresses after the forwarder has forwarded it.

How it reaches the VM

The forwarder reaches the VM over the VM’s ssh, with a key and a host key that devvm pins, and it asks for no forwarding into this machine. Only a link session asks a VM for a remote forward, on a connection of its own. Every connection starts on this machine, and the VM opens none to it. The VM sees each forwarded connection only as one to its own loopback, and on a confined tier the VM still reaches only its proxy.

A connection to a forwarded port, such as 5173, takes this path:

flowchart TD
browser["your browser, on this machine,<br>where every connection starts"] -- "localhost:5173" --> fwd["devvm's forwarder,<br>on this machine"]
fwd -- "ssh, with a key and<br>a host key devvm pins" --> sshd["the VM's sshd"]
sshd -- "127.0.0.1:5173,<br>its own loopback" --> server["your server, in the VM"]

The forwarder is devvm’s own, the same on every backend. The backend only says how the forwarder reaches a running VM’s sshd, which is a user, a key and a port on this machine’s loopback, and which file the forwarder follows to know the VM still runs, as Lima’s Ports section describes.

Its process and files

The forwarder runs as a hidden devvm command, devvm _ports, one process for each VM. devvm starts it after each start of the VM, once the backend says the VM runs, and again with the new ports when you change a running VM’s ports. devvm stop, devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop it, and a VM that stops some other way ends it, because the forwarder exits once the backend’s process for the VM is gone. Which ports a VM forwards is in the VM’s state, which devvm reads each time it starts the forwarder, so devvm ports changes the state and never the backend’s config, and the backend never hears of them. The forwarder’s log is ports.log in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/logs/, and its ports.pid, ports.status and ports.lock are in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/, beside the VM’s host keys for its current start, known_hosts, which the forwarder checks the VM against, as devvm’s ssh config does (ssh into VMs). Its control socket is ~/.local/share/devvm/run/port-<hash>.ctl, named by a hash of the VM’s name, outside the VM’s folder, because a unix socket’s path is at most 104 characters.

devvm reads every list of ports the same way, whether it comes from --ports, devvm ports or the VM’s state. Each entry is a port from 1 to 65535 or a range of them, such as 8000-8010. When the VM’s state holds a list that devvm can’t read this way, such as a file edited by hand, the VM doesn’t start and devvm names the value it couldn’t read with port_invalid, so a bad entry never becomes a port the VM didn’t ask for.

When it can’t forward

When a forwarder doesn’t start, devvm warns you and names its log (ports_forward_failed), and the VM runs on without forwarded ports.

Links between VMs

A link between VMs carries a client VM’s connections to a port that a target VM publishes. Like the forwarder, it goes over ssh, every connection starts on this machine, and it uses neither VM’s network, so no backend’s confinement changes and a confined VM still reaches nothing past its proxy over its own network. The design note has the rules, the threat check and what the prototype showed.

The addresses

Each target that a client links to gets an address of its own in 127.77.0.0/16 in that client, starting at 127.77.0.1. devvm chooses it when the client’s first link to that target is made and keeps it for every port of that target, so two targets can share a port. The client’s /etc/hosts holds a block between # devvm links begin and # devvm links end, with a line 127.77.x.y NAME NAME.devvm.internal for each target. The VM’s setup replaces the block whole at each launch, and again when links change on a running client. The setup writes the file in place, never renaming over it, and only when the block changed.

A link listens at its target’s address on the target’s own port, never on the client’s 127.0.0.1 or ::1. At each start, the setup sets net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start to 0 where it’s 1024, which is on Lima’s Alpine VMs, so a link to a port below 1024 listens on that port too. Lima’s Ubuntu and Debian VMs already have 0.

The addresses are internal to devvm. devvm link and its JSON never show them, and the forwarder never forwards them (above).

The link session

For each running client with links, devvm runs a hidden command, devvm _links VM, as one detached process on this machine. Its pid is in links.pid in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/, and its log is links.log in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/logs/. It keeps an ssh connection of its own to the client, never the forwarder’s, which starts with no forwards and asks for each link as a remote forward from 127.77.x.y:PORT in the client to a unix socket on this machine. That’s the only remote forward devvm asks a VM for. It reads the client’s links again every second and adds or cancels one forward at a time as they change, and a cancel leaves the connections that are open. A link whose address and port a program in the client already holds fails alone, with link_port_taken in the session’s log, which the next launch shows. Each line that the session’s ssh processes print starts with ssh: in its log, so no line of theirs reads as one of the session’s own, and devvm link add and the launch read only the session’s own lines.

The process ends once the client no longer runs the start it was made for, or has no links left, and devvm stop stops it with the client, which ends its connections and removes its sockets.

Every VM’s sshd allows remote forwards on 127.77.0.0/16 alone, with AllowTcpForwarding all, GatewayPorts clientspecified and PermitListen 127.77.*:*, written once into every image, so links never change or reload sshd. sshd matches the address a request names against that rule as text, so a remote forward on localhost, 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0 or ::1 is refused. Root in the client can change sshd, so those settings protect only an honest VM. What keeps the VM from choosing where its connections go on this machine is the host’s ssh client, which accepts a forwarded channel only for a forward it asked for and connects it only to that link’s socket.

Each connection

A program in the client that connects to db:5432 takes this path:

flowchart TD
app["your program, in the client"] -- "db:5432, which /etc/hosts<br>names as 127.77.0.1" --> csshd["the client's sshd"]
csshd -- "the link session's ssh,<br>which this machine opened" --> links["devvm _links,<br>on this machine"]
links -- "ssh, with the target's key<br>and pinned host key" --> tsshd["the target's sshd"]
tsshd -- "127.0.0.1:5432,<br>its own loopback" --> server["the server, in the target"]
  1. The client’s sshd carries the connection over the link session to this machine, where ssh connects it to the link’s unix socket. The socket is mode 600, in ~/.local/share/devvm/run (mode 700), and named by a hash of the client, the address and the port, because a socket’s path is at most 104 characters.
  2. devvm _links checks the link again. The link must still exist, the target must be the VM it was made for, by its ID, the port must be published, the tier rule must hold, and the target must be running, as its backend says. For a client on a confined tier, the target’s tier must also be enforced as the target runs, as devvm ls shows it, because a target that got a confined tier while it ran stays outside its proxy until its next start, and one whose self-check failed may reach the internet directly. devvm never starts the target for a connection. The link session asks the target’s backend whether the target is running and how its ssh reaches it, and the connections to that target share that answer for one second, so a burst of connections asks the backend once and devvm notices a target that stops within a second. For a client on a confined tier, the check of the target’s tier asks the backend for each connection, so it notices at once that the target stopped, and devvm logs the connection as refused because the target isn’t running, not because its tier isn’t in force. An answer that a connection closing cut short isn’t shared, so the other connections ask again. devvm makes every other check again for each connection, including the check of the target’s tier as it runs.
  3. It carries the connection over one ssh connection that it keeps to each target, with the target’s key and pinned host key, and the target’s sshd connects to 127.0.0.1:PORT in the target. That connection to a target ends when the target stops, and the next one reads the target’s host keys again, because a VM whose Lima config changed gets new ones when it boots.

An HTTP client that uses the VM’s proxy settings sends db:5432 to the VM’s proxy instead, and the proxy connects to the same link socket on this machine (links through the proxy). Steps 2 and 3 are the same for it, so the link’s checks, its cap and its events hold for both ways in.

At most 256 of a client’s connections are carried at once, and the next one is refused. A link’s socket holds at most 128 connections waiting to be accepted on macOS, and devvm _links accepts nothing while it starts a process, so it accepts a burst of connections whole before it starts any of their ssh processes: it hands them on once 5 ms pass with nothing more to accept, once the first has waited 50 ms, or once 257 wait. Each one it accepted is carried, or refused when 256 are carried already. The ssh connection to a target takes in two file descriptors for each connection it carries, more than macOS’s default limit of 256 open files allows, so devvm _links and the port forwarder give the ssh processes they start the higher limit that devvm runs with. Each connection carried or refused is written to the client’s event log, which devvm network log shows, so every VM gets an event log for its links’ connections, whatever its tier.

When links change

devvm link add and devvm link rm record the change in the client’s state on this machine, never in a VM. On a running client they send its setup again, which rewrites /etc/hosts, and they start devvm _links if it isn’t running. devvm _links reads the links again every second and writes the list that the client’s proxy reads, so the proxy reaches a new link as soon as its forward is in place. A stopped client gets the change when it next starts. Links change nothing else in the VM: no link name is in its NO_PROXY (the VM’s setup), so no daemon restarts, and on Lima no link changes the VM’s Lima config or its ssh host keys.

devvm rm of a target removes every link to it from every client’s state and updates the running clients, and devvm gc --orphans removes links to VMs whose state is gone and the sockets that a killed link session left.

Groups

A group is recorded in each of its VMs’ own state, with the name the others reach it by, so a VM made again in a folder, which gets new state, is in none. The links a group makes are links in each VM’s state like the ones devvm link add makes, marked as the group’s, so the link session, the proxy’s list and every check of a connection treat them alike. devvm works out each VM’s group links again from its own links and the other VMs’ published ports whenever one of them joins or leaves, publishes or unpublishes a port, or adds or removes a link of its own, and it records and applies only the VMs whose links changed, as above. The design note has the rules and the threat check.

item.title: Ports and size
item.description:
This page covers the ports a VM forwards to this machine and the CPUs, memory and disk it gets. You choose both when devvm makes a VM, and you can change both later with devvm ports and devvm size. Port forwarding explains how devvm’s forwarder works.

Size and ports

A new VM gets its image’s size unless you set one with --cpus, --memory and --disk, as in devvm --cpus 6. For base that’s 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk. On a machine with fewer than 4 CPUs, base gets as many CPUs as the machine has, and when 8 GiB would leave the machine less than 2 GiB of its own, base gets half of the machine’s memory, which is 4 GiB on an 8 GiB machine. When devvm builds base on such a machine, it says how many CPUs and how much memory base gets, and devvm size -g sets the size that new VMs get instead.

  • --cpus takes a whole number. --memory and --disk take a size in GiB, written 16, 16G or 16GiB, and decimals are allowed.
  • What the flags leave unset comes from the [size] table of config.toml when it sets it, else from what devvm size -g and devvm setup saved (choosing new VMs’ size).
  • devvm refuses more CPUs than this machine has, and a disk smaller than the image’s, because disks can’t shrink. It refuses them before it builds anything.
  • devvm also refuses more memory than a VM can have, because a VM that asks for all of this machine’s memory doesn’t start. A VM can have this machine’s memory less 2 GiB, counted in whole GiB, so 6 GiB on an 8 GiB machine. On a machine with 4 GiB or less, it can have half, so 2 GiB on a 4 GiB machine. When you ask for more, devvm says how much memory this machine has and the most you can give a VM, so you can run the command again with that.

A new VM forwards every TCP port from 1024 up that it listens on, unless --ports says otherwise, as in devvm --ports 5173.

  • --ports takes all, none, or ports and ranges such as 5173,8000-8010.
  • Without --ports, the default comes from ports in config.toml when it sets it, else from what devvm ports -g saved, and without either, a new VM forwards every port.
  • When you customize a new VM without --ports, devvm asks whether it forwards every port, none or the ports you type, starting from the default, and saves the answer for that VM alone (what a new VM gets).

devvm refuses a default that isn’t a valid value, as it refuses a bad flag, and for one in config.toml it names the file and the line (when devvm can’t read it).

Ports

A VM forwards the TCP ports it listens on to the same port on this machine’s localhost, so a server on :5173 in the VM is at localhost:5173 here. To change which ports a VM forwards:

devvm ports # what this folder's VM forwards: all, none or a list
devvm ports 5173,8000-8010 # only these ports and ranges
devvm ports add 5432 # one more
devvm ports rm 5173 # one fewer, as listed; the last leaves none
devvm ports none # nothing; devvm ports all forwards every port again
devvm ports -g none # what new VMs forward (default: all)
  • A change applies at once. A stopped VM forwards the new ports from its next start. On a running VM, devvm starts its forwarder again with the new ports while the VM runs on, so a server on an added port reaches this machine within a few seconds. The connections that were open through the old forwarder close, so a client that was connected through it has to connect again.
  • add and rm take ports and ranges, not all or none. devvm refuses rm on a VM that forwards every port, because there’s no list to remove from. -g also works with add and rm.
  • devvm ports -g shows what new VMs forward, followed by where it came from after a #, and devvm ports -g --json adds it as source. When config.toml sets ports, devvm ports -g refuses to change it and names the file, so edit config.toml instead (where a default comes from).
  • devvm forwards ports on every network tier, and it forwards no ports from builds.

When a VM forwards every port, devvm forwards each TCP port from 1024 up that a server in the VM listens on, whether on the VM’s loopback or on all its addresses. When a VM lists its ports, devvm forwards those ports alone, however many there are, ports below 1024 included. A port reaches this machine within a few seconds of the server starting, only on localhost (127.0.0.1 and ::1), and the forward goes away when the server stops. At most 256 ports are forwarded at once.

A VM never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, a port that another VM lists, or a port that devvm uses for its VMs’ ssh and proxies. When a port you listed is taken by a program on this machine as the VM starts, or as you change its ports, devvm warns you and the VM runs on without that port. The next start or change that finds the port free forwards it. A program that starts on a port after the VM’s forward does can still bind it on all addresses, as most servers do, and then that program’s localhost connections reach the VM.

If the forwarder can’t start, devvm warns you and names its log, and the VM runs on without forwarded ports.

UDP isn’t forwarded, on any backend. Run the UDP client in the VM instead, or tunnel it over a forwarded TCP port with socat, installed on both sides. For a UDP server on port 8125 in the VM, with TCP port 9125 forwarded:

socat TCP-LISTEN:9125,fork,reuseaddr UDP:127.0.0.1:8125 # in the VM
socat UDP-LISTEN:8125,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:9125 # on this machine

TCP is a stream, so datagrams can arrive merged or split. This suits low-rate request and response traffic, such as DNS, statsd or syslog, but not high-rate or latency-sensitive traffic, such as games, QUIC or WebRTC media.

Size

To see or change a VM’s size:

devvm size # what this folder's VM has: cpus=4 memory=8GiB disk=100GiB
devvm size --cpus 6 --memory 16 # change it; what isn't given stays
devvm size --disk 200 # a bigger disk; never a smaller one
devvm size -g --memory 16 # the size new VMs get (default: the image's)
devvm size -g # cpus=, memory= and disk= lines, empty for the image's, each with its source
  • The flags take the same values as for a new VM and have the same limits, so devvm refuses more CPUs than this machine has and more memory than a VM can have (size and ports). devvm size -g checks a default size in the same way when you set it. A VM that already has more memory keeps it and still starts, because devvm checks a size only when you set one.
  • devvm size -g ends each line with where its value came from, after a #: the path of config.toml, devvm: settings.json for what devvm size -g or devvm setup saved, or devvm: default for the image’s. When config.toml sets cpus, memory or disk, devvm size -g refuses to change that one and names the file, so edit config.toml instead (where a default comes from).
  • A stopped VM gets its new size when it next starts, such as with devvm, and until then devvm size shows what the VM has now and says what changes. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, and if you answer yes, devvm restarts it as devvm restart does. Otherwise, and without a terminal or with --no-input, the VM keeps its size until it next starts, for example with devvm restart. When devvm opens the running VM while its new size still waits, it asks once more in a terminal, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too, and a yes restarts the VM with its new size before the shell opens (restarting).
  • Disks grow but never shrink, so devvm refuses a disk smaller than the VM’s.

Choosing new VMs’ size

devvm asks for the CPUs and memory that new VMs get on your first run, before it asks which features base gets, and again whenever you run devvm setup:

devvm setup # asks its questions, the size among them
devvm size -g --cpus 6 --memory 16 # only the size, without asking

Before the two questions, devvm says how many CPUs and how much memory this machine has. Each question shows in brackets the value new VMs get now. That’s what config.toml sets or devvm size -g saved, or else base’s own size fitted to this machine: 4 CPUs and 8 GiB, or less on a machine that doesn’t have room for them (size and ports). Confirm to keep the value, or enter another one. devvm checks what you type as it checks --cpus and --memory, and when this machine can’t give it, devvm says why and asks again.

devvm doesn’t ask for a value that config.toml sets, and says so. It saves only the values you type, where devvm size -g saves them, and keeps a saved disk size as it is. When you keep both values, devvm saves nothing, so new VMs go on getting the image’s size. Either way, devvm prints the size new VMs get. A new size changes only the VMs made after it, and nothing is rebuilt, so existing VMs keep their size until you change it with devvm size.

The first run asks only in a terminal, and only when no size is set and you didn’t give --cpus or --memory. It asks once, because that run also chooses base’s features, and devvm asks only before they’re chosen. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm asks nothing, and new VMs get the image’s size. devvm setup asks only in a terminal, without --no-input, and only when you give it no flags (devvm setup). To set the size without asking, use devvm size -g --cpus N --memory GiB, which takes the same values and has the same limits.

Disk use

A VM’s disk size is how far the disk can grow, not how much space it takes. A project VM starts as a copy of its image’s disk that shares the image’s blocks, so a new VM takes almost nothing until it writes (clones and overlays):

  • macOS: the copy is an APFS clone. du counts the shared blocks as the clone’s own, so it overcounts.
  • Linux: the copy is a qcow2 overlay of the image’s disk, which holds only the VM’s changes, about 12 MB for a new VM instead of 2 GB.

Free space

Before devvm builds an image or makes a VM, it checks the free space on the disk that will hold it, and it refuses to start the step when there’s less free than the step needs:

Step macOS Linux
building base 8 GiB 8 GiB
building any other image 2 GiB 8 GiB
building shared tool images 3 GiB, and 0.5 GiB for each tool 9 GiB, and 0.5 GiB for each tool
making a VM 2 GiB 2 GiB

devvm rounds each number up to whole GiB, so building one shared tool with Lima on macOS needs 4 GiB, and building all ten needs 8 GiB. Each build checks again before it starts, so the first VM on a Mac, which builds base, needs 8 GiB free.

The numbers leave a margin over what each step took when devvm’s tests measured the free space before, during and after it. Most of a step’s space is only needed while it runs. On Lima on macOS, base took about 1 GiB with Ubuntu’s cloud image already downloaded, and downloading the image takes up to another 0.9 GiB. base’s features add up to 2.5 GiB. A build of all ten shared tools took 6 GiB at its peak and kept 1.5 GiB of images. On macOS, an image built on another and a new VM take only what they write. On Linux hosts, an image and the VM that builds shared tools start as a full copy of their parent’s disk, but a new VM’s disk holds only its own changes. A VM then grows as you work in it, and its disk never shrinks.

devvm checks the disk that holds the images and VMs, which is the disk of devvm’s Lima home. Shared tool images come out into devvm’s data folder, so a tools build also checks that folder’s disk, which needs 0.5 GiB and 0.25 GiB for each tool, rounded up: 1 GiB for one tool and 3 GiB for all ten. When devvm’s data folder is on a small temporary disk, such as a tmpfs /tmp on Linux, devvm checks that disk.

devvm doctor also warns when that disk has less free space than building base needs, but the warning doesn’t make doctor fail. When devvm refuses, see Not enough free space for how to make room.

As JSON

devvm size --json and devvm ports --json print what the commands show as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. With -g, they print the same fields for new VMs. With --json they only show, so devvm refuses --cpus, --memory, --disk or a list of ports with it.

devvm size --json has cpus, memory_gib and disk_gib, and leaves out what isn’t set. For -g, that’s what new VMs take from the image. When the VM’s size changes at its next start, pending has the cpus, memory_gib and disk_gib that change.

{
 "version": 1,
 "cpus": 4,
 "memory_gib": 8,
 "disk_gib": 100,
 "pending": {
 "memory_gib": 16
 }
}

With -g, devvm size --json also has sources, which says where each of cpus, memory and disk came from: config.toml, settings.json for what devvm saved, or built-in for the image’s (where a default comes from).

{
 "version": 1,
 "cpus": 6,
 "memory_gib": 16,
 "sources": {
 "cpus": "settings.json",
 "disk": "built-in",
 "memory": "config.toml"
 }
}

devvm ports --json has ports, which is all, none or a list of ports and ranges, written as devvm ports takes it. With -g, it also has source, which is config.toml, settings.json or built-in.

{
 "version": 1,
 "ports": "5173,8000-8010"
}

item.title: The desktop
item.description:
This page explains how devvm desktop serves a VM’s desktop on this machine, how it checks a viewer’s password and keeps the clipboard out of the VM, and why devvm uses VNC and never forwards X11. A VM’s desktop covers adding the desktop and opening it.

In the VM

The built-in desktop layer installs Xfce, TigerVNC’s Xvnc, socat for the local proxy and a command of devvm’s, devvm-desktop, into the desktop image, which only the VMs with the layer are made from (the desktop layer). Its packages come from the distribution’s archive as it is when the layer builds, and it downloads nothing else. When you run devvm desktop, devvm first checks that the VM has devvm-desktop, and refuses a VM without it (desktop_no_layer). Then it runs devvm-desktop start off, or start on with --clipboard, as the VM’s user.

devvm-desktop starts Xvnc on display :1 unless it’s running. Xvnc listens on the socket /run/devvm-desktop/vnc.sock alone, in a folder of the VM’s user’s own (mode 700), the socket itself mode 600. It listens on no TCP port (-rfbport -1), and takes no X11 connections over TCP (-nolisten tcp), so devvm’s port forwarder never sees it, even on a VM that forwards every port. It asks for no password of its own (-SecurityTypes None), because devvm checks the viewer’s password on this machine first. The clipboard settings (AcceptCutText, SendCutText, SetPrimary, SendPrimary) are on or off as asked, and on a desktop that runs already, devvm-desktop changes them in place with vncconfig. Then it starts an Xfce session on the display, in a D-Bus session of its own, with the session’s proxy settings pointed at the VM’s local proxy. Nothing starts the desktop at boot, so a VM whose desktop you never open runs none. Its log is ~/.cache/devvm-desktop.log in the VM.

The local proxy

Every request from the VM to its proxy carries the VM’s password in Proxy-Authorization, and the VM’s proxy settings carry it in their URL, http://devvm:KEY@192.168.5.2:PORT. Command-line tools take the password from that URL, but Chrome, Chromium and Firefox ignore it and ask for the proxy’s username and password instead, on every site. So the desktop’s programs use a local proxy in the VM, devvm-local-proxy, which needs no password and adds the VM’s.

The VM’s setup writes devvm-local-proxy into /usr/local/bin at each launch, mode 700 and the VM’s user’s, with the VM’s proxy address and password in it, and installs it whole, so a connection that’s already running keeps the copy it started with. The VM already holds the same password in its environment. devvm-desktop runs devvm-local-proxy start before it starts Xvnc, which starts socat unless it’s running. socat listens on 127.0.77.1:3128 alone, which is on the VM’s loopback, takes connections only from 127.0.0.0/8, carries at most 256 at once, and runs devvm-local-proxy on each connection itself. Its log is ~/.cache/devvm-local-proxy.log. The address comes from devvm (proxy.LocalProxyAddr and proxy.LocalProxyPort), which the setup gets as DEVVM_LOCAL_PROXY, and devvm-desktop sets http_proxy, https_proxy, HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY to http://127.0.77.1:3128 for the Xfce session. On Xfce, Chrome and Chromium read those variables for their proxy, and Firefox reads them first when its proxy setting is the system’s, which is its default.

For each connection, devvm-local-proxy reads the request line and the headers, waiting at most 30 seconds for each line and taking at most 100 headers. It takes only what a proxy is sent:

  • a CONNECT to a host and port, which becomes a tunnel;
  • a request for an absolute http:// or https:// URL, such as GET http://example.com/.

Anything else gets 400, and nothing of it reaches the VM’s proxy. That includes a request in origin form, such as GET /, which is what a web page sends when it reaches the local proxy as a server, so a page in the browser can’t use it. The local proxy drops the client’s own Proxy-Authorization and Proxy-Connection headers and adds the VM’s password. For a request that isn’t a CONNECT, it drops Connection and Keep-Alive and asks for Connection: close, because the password goes with each request’s head and the local proxy reads only the first, so each connection carries one request. Then it connects to the VM’s proxy, and to nothing else, sends the head and carries the rest both ways with socat. The VM’s proxy decides as it does for any request: a host the tier allows is reached, and one it doesn’t allow gets the proxy’s 403 with its reason.

devvm’s port forwarder never forwards a server on 127.0.77.1, on any port, because a forward would put a proxy that adds the VM’s password on this machine’s localhost, where other users and programs could reach it.

On this machine

devvm desktop listens on 127.0.0.1 alone, on the VM’s port. That’s the port its state records in its ports section (host.desktop) while no program on this machine has it, and otherwise a new one that no program and no VM has, which devvm chooses and records in its place under the claims lock, as it does every port it chooses for a VM. New ports come from 20000 up to just below the range this machine gives outgoing connections, which starts at 32768 on Linux by default and 49152 on macOS, because Linux refuses a listener on a port that a live outgoing connection holds. devvm reads that range from the system, and when it can’t, or the range leaves fewer than 1000 ports above 20000, it picks from 20000 to 32767. The port is among those devvm records for VMs, with their ssh and proxy ports, so no VM’s port forwarder takes it and no new VM gets it for its ssh or its proxy. devvm listens without address reuse, so a program that has the port on any address keeps it. The listener stays open until you press Ctrl+C, or until the VM no longer runs, which devvm checks every 5 seconds (desktop_vm_stopped). Nothing else listens for the desktop on this machine, at any other time.

Each connection to the port goes through devvm’s relay, which runs in devvm desktop:

  1. The relay speaks VNC’s protocol (RFB 3.8, and 3.7 and 3.3 for older viewers) as a server, and offers VNC’s own authentication alone. It sends a random challenge and checks the viewer’s answer against the VM’s password, with one check at a time, so a wrong answer holds every other viewer’s check for a second. A viewer whose answer is wrong is refused and never reaches the VM.
