Codex’s login is ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/codex/.codex/auth.json and opencode’s is ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/opencode/.local/share/opencode/auth.json, the store’s copies of ~/.codex/auth.json and ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json. The VM’s copy holds placeholders, shaped like a JWT where the tools read claims, and the bindings put the store’s API key or access token into requests for the provider’s hosts:

  • For Codex, those are OpenAI’s hosts, api.openai.com, and chatgpt.com for a ChatGPT login.
  • For opencode, they’re the hosts of Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenRouter keys, and of OpenAI and GitHub Copilot logins, but not Copilot Enterprise.

The store keeps opencode’s login in the auth.json format of opencode 1: one entry per provider, {"type":"api","key"} or {"type":"oauth","access","refresh","expires"} with its expiry in milliseconds. opencode 2 keeps its logins in the credential table of its SQLite database, ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db, and imports auth.json into it once, in the migration that makes the table, so a VM’s opencode gets the VM’s copy when it first runs there. A VM’s placeholders don’t change when the host refreshes a login, so the database’s copies keep working. After that, the store’s opencode logins reach the database through opencode auth import, as auth export entries with the IDs cred_devvm_<provider> and the logins’ placeholders (agentlogin.OpencodeImport): each API key that the proxy puts in, and the OpenAI login from one of opencode’s Codex logins. The VM’s setup sends these entries on every launch, and devvm agent login opencode --api-key --provider PROVIDER sends them at once, both on the input of devvm’s guest script opencode.sh, never in a command’s arguments. The script keeps the last entries it got in ~/.local/state/devvm/opencode-import.json in the VM. When opencode has made its database and the new entries differ from the record, or the database no longer holds one of their IDs because it was made again, such as after you delete it or a history import replaces it, it logs out of devvm’s entries from the last ones with opencode auth logout, because opencode auth import skips an ID it already has, and then imports the new ones and makes each of them its provider’s active credential with opencode auth switch, so a ChatGPT login for another account or a key saved from another VM reaches every VM at its next launch. Credentials that you added in the VM yourself have other IDs, so they stay in the database, and opencode auth switch makes one of them active again. Before opencode has made its database, the script does nothing and records nothing, because opencode 2.2.5 doesn’t always import auth.json as it makes the database, so the first launch after opencode has run imports every entry. The script imports each entry on its own, so an entry that opencode refuses doesn’t keep the others out, and devvm agent login names the providers that opencode refused. A failed import leaves the record as it was, so the next launch tries again. The script and its record live in the VM rather than in the VM’s state on the host, because only the VM knows whether its database exists and what it last imported, and a VM that is set up again or has its home copied keeps both together.

Each VM’s placeholders end in its own random value, so no other VM’s placeholder gets its secrets. devvm reads a login file only when it’s a regular file, so a FIFO or a device in its place can’t hold devvm. devvm refreshes OAuth logins on the host, one lookup at a time, and writes them back to the store’s file, so a VM never holds a refresh token. A refresh that has started finishes and is written back even when the request that needed it ends, because OpenAI may already have replaced the refresh token. When a refresh fails, or the store’s login no longer has what a binding names, the proxy puts nothing in, and its own log says to log in again with the agent and import the login again (codex_refresh_failed, opencode_refresh_failed, codex_no_key, codex_no_chatgpt), or names the login file it couldn’t read (login_read_failed). devvm copies logins it doesn’t know as they are, and warns you (codex_login_kept, opencode_login_kept). An opencode OAuth login that devvm doesn’t bind, such as Copilot Enterprise’s or one for a provider devvm doesn’t know, is the exception: its access and refresh tokens become devvm-redacted in the VM’s copy, so opencode in the VM can’t use that login, and devvm warns you (opencode_login_withheld). If devvm can’t make the VM’s copy of a login, it stops the VM’s setup (login_copy_failed).

Coding agents lists which files each agent shares.

Logins made in a VM

A login that an agent makes inside a VM goes to devvm’s store too, and the VM gets only placeholders for it. The VM’s proxy does this at the agent’s OAuth token endpoint, the one request of a login whose reply holds its tokens. Codex and opencode both log in to OpenAI at auth.openai.com/oauth/token, whether the code comes from a browser’s redirect or from a device code typed into a browser elsewhere. For opencode 2, those are its Codex logins, the methods chatgpt-browser and chatgpt-headless. Its Sign in with ChatGPT, chatgpt-token-sharing, registers a client of its own and gets its tokens from auth.openai.com/api/accounts/oauth/token, then checks the id_token’s signature against OpenAI’s keys, which a placeholder can’t pass, so devvm doesn’t capture that endpoint, and its replies get 502, as the next paragraph says. Every VM’s proxy config lists that endpoint in captures, for Codex and for opencode, whatever the VM’s image holds, because a program in the VM could install either agent itself. The endpoint’s host joins the VM’s secrets.policy on port 443 only when its image has one of them, so that agent can log in on every tier. The proxy intercepts the host’s :443 tunnels as it does a bound host’s, with a certificate from the VM’s CA, and forwards every request to it. Only a POST to the endpoint’s path is captured, and the proxy compares the path once it’s cleaned, without its path parameters and in any case, so a request for /oauth//token, /OAuth/Token/ or /oauth/token;x is captured too. A captured request goes to the endpoint’s own path, without a query, whatever the VM’s spelling of it. Any other successful reply from that host that names an access_token, a refresh_token or an id_token anywhere gets 502, whatever its type, so no other path there, such as another token endpoint’s, hands the VM a login. The proxy passes only a web page and its parts unread, which are HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and fonts, and it refuses a reply it can’t read for that, one that’s encoded or longer than 1 MiB, and an upgrade (101). No informational reply (1xx) from the host reaches the VM, because its headers could hold a cookie.

The proxy reads a captured request’s body whole, up to 64 KiB, and refuses one that names a field twice, which devvm and the endpoint could read apart. It drops the VM’s Accept-Encoding header from every request to the host, so each reply comes as it is, or as gzip that Go’s transport undoes. The request goes on unchanged, with two exceptions. After a code’s login, Codex exchanges the login’s id_token for an API key, with a token-exchange grant that asks for openai-api-key. The VM’s request carries the VM’s placeholder of the id_token, so the proxy puts the store’s id_token in its place, and only when the placeholder is that VM’s for the store’s current login. An error reply to that request reaches the VM with its OAuth error code alone, such as {"error":"invalid_grant"}, in case the endpoint’s message quotes the id_token. A refresh whose refresh token is the VM’s own, devvm-proxy-managed, or for opencode its access token’s placeholder, goes nowhere, and the VM gets the store’s login as placeholders again, because the host refreshes the login itself. devvm refuses any other grant than a code’s, a refresh’s or Codex’s exchange before the request leaves the host, because it couldn’t read the reply. The proxy reads at most 8 requests and replies to and from the host whole at once.

A successful reply never reaches the VM as it is. The proxy reads it whole, up to 1 MiB, and agentlogin.File.Capture saves its tokens in the store’s login file, in the agent’s own format, under the file’s lock, so a refresh on the host never runs at the same time. Codex’s goes in tokens of its auth.json, with the account from the id_token, and the exchange’s API key in OPENAI_API_KEY. opencode’s goes in the openai entry of its auth.json, as an OAuth login with its expiry in milliseconds and its account. A code’s reply replaces the login, and for Codex the API key of the login before it too. A refresh’s reply adds to the login, so the store keeps only the newest refresh token. Then devvm writes the VM’s bindings again, so its proxy puts the new login into requests at once. When that write fails, the login is saved still, the VM gets its reply, its proxy’s own log says why, and the VM’s next launch writes its bindings.

The VM gets a reply with placeholders in place of the tokens. Its access token’s placeholder is the one the store’s login binds, a JWT with the login’s account claims, its API key’s is the one its binding names, and its refresh token is devvm-proxy-managed, which is no token. The reply keeps only the token type and scope, says that the access token lasts until 2099, and holds nothing else of the endpoint’s reply, so the agent in the VM never refreshes the login itself. Its headers are only Content-Type, Cache-Control, Pragma and Date, so no cookie of the endpoint’s reaches the VM. A reply that’s too long, encoded in another way, or not a login devvm reads, such as one without an access token, gets 502 instead, logged as a refused block, and devvm saves nothing of it. An error reply holds no tokens, so it reaches the VM as it is, with the same headers alone. The event log gets a login event for each login saved, which names the agent, and the proxy’s own log says why a capture failed, without a value.

A login is the agent’s that the VM’s image has, of the two. In a VM with both, or with neither, the request’s User-Agent says whose login it is, through agentlogin.Pick. opencode runs on Bun, so a request whose User-Agent starts with Bun/ or opencode/ is opencode’s, and any other is Codex’s.

Claude Code logs in at platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token, and older releases at console.anthropic.com/v1/oauth/token, so every VM’s proxy config lists both in captures for Claude Code, and their hosts join the secrets.policy of a VM whose image has it. Anthropic doesn’t document these requests: devvm reads them from Claude Code 2.1’s bundle, so a release that changes them can break the capture, and the network end-to-end section drives the real Claude Code’s login against a fake endpoint to catch that. Claude Code sends JSON with its public client ID, 9d1c250a-e61b-44d9-88ed-5944d1962f5e, and PKCE, without a client secret. A code’s request holds grant_type, code, redirect_uri, client_id, code_verifier and state, and a refresh’s grant_type, refresh_token, client_id and scope. The reply holds access_token, refresh_token, expires_in and scope, with the account and the organization.

claude setup-token sends a code’s request too, with expires_in of a year added, and asks only for the user:inference scope, so agentlogin.SetupToken tells it apart by that field. Its reply’s access token, which must start with sk-ant-oat01-, becomes the claude secret (secrets.Store.Save), and the VM gets the secret’s placeholder in its place, which claude setup-token then prints. Any other code’s login goes in the store’s .claude/.credentials.json, as Claude Code keeps it on Linux: claudeAiOauth with accessToken, refreshToken, expiresAt in Unix milliseconds and scopes. A new login whose scope lacks user:inference gets 502, because it can’t use the model: that’s an Anthropic Console login, which Claude Code would use to make an API key at api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/claude_cli/create_api_key with the access token the VM never gets. A login or a refresh whose scope has org:create_api_key gets 502 too, whatever else it has, because the proxy puts the login into every request to api.anthropic.com, so a VM could make an API key with it and get the key itself. The access token must start with sk-ant-oat01- and hold no space, quote, backslash or control character, in a capture’s reply and in the host’s refresh’s. Only a VM whose image has Claude Code captures a Claude Code login, because a capture replaces the login every VM with Claude Code uses, so another VM’s gets 502 and devvm saves nothing. The VM’s reply holds sk-ant-oat01-devvm-proxy-managed-oauth-<salt> as its access token and devvm-proxy-managed as its refresh token, so the VM’s ~/.claude/.credentials.json, which Claude Code writes from it, holds no token. A refresh with devvm-proxy-managed goes nowhere, and the VM gets the placeholders again.

devvm keeps one Claude Code login. Saving the claude secret, captured or with devvm secret set claude, deletes the store’s .credentials.json, and capturing an OAuth login deletes the saved claude secret, so the newest login wins. Both happen under the lock of the store’s logins/claude folder, so two at once never leave neither, and a saved token that can’t be deleted is a warning in the proxy’s log, as the login is saved. A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in devvm’s environment wins over both, as it does in Claude Code (secrets.ClaudeOf(store).Login). A launch gives the VM CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN with its placeholder when there’s a token, and otherwise the VM’s copy of .credentials.json, with that placeholder, no refresh token and an expiry of 2099 (agentlogin.File.VMCopy), never both. The VM’s bindings hold both logins’ placeholders, the claude secret’s and claude-oauth, each putting a value into Authorization for api.anthropic.com, whenever devvm keeps either login, and secrets.Store.Get gives each the login devvm keeps now. So a VM that started with the login that the newest replaced keeps working until its next launch gives it the new one. Claude Code sends the anthropic-beta header that names oauth-2025-04-20 itself, so the proxy only swaps the placeholder.

The host refreshes the OAuth login when its access token is due, as Codex’s is: a JSON refresh to platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token with Claude Code’s client ID and the login’s scopes, through the company proxy the VM’s proxy goes through, written back under the file’s lock (agentlogin.File.Get). When the refresh fails, the proxy’s log says to run devvm agent login claude again (claude_refresh_failed).

devvm agent login claude runs claude auth login --claudeai in the VM, or claude setup-token with --setup-token, without the VM’s CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Claude Code shows the address that comes back to platform.claude.com/oauth/code/callback, which shows the code to paste, so devvm forwards no port. Once the store has a new login of the kind asked for (secrets.ClaudeOf(store).Sums), devvm sets the VM up again, so its environment and files hold the login devvm keeps now.

Any VM with the agent can replace the store’s login, because the store keeps one login for each agent. A VM you don’t trust can log your other VMs in to an account of its choosing, and their requests then go to that account. Claude Code’s long-lived tokens have the same shape whatever asks for one, so a token that Claude Code mints in a VM for another use, such as claude /install-github-app’s, becomes devvm’s Claude Code login too, and what the VM gets is its placeholder, which works only through its proxy. A VM with Claude Code can also use the login, through its proxy, for whatever else its scopes allow at api.anthropic.com, beyond the model, such as reading the account’s profile, and devvm doesn’t limit the paths it goes to. Neither does devvm guard Anthropic’s other hosts: if one of them also answered /v1/oauth/token, a VM could exchange its code there and keep the login’s tokens, though none is known to. On the open tier, a program in the VM can go around its proxy, and then it gets the login’s tokens itself and devvm saves nothing.

Unit tests: TestCaptureLogin, TestCapturePaths, TestCaptureEarlyHintsAnswerAndSaved, TestCaptureErrorPasses and TestCaptureRefuses (internal/proxy) check what goes out and what the VM gets, its headers included, which paths are captured and the one they go to, that tokens from another path are refused, that no 1xx reaches the VM, an answered request and a login saved without its bindings, that an error passes, with its code alone after a real value went out, and that what can’t be read is refused; TestCodexCapture, TestOpencodeCapture, TestClaudeCapture, TestClaudeSetupToken, TestClaudeOAuthGet, TestCaptureRefuses and TestEndpointsAndPick (internal/agentlogin) check each agent’s file, the VM’s placeholders and copies, the exchange, the VM’s own refresh, a Console login refused, setup-token’s request told apart, the host’s refresh of Claude Code’s login and repeated fields; TestOneClaudeLogin, TestClaudeBindings and TestClaudeOAuthVMCopy (internal/secrets) check that the newest Claude Code login replaces the other, the environment’s token wins, both bindings get the login devvm keeps, and the VM’s copy holds placeholders; TestCapturer (internal/netpolicy) checks that every VM’s config has the endpoints on every tier, which agent a capture is, and that it writes the VM’s bindings. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, network): a fake token endpoint behind a company proxy of the run’s own, which the VM reaches through its proxy; the store gets the real tokens and the API key, the VM’s replies hold placeholders and no refresh token, no log holds a value, and the VM’s next launch gets the login as placeholders. For Claude Code, the same company proxy fakes Claude’s token endpoint and Anthropic’s API: claude setup-token’s request makes the claude secret and the VM gets its placeholder, the real Claude Code’s claude auth login through devvm agent login claude saves the login in the store and leaves placeholders alone in the VM, the API gets the store’s token for the VM’s placeholders, and a login that’s due makes the host refresh it at Claude’s endpoint through the company proxy.

MCP servers

On each launch, devvm merges the settings and MCP servers from the store’s .claude.json, ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude.json, into the VM’s own ~/.claude.json:

  • Each of your servers replaces the VM’s server of that name whole.
  • devvm removes the servers it copied before that you no longer have.
  • Servers added in the VM stay.

The copy holds only your settings, onboarding and account state, and MCP servers. Everything else stays out, such as primaryApiKey, customApiKeyResponses and your per-project entries, which devvm agent import already leaves out of the store, and the VM keeps its own value of each. So the VM keeps its own per-project entries, such as trust and allowed tools, and yours never go in. If devvm can’t read the store’s .claude.json, it stops the VM’s setup (login_copy_failed).

On every tier, an HTTPS server’s headers become bindings for its host, which must be a DNS name on port 443. devvm replaces these with devvm-redacted: env values, plain-HTTP servers’ headers, user info and secret-looking values in URLs, and secret-named or key-shaped arguments. A server’s command and headersHelper, which are shell commands, lose the same words as other text in settings files (keys in settings files).

Keys in settings files

devvm also takes the keys out of the VM’s copies of the agents’ settings files, which are ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.codex/config.toml and opencode’s .json, .jsonc and .toml files. Those are JSON, JSONC or TOML, and devvm parses each file whole and writes the VM’s copy from what it parsed, so a JSONC file’s copy is JSON and a TOML file’s copy has no comments. devvm replaces these with devvm-redacted, and names what it replaced (config_redacted):

  • Every value under a key that looks like a secret’s (*key*, *token*, *secret*, *password*, Authorization), and every string in a list or a table under such a key, but key bindings, such as opencode’s keybinds.
  • Any string that starts like a known key or token, such as sk-, ghp_ or eyJ, wherever it is.
  • Every value in an env or headers table, whatever its name: env, environment, headers, http_headers, and Codex’s shell_environment_policy.set. A number of up to five digits, true and false stay, because they’re switches and ports. In Claude Code’s own env, the top-level one of settings.json, its configuration variables stay too: ANTHROPIC_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL, the ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION families, CLAUDE_CODE_*, DISABLE_*, MAX_* and *_TIMEOUT_MS. A variable whose name has KEY, TOKEN as a word, SECRET, PASS, AUTH, CREDENTIAL, COOKIE or HEADER in it is redacted all the same, such as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, and so is its value when it’s a URL.
  • In a URL anywhere in the file, a string’s whole value or a part of other text, its user info and its secret-looking query values and path segments.
  • In every list, the arguments that MCP servers’ arguments in ~/.claude.json lose: the value after a secret-named flag, such as --api-key X, the value of --token=X, and any that looks like a key.
  • In any other string, such as a hook’s command or an argument that holds a header, each word that starts like a known key, and the credential after Bearer or Basic, quoted or not, when it has 16 or more characters, with a digit, +, / or = among them, which words don’t have, and isn’t a path. devvm replaces only those words, so curl -H 'x-api-key: sk-…' URL becomes curl -H 'x-api-key: devvm-redacted' URL, and a reference such as Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN} stays. MCP servers’ arguments, command and headersHelper in ~/.claude.json lose the same words.

Values that only name where a secret is stay as they are. Those are an environment variable’s name (env_key = "OPENAI_API_KEY"), {env:X}, ${X} and a path. devvm refuses a file that doesn’t parse as its format, instead of copying any of it unread, so the VM doesn’t get that file (config_not_copied). The VM doesn’t get opencode’s other files in ~/.config/opencode either, such as a .env, because devvm can’t take secrets out of them, apart from its Markdown files, such as AGENTS.md, which hold instructions for the agent (config_not_copied). An MCP server or a provider that needs one of those keys in the VM has to get it another way.

Saving the copies back

devvm agent save reads the VM’s copies back, and they hold devvm-redacted and the proxy’s placeholders where devvm’s agent store has your secrets (saving a VM’s settings). devvm parses the VM’s file whole, and when it holds a placeholder, devvm also makes the copy the VM got from the store’s file again: the same redaction for a settings file, and for ~/.claude.json the copy with the VM’s own salted placeholders. Each placeholder gets the store’s value at the same path, but only when the copy had the same placeholder there, and when the table the placeholder is in and the table above that one, below the file’s top level, are the same as in the copy. Those tables say where the secret goes, such as an MCP server’s url beside its headers, a provider’s baseURL beside its apiKey and an env table’s base URL beside its key, so a VM can’t keep a placeholder and point it at another host. A placeholder that fails the check leaves the whole file out of the save (agent_save_placeholder), and so does a placeholder in a file without a format devvm parses, such as a skill. A file with placeholders put back is written as devvm writes the VM’s copies, as JSON or as TOML without comments, and a file without placeholders is saved as the VM has it.

What stays in the VM’s copies

Taking secrets out of a file works only where devvm can tell a secret from the rest, so some go into the VM on every tier, and keys devvm can’t tell apart lists them among what devvm leaves open:

  • The agents’ mounted folders. devvm mounts Claude Code’s skills, agents, commands, output-styles and plugins, Codex’s prompts and skills, and opencode’s subfolders whole and read-only, so every file in them reaches the VM, a .env in ~/.config/opencode/plugin included. So does a plugin marketplace’s git config in ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces, which holds a password or a token when you added a private marketplace with one in its URL. These folders hold code that the agent runs, such as plugins, hooks and the scripts that skills call, so a copy with only settings and Markdown, as opencode’s config folder’s files get, would break them. A copy without files whose names look secret, such as .env or *.pem, would miss a key in any other file, and it would need a copy of each folder, which can be large, on every launch, while a mount shows the changes to devvm’s agent store at once. So devvm mounts them as they are, and the coding agents page says to keep secrets out of them.
  • Free text of an unknown shape. A key in other text, such as a hook’s command, stays when it neither starts like a known key nor follows Bearer or Basic, because devvm can’t tell it from a word.
  • Logins devvm can’t bind. The entries of Codex’s auth.json that devvm doesn’t know, opencode’s API keys for providers other than Anthropic, OpenAI and OpenRouter, and opencode’s well-known logins ("type": "wellknown", which an organization’s own config sets up) go into the VM’s copy as they are, because devvm doesn’t know which hosts they’re for, so the proxy couldn’t put them in. A local model server’s key is one of these. devvm names each (codex_login_kept, opencode_login_kept).

The self-check

A confined tier holds only while the VM runs on the process that devvm started confined. A process can’t leave its sandbox, but limactl start starts a new Lima process, unconfined. So on every launch, and whenever an export or devvm rm’s check of a --clone VM needs the VM running, whether devvm started the VM or found it running, devvm checks two things, from the host:

  1. That the VM still runs on the process devvm started. The VM can’t fake this check.
  2. That a direct connection from the VM to the internet fails. The VM answers this check, so it catches only the honest case.

devvm records the result in the VM’s state, as ok or unenforced in the net section’s made.check. When the check fails, what devvm does depends on why:

  • The VM wasn’t started confined, because it was started outside devvm or has been running since before devvm network moved it from open to a confined tier. In a terminal, devvm offers to restart the VM confined (net_unenforced_restart), and if you decline, it warns you and goes on (net_unenforced). Without a terminal, or if the VM is still unenforced after the restart, devvm stops the VM and ends without opening a shell (net_unenforced_stop). The next devvm starts the VM confined.
  • The VM was started confined, yet it gets out, because it reaches the internet through something devvm didn’t set up, such as a second network. A restart wouldn’t help, so devvm stops the VM and ends (net_direct_route).

This is the check, and what devvm does when it fails:

flowchart TD
launch["every launch"] --> proc["on the process<br>devvm started?"]
proc -- "yes" --> direct["a direct connection<br>from the VM fails?"]
direct -- "yes" --> ok["check: ok"]
proc -- "no" --> un["check: unenforced"]
direct -- "no" --> un
un --> confined["started confined?"]
confined -- "yes: another<br>way out" --> route["stops the VM<br>and ends"]
confined -- "no" --> term["a terminal?"]
term -- "no" --> stop["stops the VM, no shell;<br>the next devvm starts<br>it confined"]
term -- "yes" --> offer["restart it confined?"]
offer -- "no" --> warn["warns, goes on"]
offer -- "yes" --> again["enforced now?"]
again -- "yes" --> ok2["check: ok"]
again -- "no" --> stop

An open VM isn’t confined, so its self-check is another one: a command in the VM asks its proxy for http://devvm.proxy/blocked through the proxy that the VM’s /etc/environment names, the variable’s name in the command and never the password. When the proxy doesn’t answer, devvm warns you (net_proxy_unreachable) and goes on, records no result, and the VM keeps running.

devvm ls and devvm network show such a VM’s tier as unenforced. That’s a VM whose last self-check failed, or a running VM that isn’t on the process devvm started confined, which devvm checks on the host each time.

On Lima, “the process devvm started” is the VM’s Lima process, which devvm starts confined.

Log files

The proxy writes every decision (tunnel, intercept, forward, blocked, or nix-cache for a request to the shared Nix cache) as a JSON line in network.jsonl in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/logs/. A line holds the time, the VM, the host and port, the method and path when the proxy sees them, the rule or the reason, and the names of the secrets it put in, never their values.

The proxy’s own lines, such as what it loaded and what failed upstream, go to proxy.log next to it. An upstream error stays there, because it can name addresses that the VM shouldn’t learn. So when a name doesn’t resolve, or a tunnel can’t connect, the VM’s 403, its http://devvm.proxy/blocked and the event log give only the reason can't resolve it; see proxy.log on the host or connect failed; see proxy.log on the host. The error itself, which can name this machine’s DNS server or the company proxy’s address and what it answered, goes to proxy.log alone. A name that resolves to an internal address gets the reason it resolves to an internal address; allow the address itself to reach it, which tells the VM that much and not the address (attack vectors). Only you can read the VM’s logs folder and its run folder, and devvm’s run logs never hold a VM’s password. The VM chose the hosts and paths, so devvm network log drops control characters in them.

The event log also holds the VM’s links’ connections, which devvm _links writes in the same format: link for a connection it carried, and link_refused, link_target_stopped or link_limit for one it refused, with the link’s name as the host and the target VM in target. An open VM’s event log holds its proxy’s events and its links’, but nothing it reached directly.

The proxy is the only program that writes proxy.log, and the event log has devvm _links as its only other writer. The proxy rotates each log before a line would take it past 10 MiB, and devvm _links writes the event log with the proxy’s own code, so it rotates the log by the same rule and a VM that runs for months keeps at most about 20 MiB of each. A line never spans two files, and lines from the proxy’s connections at the same time are written one after another, so a rotation loses none and splits none. Before each line, each writer checks that the file it has open is still network.jsonl, and when the other writer has rotated it, the writer opens the new network.jsonl and writes there, so its lines go on reaching the file that devvm network log --follow follows. Each writer takes the log’s size from the file, so it counts the other writer’s lines too. A writer rotates the log while it holds a lock on the file and checks the name again first, so when both reach the limit at once, only one renames the file and the other writes to the new one. A rotation renames network.jsonl to network.jsonl.1, which replaces the one that was there, and starts a new network.jsonl. proxy.log is also the proxy process’s output, where its last error goes when it stops, so the proxy copies it to proxy.log.1 and empties it instead, and that error still reaches the current file. Every log file and its .1 file is readable only by you (mode 600).

devvm network log reads network.jsonl.1 before network.jsonl, so the history it shows and the blocks that devvm network log --blocked counts carry on across a rotation. devvm network log --follow reads the renamed file to its end and then follows the new one from its start. devvm rm deletes the .1 files with the rest of the VM’s logs.

devvm _proxy

devvm runs the proxy as itself, devvm _proxy -config FILE, and nothing else is in its arguments. Its flags take one dash or two, and its errors end in one line, The VM's proxy failed: … (proxy_failed).

The config is one JSON file, proxy.Config, which a VM’s proxy and a build’s proxy both run with. For a VM it’s proxy.json in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/, and for a build it’s proxy.json in the build proxy’s folder. devvm writes it whole, mode 600, before each start. It holds the VM’s password and the company proxy’s credentials from the environment, though never config.toml’s password, which the proxy looks up itself, so it’s never in a process’s arguments, which other users can see. The proxy reads it once, as it starts, and refuses to start unless it’s a regular file, not a symbolic link, owned by the user the proxy runs as and readable and writable by nobody else, at most 1 MiB, of "version": 1, with no field the proxy doesn’t know. It also refuses a config without a password, one whose listen isn’t a loopback address and port, one with ca and no ca_key or the other way around, and one with a nix_cache_max below 0. A config of another version is never read, so a proxy and the devvm that started it always agree on what each field means.

Field What
version 1
listen the loopback address and port to listen on, port 0 for any free one
vm the VM’s name, for the log
password the VM’s password, which every request carries in Proxy-Authorization with the user devvm; required
builtin_policies the built-in policies, paths in devvm’s own files, read from the binary once as the proxy starts, ahead of policies; a missing one refuses to start
policies your policy files, in order, each read again when it changes; a missing one has no rules
log the JSON-lines event log (none: standard output), rotated past 10 MiB
proxy_log the file that the proxy’s output goes to, which is its own log, rotated past 10 MiB by copying
lifeline the hostagent’s pid file: exit once it no longer holds what it held when the proxy first saw its process running, or that process is gone
ca, ca_key the VM’s own CA, for interception: its certificate and key
ca_next, ca_next_key with ca: the VM’s next CA, which signs from an hour after its start
secrets the VM’s bindings file, read again when it changes; the proxy looks each binding’s value up in its own process
upstream_cas the CAs in your CA folder (PEM), which the proxy’s own TLS connections trust besides the system’s
upstream the company proxy: https, http and no_proxy, as HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY or config.toml’s [proxy] had them, and secret, the secret the proxy looks up as the password of a URL that names a user and none of its own; allowed hosts are reached through it
upstream_unresolved with upstream: names this machine can’t resolve go there even when only ** allows them, which builds’ proxies get
nix_cache serve the shared Nix cache at http://devvm.proxy/nix/ from this folder, which it makes, only yours (mode 700)
nix_cache_max with nix_cache: the cache’s cap, in bytes (none: 10 GiB)
links the VM’s links’ list, which devvm _links writes: reach each link through its socket, before any rule (links through the proxy); a missing list has no links
link_sockets with links: the folder of the links’ sockets, devvm’s run folder; without it, no link is reached
devvm_sha256, ca_sha256, ca_next_sha256 the SHA-256 of devvm’s binary, of the VM’s CA certificate and of its next CA’s that the proxy started with; the proxy doesn’t read them, and they’re there so that a new binary or a new CA makes another config (how long a proxy runs)

-config is the proxy’s only flag, and running the proxy is its only mode. What only this machine does for a VM’s proxy runs inside devvm itself, never through the proxy’s arguments. devvm makes each VM’s CAs with trust.InitCA, and internal/agentlogin makes the VM’s copies of agents’ logins and settings files, their bindings and their values.

item.title: .git protection
item.description:
This page explains what devvm locks in a project’s git folder, when it locks and checks the locks again, and what the locks can’t stop. .git protection covers what still works, turning protection on or off, strict, and what isn’t covered.

On macOS devvm locks with the user-immutable flag (chflags uchg), which even root in the VM can’t clear. A read-only mount wouldn’t hold, because root in the VM can unmount it.

What’s locked

devvm locks these paths:

  • .git/hooks and .git/config. A repo without a hooks folder gets an empty one, locked, so the VM can’t make one.
  • The same paths for each submodule devvm finds, submodules of submodules included. Those are the git folders under .git/modules, and those in the working tree, which are sub/.git or the folder that a sub/.git file points to. devvm finds the submodules from the index, which it reads with core.fsmonitor off.
  • .git/config.worktree, when extensions.worktreeConfig is on. devvm creates it empty if it’s missing.
  • What linked worktrees elsewhere on your machine read from here, which is .git/worktrees/<name>/commondir and config.worktree.
  • The project folder’s .git file, if the project folder is itself a linked worktree. The repo it points to is outside the VM.

When devvm locks

devvm records a new VM’s mode in its state before its backend makes the VM, so the mode is never unset: on with locks (macOS), off when you pass --no-git-protect or on hosts without locks, and clone for a --clone VM, which mounts no .git. devvm locks once the backend has made the VM, and again on each launch that finds the VM stopped and on devvm stop, so nothing in the VM can race the locks. A VM whose creation stopped before its first locks, or that devvm adopt moved to this folder, is locked on its next launch as a new VM is, without reports. A running VM keeps the locks it had, and devvm stop or the next launch that finds the VM stopped, such as devvm restart, sets new ones. devvm git-protect on a running VM saves the mode in the VM’s state (the git section’s next).

Each time it locks, devvm records in the VM’s state what it locked and found: the identity of .git (its device and inode, and its birth time where the file system keeps one), every git folder it locked besides .git (those under .git/modules and the submodules’ in the working tree, in one list), and a hash of what the locked files hand over to the project folder. The next check compares with those, so it reports what changed since. The same places first check .git under the mode the VM ran with, so a .git that the VM replaced meanwhile is still named (git_replaced), and then set the new mode, which locks .git as it is then.

A new VM that’s interrupted before its first shell is deleted, and devvm takes its locks off. When devvm rm deletes a VM, devvm also takes its locks off. It unlocks what it would lock now and every git folder the VM’s state records locking, so a submodule whose entry the VM dropped from the index since is unlocked too.

Symlinks

devvm never locks or creates anything through a symlink, because the VM could plant one under .git to make devvm lock a file elsewhere. devvm reports a path that is a symlink, or is under one, instead of locking it (git_not_locked). devvm also checks each lock again once it’s set. If the path moved in the meantime, devvm unlocks it where it landed and reports it (git_lock_raced).

On each launch

Every launch of an existing VM, every export of its agents’ history, and devvm stop check .git again. devvm reports each of these once:

  • A .git that was replaced since devvm locked it (git_replaced). devvm then does nothing else, so check the new .git, and look for the old one, renamed.
  • A repo that appeared in the folder after the VM was made (git_appeared), which devvm then locks.
  • A submodule git folder that appeared, in the working tree or under .git/modules (git_embedded_new), which devvm then locks. devvm compares with the git folders it recorded last time, so devvm git-protect on after a VM was made without protection names none: it locks .git as it is then, as trusted.
  • Hooks in a hooks folder that wasn’t locked, because it wasn’t there to lock or belongs to a new submodule (git_hooks_unlocked).

devvm also reports these, the first two on every launch and the last when they change:

  • A commondir (git_commondir).
  • Linked worktrees whose commondir leads elsewhere (git_worktree_stray).
  • Includes and hook links into the project folder (git_include_inside, git_hook_link_inside), which not covered describes.

What a lock can’t stop

The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, add .git/commondir to point git at another config, or do the same with a linked worktree’s folder in .git/worktrees. When devvm creates the VM, and on each launch, it reports a commondir that’s there, linked worktrees whose commondir leads somewhere else, and paths it couldn’t lock because they’re symlinks. devvm doesn’t repair anything, so check what it names before you run git in the folder. When you don’t trust what runs in the VM, use --clone, which mounts no .git at all.

The VM writes .git/index, because it has to in order to commit, so it can also add a submodule with its own config, which git status on the host reads. A submodule’s core.fsmonitor therefore also runs on the host. devvm names a new submodule on the next launch, but git on the host reads it before that, unless the VM is strict.

devvm’s own git commands on the host run no program that a repo’s config or .git names, a submodule’s included, whatever the VM wrote there. devvm runs each one with these settings, given as GIT_CONFIG_COUNT pairs, which git takes over any config file:

  • core.fsmonitor=false, core.hooksPath=/dev/null and core.alternateRefsCommand=true, so git runs no fsmonitor, no hook from a hooks folder and no command for an alternate object store’s refs.
  • hook.EVENT.enabled=false for every event githooks(5) lists, and hook.NAME.enabled=false for each hook the repo’s config names, so git 2.54 and newer run no hook that a config defines.
  • filter.NAME.clean, smudge and process emptied, and filter.NAME.required=false, for each filter driver the repo’s config names, so git hashes files without running a filter and doesn’t fail on a required one.
  • protocol.allow=never and protocol.ssh.allow=always, so git reaches nothing but ssh, not a path, file://, ext::, git:// or http. A repo’s config could still allow one protocol by its own key, such as protocol.ext.allow=always, which git takes over protocol.allow, so devvm also sets GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL=ssh, which git takes over every protocol setting.
  • maintenance.auto=false and gc.auto=0, so a fetch starts no maintenance or gc.

Its ssh is false, which reaches nothing, in place of a repo’s core.sshCommand (GIT_SSH_COMMAND=false, with GIT_SSH_VARIANT=ssh over a repo’s ssh.variant), unless the command is a --clone VM’s push or fetch, and it fetches nothing lazily (GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1), so a repo that says it’s a partial clone can’t make git rev-list or git status connect anywhere for an object it lacks.

It runs without any GIT_* variable of devvm’s own environment, such as GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE or GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, so a hook or a rebase you run devvm from can’t point it at another repo or config, and it reads your global config from its usual place. It keeps only the absolute folders of PATH, because git looks programs up, ssh among them, from the repo’s folder, and it runs with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. Its git status adds --no-optional-locks, so it writes no index, and --ignore-submodules=all, so it never enters a submodule, whose own config could name filters of its own.

A --clone VM’s push adds --no-verify, --no-recurse-submodules and --no-signed, so no signing program runs, and its fetch adds --no-recurse-submodules and an empty --refmap=, so it updates only the branches its own refspecs name, never those of a remote that the repo’s config names after the clone’s address. Both run git with devvm’s own GIT_SSH_COMMAND, which ignores the host, port and options git passes to ssh. It always connects to the VM’s own address and port, the host’s loopback port that the VM’s backend gives, as the VM’s user with the VM’s own key, and it reads no ssh config (-F none). It checks the host keys devvm pinned for the VM’s current start, with the VM’s own known hosts file and no global one, -o HostKeyAlias= the VM’s name and -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes, and it runs with -o BatchMode=yes, -o ForwardAgent=no and -o ClearAllForwardings=yes. In the VM it runs only git-receive-pack or git-upload-pack, whichever git asks for, on the clone’s path, and it refuses any other command. So no url.*.insteadOf, pushInsteadOf or remote URL in the repo’s config can send the push or the fetch to another host or to another path, and they forward neither your agent nor any port. A repo’s core.sshCommand doesn’t apply, because devvm sets GIT_SSH_COMMAND, and its diff.external, textconv drivers and pager never run, because none of devvm’s commands shows a diff or writes to a terminal.

Before a --clone VM is made, and again before its push, devvm checks that what git reads in the folder is the repo’s own, so the push can’t copy another repo into the VM. The folder’s .git is a folder with no commondir, or it’s the .git file of a linked worktree whose link git made both ways. That .git file names <repo>/.git/worktrees/<name>, that entry’s gitdir file names the folder’s .git back, and its commondir leads to that <repo>/.git, which has no commondir of its own. Neither the git dir nor the common dir has objects/info/alternates, or a packed-refs or reftable that’s a symlink, or anything in objects or refs that’s a symlink, such as a pack folder or a loose object’s folder that leads to another repo’s objects. Then git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir --git-common-dir must name the same two folders. A worktree’s push sends only its branch and that branch’s upstream, when the upstream is one ref, so the repo’s other branches stay on this machine. A branch.<name>.merge that’s a pattern, such as refs/heads/*, would make the upstream push every branch, so devvm then pushes only the branch.

devvm finds the hook and filter names to turn off with one git config before each command, so a VM that keeps swapping the repo’s config could show that git config one config and the command another. Every hook event is turned off by its name as well, which covers config hooks on git that has the event setting, so the gap is a filter that the swap hides, which git status could then run on a file whose stat changed. It needs a VM that writes the repo’s .git, so on macOS, where .git/config is locked, it needs a repo devvm doesn’t lock, such as one nested in a parent folder’s mount.

Two things a repo’s config can still do, and neither runs code. An include.path can make devvm’s git config --get user.name read your name and email from another file in git’s config format, which then go into the VM as its git identity. A config file or included file that is a FIFO makes git, and so devvm, wait until you press Ctrl+C.

item.title: devvm agent save
item.description:
Copy the agents’ settings from this folder’s VM into devvm’s store

Synopsis

Copy the settings of AGENT, claude, codex or opencode, or of every agent this folder’s VM has, from the VM into devvm’s store, so every VM with the agent gets them, never its logins or history. It shows what changed and asks first, so it runs only in a terminal without –no-input, and devvm starts a stopped VM for it.

devvm agent save [AGENT...] [flags]

Examples 

 devvm agent save # show what changed in every agent's settings, then save them
 devvm agent save claude # save only Claude Code's

Options 

 -h, --help help for save
 --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside
 --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm agent save explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm agent: Fill devvm’s store of the agents’ settings and logins that every VM gets

item.title: Images and tools
item.description:
Every VM is a copy of an image. An image is base with your choice of layers on it, and nothing else. A VM also gets the shared tools you chose for it, such as node or Claude Code, which are mounted into it and are never part of an image. This page covers what base and the layers bring, adding layers to a VM, how the shared tools work, what a new VM gets, and how to rebuild, list and delete images. Images and caching explains how devvm builds, pins and caches them, and toolchains and coding agents list the shared tools.

flowchart TD
ubuntu["Ubuntu's cloud image,<br>or a --from image"] --> base["base, with<br>the features you chose"]
base --> docker["docker, a layer<br>on base"]
base -. "a copy" .-> vm1["VM of base,<br>with node"]
docker -. "a copy" .-> vm2["VM of docker,<br>with node and claude"]
tools[("shared tools:<br>node, claude…")] -- "mounted<br>read-only" --> vm1 & vm2

Base

base is the image that every other image is built on. It is Ubuntu 26.04’s cloud image with git, build-essential, ripgrep, jq, sqlite3 and mise added, followed by the optional features you chose, such as oh-my-bash and fzf. Docker comes as a layer of devvm’s, so you choose it when you customize a new VM, or give devvm --layers docker. With --from, base starts from a container image instead of Ubuntu’s (details).

A VM made from base gets 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk unless you give it another size, and on a small machine it gets fewer CPUs and less memory (size and ports).

base drops the server extras that Ubuntu’s cloud image comes with, which are snapd, multipath, ModemManager, udisks, firmware updates, crash reporting, tracing tools, kernel headers, and apt’s background updates and upgrades. That saves 0.9 GB of disk and 100 MB of memory per VM. The everyday tools stay, such as htop, tmux, lsof, strace, tcpdump, rsync and nano.

The first time devvm builds base on this machine, it starts from the newest release of Ubuntu’s cloud image and installs the newest packages from Ubuntu’s archive, or first from a mirror you set. devvm keeps a copy of each package it installed, so building the same base again, such as after devvm images rm base, installs exactly those packages from the copies, with no network for them. devvm rebuild base starts again from the newest image and packages. Your VMs use Ubuntu’s live archive, and base keeps no package lists, so run sudo apt update in a VM before you install a package, and apt upgrade then gets the current updates.

Layers

An image is base with layers on it, named bottom first and joined with +, so foo+bar is bar on foo on base. You can leave base itself out, which makes base+foo the same as foo. An image name never holds shared tools, which aren’t layers, so devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm refuse a shared tool’s name, such as node, and point you to devvm tools.

A layer is a script that bash runs in the image’s VM as the VM’s user, who has sudo. It is either one of devvm’s built-in layers or one of yours, at ~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.sh. A layer’s name is made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starts with a letter or digit, and is neither base, a built-in layer’s name nor a shared tool’s name. devvm refuses any other name in an image, and it refuses a layer whose script is missing. devvm layer new NAME starts a layer of your own (details).

devvm build foo+bar # builds base, foo and foo+bar, unless they're built
devvm rebuild foo # builds foo again, and deletes the old foo and foo+bar

Built-in layers

devvm ships three layers, desktop, docker and nix. You choose them like any other layer, in the list devvm shows for a new VM or as in devvm --layers docker, and you build one with devvm build nix. To give every new VM one, choose it with devvm setup --layers, and to give a VM you have one, run devvm layer add (adding layers to a VM). Their names are reserved, so devvm refuses devvm layer new docker and never reads a desktop.sh, docker.sh or nix.sh of yours. The hosts that each layer needs are in its own allowlist.

desktop

The desktop layer installs an Xfce desktop with TigerVNC’s server, which devvm desktop opens in Screen Sharing, and adds about 370 MB to the image. Its packages come from the distribution’s archive as it is when the layer builds, which on a base made --from alpine means Alpine’s own packages, and they aren’t pinned. It needs no hosts of its own on the allowlist tier, and a VM without the layer has no desktop.

docker

The docker layer installs Docker’s engine, CLI, BuildKit and Compose from Docker’s apt repository, adds the VM’s user to the docker group, and starts the daemon at each boot. On a base made --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s own packages instead. A VM without the layer has no Docker. A VM with the layer can be on any network tier like any other, because its containers’ connections go through the VM’s network, which devvm confines from outside the VM (network tiers).

nix

The nix layer installs Nix with flakes and the nix command turned on, and direnv with nix-direnv, so a project’s flake.nix, shell.nix or devenv.nix can supply its toolchain. Each VM has a Nix store and daemon of its own, which no other VM and nothing on this machine shares. VMs share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache through a cache on this machine that only devvm fills. Nix projects explains that cache, and how a flake’s dev shell and the shared tools work together.

The nix layer works on a base from Ubuntu, Debian or Alpine. On a base made --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s xz package, which isn’t pinned, and runs Nix’s daemon as an OpenRC service.

Adding layers to a VM

A VM keeps the layers devvm made it with, because a layer’s script changes the VM’s disk. devvm layer add LAYER... gives a VM more layers by making it again. devvm builds an image with the new layers on top of the VM’s own, in the order you give them, and gives the VM a new disk, copied from that image. A VM of docker with desktop added is made again from docker+desktop, so the images it already uses stay as they are. devvm names the layers the VM has already and leaves them where they are, and when the VM has all of them, devvm says so and changes nothing.

devvm layer add desktop # make this folder's VM again with the desktop layer on top
devvm layer add docker nix # docker, then nix on top of it
devvm layer add desktop --force # the same without asking, as a script must

Everything on the VM’s disk that devvm doesn’t keep is lost, so in a terminal devvm names the image and asks first, with no as the default. Without a terminal, it refuses unless you give --force. When the VM has a coding agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history, as devvm rm does, unless you give --no-export (history). In a subfolder of a folder with a VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to make that folder’s VM again, and refuses without one.

devvm refuses before it changes anything when a name isn’t a layer, or is a shared tool’s name, which devvm tools add adds instead. It also refuses when the VM’s backend can’t run one of the layers, when the VM’s creation didn’t finish, and for a --clone VM, whose clone of the repo is on its disk. To give a --clone VM more layers, run devvm clone off, which offers to fetch the clone’s work first, then devvm layer add and devvm clone on (switching a VM that exists).

devvm then works in this order:

  1. It builds the new image, so a build that fails leaves the VM as it was.
  2. It exports the agents’ history and saves the VM’s home folder on this machine.
  3. It stops the VM and sets its old disk aside under another name.
  4. It makes the VM again from the new image, with the same name and settings, and starts it.
  5. It copies the home folder onto the new disk and deletes the old disk, then opens a shell in the VM.

Until the new VM has started with its home folder, a step that fails, or Ctrl+C, deletes the new disk and puts the old one back as it was. While one devvm makes a VM again, another devvm that would make the same VM again refuses, and so does devvm in its folder, so wait for the first to finish. While devvm makes the VM again, the old disk, the new one and the saved home folder take room on this machine at the same time, and devvm checks for free space before it starts.

What a VM made again keeps

devvm keeps the project folder, which is on this machine, and everything it keeps for the VM: its name, its shared tools, its size, its ports, its network tier and allowlist, its secrets’ bindings, its SSH agent choice and its .git protection. It also keeps the VM’s links, group and published ports, its desktop’s password and port, and what its devcontainer.json gave it. The commands in its devcontainer.json that run once, such as postCreateCommand, run again on the new disk. The VM gets new SSH host keys, which devvm pins as it does for any new VM, and it keeps its identity, so links to it still reach it.

devvm keeps the VM’s home folder too. It reads the folder as the VM’s user before it stops the VM, and copies it onto the new disk before devvm’s own setup runs there. What other shells in the VM write after devvm reads the folder is lost, so close them first. A file that the new image puts in your home itself, such as ~/.bashrc, stays the image’s, so put shell settings of your own in a file of yours in ~/.bashrc.d. devvm leaves out what the new VM gets from devvm itself: ~/.config/devvm, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, the agents’ logins, and the agents’ folders and files that devvm links or copies from this machine. It leaves out ~/.cache too. devvm keeps only files, folders and symlinks, without setuid bits, and nothing from a filesystem mounted inside your home. --clean-home gives the VM the new image’s home folder instead.

Everything else on the VM’s disk is lost: the packages you installed with apt, programs installed outside your home, Docker’s images, containers and volumes, the Nix store, and the processes that ran in it. When saving the home folder fails, devvm keeps the VM as it was, and --clean-home goes ahead without it.

A remake that stops halfway

If devvm itself is killed while it makes a VM again, such as when this machine loses power, the VM’s state records the remake. The next devvm, devvm layer add, devvm layer rm, devvm update, devvm clone on or devvm clone off in the folder finishes it without asking. When the new VM already has its home folder, devvm only deletes the old disk. When the old disk is still set aside otherwise, devvm puts it back and makes the VM again from the start, and when it’s gone, devvm makes the new VM with the home folder it saved. Until then, other commands on the VM refuse and name devvm, and devvm rm deletes the VM together with its old disk.

Taking layers out of a VM

devvm layer rm LAYER... takes layers out of a VM by making it again, in the same way that devvm layer add puts them in. devvm builds an image of the VM’s other layers, in the order they had, and gives the VM a new disk, copied from that image. A VM of docker+nix+desktop without nix is made again from docker+desktop, and a VM without any of its layers is made again from base. devvm names the layers that the VM doesn’t have and leaves them out, and when the VM has none of them, devvm says so and changes nothing.

devvm layer rm desktop # make this folder's VM again without the desktop layer
devvm layer rm docker nix # take out docker and nix
devvm layer rm desktop --force # the same without asking, as a script must

The VM keeps what a VM made again keeps, its home folder included, and everything else on its disk is lost, such as what the layers you took out installed and Docker’s images. So devvm asks first in a terminal, with no as the default, and refuses without one unless you give --force. It takes the same flags as devvm layer add, works in the same steps and refuses the same VMs, before it changes anything: a --clone VM, one whose creation didn’t finish, and one whose backend can’t run the layers left. It also refuses base, a shared tool’s name, which devvm tools rm takes out instead, and a name that isn’t a layer. You can still take out a layer of yours whose script you deleted, and that’s the one way to make such a VM again with its home folder and settings, because devvm layer add and devvm update need every layer’s script to build the VM’s image.

Shared tools

The toolchains and coding agents are shared tools, not image layers. A VM of any image can have them, in any mix, such as node and Claude Code on base, or go and Codex on foo. A VM’s state lists its shared tools apart from its image. Toolchains lists the toolchains, with what each brings, and supported agents lists claude, codex and opencode.

devvm builds each tool version once and mounts it read-only into every VM that has it, so any mix of tools works without building anything new, and ten VMs with node share one copy of it. The builds are in ~/.local/share/devvm/tools. Each C library gets a build of its own, so when an Alpine VM and an Ubuntu VM both have node 24, devvm images lists two builds of that version (what devvm keeps). An Alpine VM’s builds are only ever shared with VMs on the same container image, as shared tools and glibc explains. mise runs the tools:

  • They work as usual. Each toolchain’s commands, such as npm i -g (into ~/.npm-global) or go install (into ~/go/bin), work from any shell, including bash -c from agents and from editors over SSH. Global installs go into your home, as each toolchain’s section says.
  • A project’s own version files win. .nvmrc, .node-version, .python-version, rust-toolchain.toml, the toolchain line in go.mod and the SDK version in global.json pick their version, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used. mise also reads a mise.toml in the project folder, and devvm trusts it without asking, because the folder is yours.
  • They’re read-only. A VM can’t change the shared tools, even as root. The tools can’t update themselves, and rustup component add can’t change the shared toolchain.
  • They’re mounted, or the launch stops. When one of a VM’s tools is missing or the VM can’t mount it, devvm stops the launch and names the tool, and the VM never downloads its own copy in its place (a shared tool doesn’t mount). Only the versions that a project’s own version files pick install into the VM.

devvm doesn’t pin the tools’ versions, because agents like Claude Code release several times a week. It follows the newest release of each tool, with Node 24 for node and opencode 2 for opencode. The first time a tool is needed, devvm looks up its newest release, which needs this machine to be online once. When it makes a new VM, devvm also checks for newer releases if its last check was more than a day ago, and DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK=1 turns that check off.

A new VM gets the tools chosen for it when devvm makes it, and keeps those versions. devvm tools shows them, and in a terminal lets you choose them. devvm tools add, devvm tools rm and devvm tools update change them too, as does the first step of devvm update, and changing them never changes the VM’s disk (adding and removing tools).

What a new VM gets 

flowchart TD
run["devvm in a folder<br>without a VM"] --> defaults["the defaults: the folder's toolchains,<br>devvm setup's agents and layers"]
defaults --> flags["each flag given replaces its part:<br>--tools, --agents, --layers, --network, --cpus, --memory"]
flags --> summary["the summary says what the VM gets"]
summary --> term{{"a terminal, without --no-input,<br>and something left to choose?"}}
term -- "no" --> copy
term -- "yes" --> ask{{"Customize it? [y/N]"}}
ask -- "Enter" --> copy
ask -- "y" --> pick["the list, then the tier,<br>then the CPUs, memory and disk"] --> copy
copy["its image built if it isn't,<br>and the VM is a copy of it,<br>with its shared tools mounted"]

Before devvm makes a new VM, it shows a summary of what the VM gets. The summary names each toolchain, coding agent and layer with why the VM gets it, such as for package.json, from devvm setup or from --tools, and then the VM’s size, its network tier, its ports and the folder’s devcontainer.json, when there is one:

==> This folder's new VM, devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c, gets:
 toolchain node, for package.json
 agent claude, from devvm setup
 layers: none
 size: 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk
 network tier: allowlist
 ports: all
 devcontainer.json: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, which devvm --no-devcontainer skips
Customize it? [y/N]

In a terminal, devvm then asks whether to customize the VM, with no as the default, so confirming makes it as shown. When you customize it, devvm shows the three parts in one list under three headings, Toolchains, Coding agents and Layers, with what the summary showed already chosen (choosing in a list). The Layers heading says that a layer is extra software built into the VM’s image:

Choose what devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c gets. Use up and down to move, space to toggle and enter to confirm.
Toolchains
> [x] node for package.json
 [ ] python
 [ ] rust
 [ ] go
Coding agents, which you start in the VM's shell
 [x] claude from devvm setup
 [ ] codex
 [ ] opencode
Layers: extra software built into the VM's image, such as docker, nix or desktop
 [ ] desktop an Xfce desktop, which devvm desktop opens
 [ ] docker Docker's engine, CLI, BuildKit and Compose
 [ ] nix Nix, direnv and nix-direnv

Then devvm lists the four network tiers, each with what it reaches, unless you gave --network, and you choose one, starting from the tier the summary showed: allowlist, or the tier you saved for new VMs with devvm network -g (choosing a tier). Next, unless you gave --ports, devvm lists the ports the VM can forward: every port, none, which you add later with devvm ports add, or the ports you type, which devvm checks as --ports checks them and asks for again when they aren’t a list. The list starts on what the summary showed, every port unless config.toml or devvm ports -g set another (size and ports), and the ports you choose are this VM’s alone. Last, it asks for the VM’s CPUs, memory and disk, starting from the summary’s, and confirming keeps each one. Each question is skipped when you gave its flag, --cpus, --memory or --disk. Before the disk’s question, devvm says that the disk can grow later with devvm size --disk but never shrinks, and that it takes up only the space the VM writes. A disk smaller than the image’s, 100 GiB for base, is refused as --disk refuses it, and devvm asks again, as it does for a value that isn’t a size. The size you type is this VM’s alone, and devvm saves it for no other VM.

Each part has a default:

  • Toolchains: the ones the folder’s files call for, each naming its file in the summary and the list, such as package.json.
  • Coding agents: the ones you chose with devvm setup, which the summary and the list say. The summary says from config.toml for the ones that config.toml sets. Until you choose some, there are none.
  • Layers: the ones you chose with devvm setup, bottom first, which the summary and the list say in the same way. Until you choose some, there are none. A layer that a project file calls for, such as nix for a flake.nix, names the file in its row of the list but isn’t chosen unless devvm setup chose it, so you choose it when you want it.

Three flags choose the parts on the command line. --tools takes the toolchains, as in --tools node,python, --agents takes the coding agents, as in --agents claude,codex, and --layers takes the layers bottom first, as in --layers docker,mine. Each is the exact list for its part and replaces that part’s default, and none chooses none of it, as in --agents none. A part whose flag you leave out takes its default. devvm checks each name before it does anything. For a name that belongs to another part, such as --tools claude, it names the flag that takes it, and for a name it doesn’t know, it suggests the closest one.

A part, tier or size that a flag gives is taken as given, and the summary says so. devvm still asks whether to customize the VM while anything is left to choose, because a flag answers only its own part. When you customize it, the list shows a part that a flag gave greyed out, and the cursor skips it. devvm skips the list when --tools, --agents and --layers give all three parts, skips the tier when you give --network or saved a tier, skips the ports when you give --ports, and skips the CPUs, the memory or the disk when you give --cpus, --memory or --disk. devvm doesn’t ask at all when the flags give every part, the ports, the CPUs, the memory and the disk, and the tier is given or saved. It doesn’t ask about the tier on a backend whose VMs can only be open, either.

Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm asks nothing and doesn’t fail. The VM gets what the summary shows, and the summary ends with the flags that choose others.

devvm looks at the folder’s top level for the files that call for a toolchain, in this order:

Toolchain Files
node package.json, bun.lock, bun.lockb
python pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, uv.lock, setup.py, Pipfile
rust Cargo.toml
go go.mod

If more than one toolchain matches, the VM gets them all, so package.json and pyproject.toml give node and python. A Nix project’s files call for the nix layer, whose row names them. Those files are flake.nix, shell.nix and devenv.nix, and a default.nix that makes a shell with mkShell. In a folder with none of these files, the default is no toolchains, so a VM made without a terminal or flags gets devvm setup’s layers and agents.

A folder’s devcontainer.json adds what its features map to, such as toolchains or the docker layer, to the defaults, each naming the file in the summary and the list (devcontainer.json). Its layers go on top of devvm setup’s.

The VM’s image is base with its layers, in the order you give them, bottom first, so --layers docker,mine makes the image docker+mine. When you check layers in the list, devvm setup’s stay in their order at the bottom, and the ones you add go on top in the list’s order. Its shared tools are a list of their own, the toolchains first, then the agents.

If the image isn’t built yet, devvm builds it first, then the shared tools the share lacks, and the VM is a copy of the image with its shared tools mounted. A VM keeps the image and tools it was made from, and the options for a new VM change nothing on a VM that exists, which ignores them with a warning. The warning names the command that changes the same on that VM, such as devvm tools, which changes its shared tools, for --tools, devvm layer add, which adds layers, for --layers, and devvm size for --cpus, and for --from and --no-devcontainer it names none. Only devvm takes these options, and another command given one fails as it does for any flag it doesn’t know (flags and values).

Choosing in a list

devvm’s lists work the same way everywhere: the new VM’s list, its network tiers and ports, devvm tools, and base’s features in devvm setup. Up and down, or k and j, move. In a list where you choose several, such as the toolchains, coding agents and layers, space chooses or unchooses the row under the cursor. In a list where you choose one, such as the network tiers, moving chooses it. Enter confirms. A row that’s greyed out, such as a part a flag gave or a VM’s layers in devvm tools, can’t change, and the cursor skips it. At a question with a value in brackets, such as a size, Enter keeps that value.

Rebuilding

When you edit a layer’s script, devvm builds that layer again the next time it’s used, together with every layer built on it, and it reuses the layers below. A new choice of base’s features rebuilds base and everything on it in the same way.

devvm rebuild IMAGE builds an image again from its parent as the parent is now, where IMAGE is base or a stack of layers, such as docker or foo+bar. That’s how you get the newest packages that a script installs without a pin. On Lima, devvm rebuild base also starts base again from the newest release of Ubuntu’s cloud image, which devvm otherwise picks only the first time it builds base on this machine. devvm also builds the images on it again, on the new image, the next time they’re needed. When there are such images, devvm lists them first and, in a terminal, asks before it goes on. After the build, devvm deletes the old images that no VM uses.

Shared tools aren’t images, so devvm rebuild refuses a shared tool’s name, and devvm update and devvm tools update get their newer versions. Rebuilding explains how devvm tells which images to build again.

Outdated VMs

A VM keeps the image it was made from. When that image, or one it’s built on, changes after an edited script, another choice of base’s features or a rebuild, the VM is outdated. devvm then warns on each launch, names the images that changed and devvm update, and leaves the VM as it is.

devvm update brings this folder’s VM up to date in two steps. First it moves the VM to the newest shared tools, as devvm tools update does, and that needs no question, because the shared tools aren’t part of the image and nothing on the VM’s disk changes (adding and removing tools). Then, when the VM is outdated, devvm makes it again from its own image as it builds now, with the same layers, in the same way that devvm layer add makes a VM again with more layers. devvm builds the image first, then gives the VM a new disk copied from it, and keeps its home folder, the project folder and its settings (what a VM made again keeps). Everything else on its disk is lost, such as the packages you installed with apt and Docker’s images, so in a terminal devvm names the images that changed and asks first, with no as the default. When the folder’s devcontainer.json changed since devvm made the VM, or is gone, or has appeared, devvm also makes the VM again, after asking, as the file says now (updating a VM from the file).

devvm update # move the VM to the newest shared tools, and to its image's new build after asking
devvm update --force # the same without asking, as a script must
devvm update --clean-home # the same, with the new image's home folder

When only the shared tools are newer, devvm moves the VM to them and opens a shell in it without asking, because newer tools don’t need the VM made again. When you answer no, devvm keeps the VM with any newer shared tools it moved to, and opens a shell in it if there were some. Without a terminal, devvm refuses an outdated VM unless you give --force, and it refuses before it changes anything, the VM’s shared tools included.

When the VM has the newest shared tools and nothing it was made from has changed, devvm says that the VM is current and changes nothing. To make a current VM again with the newest packages that a script installs without a pin, run devvm rebuild on its image first, which makes the VM outdated, then devvm update (rebuilding). devvm update takes the same flags as devvm layer add, and it refuses the same VMs, before it changes anything: a --clone VM, one whose creation didn’t finish, and one whose backend can’t run its layers. It exports the agents’ history first unless you give --no-export, and --clean-home gives the VM the new image’s home folder instead of its own. In a subfolder of a folder with a VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to make that folder’s VM again, and refuses without one. The steps, and what happens when one fails, are those of adding layers to a VM.

For a VM made with --from, devvm tells whether the VM is outdated from the container image’s digest that it last recorded, without looking anything up. When devvm makes the VM again, the build looks up the digest as every build does, so a tag that has moved since gives the VM the container image’s newer version too, and a pinned digest stays as it is (--from).

devvm tools update moves the VM to newer shared tools alone, and it never makes the VM again, even when the VM is outdated (adding and removing tools).

Listing images

devvm images prints two tables, each with a header, and it shows what a row lacks as -. The first table lists the images by name, with unfinished builds last:

Column
IMAGE its name, such as base or foo+bar
FROM what its base started from: the --from image, or Ubuntu’s cloud image with its release’s date, ubuntu 26.04 (20261001)
DIGEST the first 12 hex digits of that image’s SHA-256
KEY its key, which devvm images rm also takes
STATE current, stale when what it’s built from has changed since it was built, unfinished for a build that didn’t finish, or building while another devvm builds it
SIZE the disk it takes, in powers of 1024 (2.1G). On macOS an image is a clone of its parent’s disk, and the blocks they share count for both

The second table lists the shared tools that devvm has built, by the name you choose them by, such as node for node, pnpm and bun. The toolchains come first, then the agents, with each tool’s versions newest first:

Column
NAME a toolchain’s name, such as node, or an agent’s, such as claude
TOOL, VERSION the tool and its version
LIBC the C library (gnu, or musl for an Alpine base) that this build is for, because each gets a build of its own, or - when devvm can’t tell
SIZE the disk it takes
VMS how many VMs have it
STATE current for the version new VMs get, in use for another version a VM has, unused for neither, not built for the current version of a tool devvm has other versions of, and not installed when devvm has no version of it

After the tables, devvm says on stderr how many images are stale or unfinished and how much disk the unused tools take, when there are any. It ends with the disk that the images and shared tools take together, and when the shared Nix cache holds anything, the disk it takes of its cap. devvm space shows the rest of what devvm keeps (what devvm keeps).

devvm images –json

devvm images --json prints the same as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and devvm still says the same on stderr. images and tools have the tables’ columns as fields, with sizes in bytes, and each also names the backend that has it or built it, lima. An image’s digest is the full SHA-256 of what its base started from, and sized says whether devvm knows its size. A tool image’s built says whether devvm has built it, and only a built one has backend and libc. A value an image lacks, such as an unfinished build’s name, is "". total is the disk the images and shared tools take together, unused_tools is the part the unused tool images take, and nix_cache has the shared Nix cache’s files, the disk they take and its cap.

{
 "version": 1,
 "images": [
 {
 "name": "base",
 "from": "ubuntu 26.04 (20261001)",
 "digest": "sha256:8eb876c2ccc4b6ff89e4a65d511815923b285e04503ba465809bf587f763da24",
 "key": "7a76021c46ef",
 "state": "current",
 "size": 2254857830,
 "sized": true,
 "backend": "lima"
 }
 ],
 "tools": [
 {
 "name": "node",
 "tool": "node",
 "version": "24.11.0",
 "built": true,
 "backend": "lima",
 "libc": "gnu",
 "size": 125829120,
 "vms": 1,
 "state": "current"
 }
 ],
 "total": 2380686950,
 "unused_tools": 0,
 "nix_cache": {
 "files": 0,
 "size": 0,
 "cap": 10737418240
 }
}

Deleting images

devvm images rm IMAGE|KEY... deletes images. You name each one by its name or by the key that devvm images shows:
