  • A name means its image as it is now, on base from --from when you give it. A stale or unfinished image has only its key.
  • Each image must be built, or devvm deletes nothing. Shared tools aren’t images, so devvm refuses a name that has one, such as node+foo, and devvm gc deletes the shared tools no VM has.
  • devvm also deletes nothing while another devvm is building one of the images, so run the command again once that build ends. devvm gc and devvm rebuild leave such an image alone too.
  • A deleted image is built again the next time it’s needed. VMs made from it keep working, because on macOS they’re clones of its disk. On Linux hosts, devvm refuses to delete an image whose disk VMs are overlays of, and names those VMs.

Cleaning up

devvm gc deletes four things. The first is what devvm images lists as stale or unfinished. The second is the shared tools it lists as unused. The third is the older versions of the mise that devvm runs on this machine to look up the tools’ versions, which an upgrade of devvm leaves behind, except one that changed in the last hour, because another devvm may be downloading it. The fourth is the shared Nix cache’s least recently used files, while it takes more than its cap, the nix-cache.size retention setting, which is 10 GiB when it’s off. devvm’s mise and the shared Nix cache are both in cache/ in devvm’s data folder, which holds only what devvm makes again when it needs it, so you can also delete that folder yourself at any time. gc lists them all first and, in a terminal, asks. Without a terminal, it deletes nothing unless you give --force, which deletes without asking, in a terminal too.

  • devvm gc --tool-images also deletes the current shared tools that no VM has, such as a toolchain you tried once, for every C library. devvm gc --tool-images node claude deletes only those tools’ builds, by the names you choose them by, so node also covers pnpm and bun. A tool that a VM’s state lists stays, including a stopped VM’s, and a tool that no VM has goes however recently it was built. While devvm is making a VM, or giving one new shared tools through devvm tools add or devvm tools update, that VM may not list the tools it picked yet, so gc keeps every current shared tool that no VM has, names them, and deletes the rest of what it would. Run it again once that’s done. A tool that devvm is still building never reaches gc, because gc waits for the build to finish before it lists anything. A VM that has a deleted tool builds it again when it needs it.
  • The devvm making a VM holds a lock from before it picks the VM’s tools until the VM’s state lists them, and the system lets go of that lock as soon as that devvm ends, so one that crashed or that you killed never leaves gc keeping tools. A devvm that starts to make a VM while devvm gc --tool-images runs, or while retention deletes shared tools, waits for it to finish and says it’s waiting. In a terminal, gc holds that lock while it asks you, so answer it first.
  • When a shared tool that a new VM’s state lists is gone before the VM’s first shell, for example because you deleted it by hand, the VM’s setup can’t mount it. devvm then names the tools it couldn’t mount and stops, and the VM stays. Run devvm tools update in the folder, which builds the missing tools again and opens the VM.
  • devvm gc --history also deletes the exports of agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm saved, which are the only copy of a deleted VM’s history, and --older-than DURATION keeps those newer than that duration, such as 12h, 30d or 2w. gc never deletes exports without --history.
  • devvm gc --nix-cache also deletes the rest of the shared Nix cache. VMs download its packages again when they need them.
  • devvm gc --orphans also deletes what devvm keeps for VMs that their backend no longer has, such as one you deleted with limactl delete instead of devvm rm, and with it the hold their state has on their shared tools (leftovers).
  • devvm gc --caches then frees devvm’s share of Lima’s own caches, such as its downloads of Ubuntu’s cloud image, after asking, or without asking with --force, which it needs without a terminal (Lima’s caches).
  • devvm gc --retention then applies the retention settings at once, which devvm otherwise applies at most once a day. They’re all off until you set them.
  • When Lima can’t list its images while one of your VMs uses it, for example because Lima isn’t installed, gc warns and leaves Lima’s images, shared tools, VM leftovers and caches alone. It also leaves the shared tools whose record doesn’t name the backend that built them, because they may be Lima’s. gc still succeeds, so run devvm doctor to see what’s wrong with Lima, then run gc again once it answers. devvm images fails instead, because it lists all the images or none.
  • gc never deletes VMs, and it keeps current images, which devvm images rm deletes (deleting images). Without --tool-images it keeps the current shared tools. It always keeps every shared tool that any VM has, including a stopped VM’s and that of a VM deleted outside devvm whose state is left, until --orphans deletes that state.
  • On Linux hosts, a stale image whose disk VMs are overlays of stays, and devvm says which VMs use it.
  • After an Alpine VM is gone, the shared tools built for Alpine are unused, unless you give gc that --from.

Images and caching has the details of what counts as current and unused. To see what gc would free before you run it, and what takes the rest of the space, run devvm space (what devvm keeps).

item.title: Customizing images
item.description:
You customize images with your own layers, which add what a project needs, and by choosing base’s features, which are devvm’s optional extras that every VM gets. Your layers live in ~/.config/devvm ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devvm), not next to devvm’s binary, so upgrading devvm keeps them. To give every new VM something of your own, write it as a layer and make it one of the layers new VMs get (extras of your own).

Your own layers 

devvm layer new mailpit # writes ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh and mailpit.policy
$EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh
devvm --layers mailpit # a new VM with your layer; or devvm build mailpit

When you customize a new VM, its list also shows your layers under Layers, so you can choose mailpit there instead of giving --layers (what a new VM gets). To give every new VM your layer, choose it with devvm setup --layers mailpit, or add it to the layers key in config.toml (layers for new VMs). When you delete a layer’s script that you chose there, new VMs are made without it, and devvm warns you.

A layer is a script, ~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.sh, that bash runs once as the VM’s user, who has sudo, in an image on top of its parent. devvm layer new NAME writes a starter script, and also NAME.policy next to it unless that file exists. It refuses to overwrite a script that exists.

  • Names are made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and start with a letter or digit. A name can’t be base, a built-in layer’s name (desktop, docker or nix) or a shared tool’s name (node, claude and so on). A command’s name, such as log, is fine, because devvm takes layers only through --layers, the list and image names.
  • Built-in layers go in the same image names as yours, bottom first, as in devvm --layers docker,mailpit, which makes the image docker+mailpit.
  • Put interactive shell setup in ~/.bashrc.d/<name>.sh, which every VM’s ~/.bashrc reads, and PATH changes in ~/.profile.
  • Download files with devvm-fetch URL SHA256 OUT, which base installs. It fails when the file’s checksum doesn’t match.
  • NAME.policy lists the hosts that VMs with the layer can reach on the allowlist tier, one rule per line.
  • Editing the script rebuilds its image, and the ones built on it, the next time they’re used (rebuilding).
  • A layer’s script changes the VM’s disk, so devvm layer add mailpit gives a VM you have the layer by making the VM again, keeping its home folder and settings (adding layers to a VM), and devvm layer rm mailpit takes it out again in the same way (taking layers out of a VM).

To edit layers with an agent in a VM, keep them in a repo of their own and copy them in, because devvm refuses a VM for a folder inside ~/.config/devvm (details).

Example: mailpit

This layer installs Mailpit, which catches the emails your app sends while you develop it, and starts it with the VM. Point your app’s SMTP settings at localhost:1025, and read the emails at localhost:8025 in your browser, because devvm forwards both ports to your machine. Put these lines in ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh, below the starter’s set -euo pipefail:

mailpit_version=1.32.0
mailpit_sha256_amd64=4b5993c978e8604c70d43927e2ad103b311bba3b1822fa0cf1d4ee4ec890a93c
mailpit_sha256_arm64=e1e45d1dc72bd497fb262a1e4100178eee057c42c5fc36d143eb8621769e1137

case "$(uname -m)" in
 x86_64) arch=amd64 sha256=$mailpit_sha256_amd64 ;;
 aarch64) arch=arm64 sha256=$mailpit_sha256_arm64 ;;
 *) echo "mailpit: no build for $(uname -m)" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
devvm-fetch "https://github.com/axllent/mailpit/releases/download/v$mailpit_version/mailpit-linux-$arch.tar.gz" \
 "$sha256" /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz
sudo tar -xzf /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz -C /usr/local/bin mailpit
rm /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz

printf '%s\n' '[Unit]' 'Description=Mailpit' '[Service]' 'ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/mailpit' \
 'DynamicUser=yes' '[Install]' 'WantedBy=multi-user.target' |
 sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/mailpit.service >/dev/null
sudo systemctl enable --now mailpit

The version and each download’s SHA-256 sit at the top, so devvm-fetch refuses a download that doesn’t match. To update Mailpit, change all three and rebuild the image. The downloads come from GitHub’s releases, which base’s allowlist has, so mailpit.policy can stay empty. On a base made --from an Alpine image, start it with OpenRC (rc-update, rc-service) instead of systemd.

Base image features

Features are optional extras that devvm builds into base after base’s own setup, so every VM has them.

Feature What it adds
omb oh-my-bash: a themed prompt, completions and aliases, with auto-update off
fzf fuzzy Ctrl-R history and Ctrl-T file search
cli-tools bat, fd, eza, zoxide (z), btop, tree, tldr

The desktop that devvm desktop opens isn’t a feature but a built-in layer, desktop, so only the VMs you choose it for get it.

Choosing features

On its first run, devvm asks which features base gets, after the size and coding agents that new VMs get and before it shows what the folder’s new VM gets. devvm build and devvm rebuild ask too, until the features are chosen. The list starts with every feature chosen, and you choose in it as in any of devvm’s lists. Without a terminal, devvm chooses every feature. devvm prints the choice and saves it, in the order the features run. When features in config.toml chooses them, devvm doesn’t ask.

To change the choice:

devvm setup # asks again, starting from the current choice
devvm setup --features fzf,omb # without asking
devvm setup --features none # without asking, and base gets no features

In a terminal, devvm setup asks for the features among its other questions, which devvm setup lists in order. --features asks for none of the others. Without a terminal, devvm setup keeps the choice. devvm refuses a name that isn’t a feature, and an empty --features '', and then nothing changes. You can also choose them by hand with features in config.toml, such as features = ["fzf", "omb"], which wins over what devvm setup saved, and then devvm setup --features refuses to change them. features = [] chooses none, and devvm skips a name without a script, with a warning.

A new choice makes base and the images built on it rebuild the next time they’re used, and devvm setup says so. The old images are then stale, and devvm gc deletes them.

Extras of your own

Base’s features are the ones in the table above, and devvm ships all of them. To give every new VM an extra of your own, such as your shell setup or a tool you always use, write it as a layer of your own and choose it as one of the layers new VMs get:

devvm layer new dotfiles # writes ~/.config/devvm/layers/dotfiles.sh
$EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/dotfiles.sh
devvm setup --layers dotfiles # every new VM gets it

A new VM’s summary then shows dotfiles, and when you customize the VM, its list shows dotfiles under Layers, already chosen because devvm setup chose it, so you can leave it out of that VM (layers for new VMs). A layer is an image built on top of base, so the images that have it are named with it, such as dotfiles or docker+dotfiles, and editing its script rebuilds only those images, never base.

item.title: devvm build
item.description:
Build an image and the images under it, unless they’re built

Synopsis

Build an image and the images under it, unless they’re built. IMAGE is base, or layers joined with + bottom first, so foo+bar is bar on foo on base. An image holds no shared tools: a VM gets those when devvm makes it, or with devvm tools.

devvm build IMAGE [flags]

Examples 

 devvm build docker # build base and the docker layer on it
 devvm build foo+bar # build base, foo and foo+bar

Options 

 --from IMAGE the container IMAGE base starts from, such as node:24, instead of Ubuntu's cloud image (default: $DEVVM_FROM)
 -h, --help help for build

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm build explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm: Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first

item.title: Security model
item.description:
devvm treats everything in a VM as untrusted, including a coding agent with root, because the VM’s user has passwordless sudo. This page explains how devvm keeps that code away from the rest of your machine. Staying safe lists what a VM can reach and the habits that keep you safe, and Attack vectors goes through common attacks one by one and lists what devvm leaves open.

All of it rests on the VM’s boundary.

What devvm protects, and how

Only the project folder

A VM mounts its project folder read-write at the same path. The only other things it mounts from the host are the shared tools and its agents’ config folders, both read-only, so it never mounts your home folder, which Lima’s own templates do. A --clone VM doesn’t mount the project folder either. It has its own clone, and its work reaches the repo only when you fetch it. When you run devvm in a subfolder and it uses the project folder’s VM, that VM mounts nothing more than it already did (a subfolder’s VM).

devvm refuses a project folder that would hand the VM more than the project:

  • A folder that is or holds your home folder, devvm’s settings (~/.config/devvm), its state (~/.local/share/devvm, which holds its binaries and other VMs’ disks) or its Lima home (unsafe_folder).
  • A folder inside devvm’s own folders (unsafe_folder_inside). A VM in ~/.config/devvm/layers could rewrite the scripts that every image build runs, and a VM in devvm’s data folder could rewrite the files devvm runs on the host.

--unsafe-folder mounts such a folder anyway, and devvm says so. A --clone VM mounts nothing, so devvm doesn’t refuse its folder.

One VM per folder

A VM belongs to the folder it was made for, which devvm knows by its path and by the folder itself: its device and inode, and its birth time where the file system keeps one. When you delete a folder and make it again at the same path, or clone another repo where an old one was, devvm refuses to give the new folder the old folder’s VM, so the new folder never quietly gets what’s in the old VM’s disk. devvm rm deletes the old VM and devvm adopt gives it to the new folder, and each does so only after you confirm (a folder made again). When you move or rename the folder, the folder at its new path is the same folder, so devvm offers it the VM, and moves the VM only after you confirm (a moved or renamed folder). It never offers a VM to a copy, to a folder another user owns, or on a file system that may give a new folder the inode number of a deleted one, so a VM never moves to a folder that only looks like its own.

A project’s devcontainer.json

A project’s devcontainer.json belongs to the project, and so to the VM, which can rewrite it for the folder’s next VM, or for the VM itself when you run devvm update. devvm reads it only when it makes a VM, new or again, and uses only what it can do inside the VM. Nothing in it runs on this machine, so initializeCommand never runs. Nothing in it reaches this machine’s files, because devvm doesn’t follow a link out of the folder, or this machine’s environment, because devvm refuses ${localEnv:…} before it makes anything. It can’t add a mount or change the VM’s network tier or other confinement.

Its commands run in the VM as the VM’s user, confined like anything else in it. Its features can only be devvm’s own layers, so devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script, and it refuses docker-outside-of-docker. devvm uses its image only when the image’s registry gives it to anyone who asks anonymously, so it never uses a container image that only your Docker has or that only your registry login reaches. It refuses a registry named localhost or by an address that isn’t the internet’s, and its lookup connects only to the internet’s addresses, so it never uses an image on this machine or its network, except through a company proxy, which resolves the registry’s name itself (attack vectors).

An existing VM never changes when the file does, until you run devvm update, which says it reads the file again and asks before it makes the VM again. The file read again is held to the same refusals as a new VM’s, and it can’t replace a base you chose with --from, bring back a port you took out with devvm ports rm, or change its network tier, size, SSH agent or .git protection, which devvm keeps.

Its forwardPorts are added to the VM’s ports, as devvm ports add adds them, even beyond a list you narrowed, both when devvm makes the VM and when devvm update reads the file again. They go through the one port forwarder, so they listen on this machine’s loopback alone (127.0.0.1 and ::1), never take a port that a program on this machine has, and never take a port another VM forwards (port forwarding). What a cloned repo’s file opens is so only what devvm ports add could open, but it reaches whatever on this machine connects to those ports, a browser’s pages included (attack vectors).

Read-only and confined builds

devvm builds images with nothing from the host mounted, and it confines their builds so that they reach the internet but not your machine’s own services (details). Credentials never go into images.

A tool build writes into a folder of its own and never into the shared tools, and devvm checks each tool image, moves it in and writes its record, with its hash (details). Tool images for glibc, which any VM may mount, build only in devvm’s own Ubuntu base, never in a --from image, and musl ones are keyed by the digest of the --from base they build in, so a container image’s code never reaches another VM’s tools. devvm’s VMs live in a Lima home of their own, so Lima settings you made for other VMs never reach them. devvm also refuses a VM with a network it didn’t give the VM, because that network would reach around the proxy (details).

.git protection

The VM can’t change the parts of .git that run code on the host, because devvm locks hooks and config with a flag the VM can’t clear (details).

Network tiers

A VM on a confined tier, internet, allowlist or none, reaches nothing but its own proxy on the host and the links you added to it. On macOS its Lima process runs under a macOS sandbox, and on Linux QEMU’s network is restricted (details). Even root in the VM can’t get around that. A link’s connections don’t use the VM’s network, because this machine carries them over ssh, and only to a port that another VM on the same tier or a stricter one publishes. An open VM runs on its backend’s own network, and its proxy applies no rules.

The proxy applies the tier’s rules, and it refuses the host’s own addresses and internal addresses unless a rule names them (the proxy). The one thing that VMs share through their proxies is the shared Nix cache, for those with the nix layer. Only the host writes it, with packages from cache.nixos.org whose signature it checked, and nothing a VM sends is stored, so a VM can make the host fetch but can’t change what another VM gets. After each start, devvm checks that the VM still runs confined and can’t connect out directly, and it stops a VM that fails the check instead of opening it (the self-check).

ssh into VMs

ssh and editors reach a running VM by name through the entries that devvm writes (ssh access by name). Each entry is built so that ssh connects only to that VM and the connection gives the VM nothing else of this machine’s:

  • Each entry checks the VM’s own host keys, which devvm keeps in the VM’s folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/known_hosts, as a record of the VM’s current start. devvm reads them from the VM through its backend, instead of over the network, once each start, after the VM runs, and the record names the start it was read for, so the keys of an earlier start are read again rather than trusted, whoever started the VM. devvm also removes the record before each start of its own. A VM whose Lima config changed gets new host keys when it boots. A VM whose keys devvm can’t read gets no entry, and ssh refuses a host key that doesn’t match. devvm’s port forwarder, the sessions of links between VMs and a --clone VM’s git all check the VM against the same record.
  • Only host keys go into the record. devvm keeps a line the VM shows only when its key decodes and names its own type, which works for every key type ssh has, and it drops certificates, markers such as @cert-authority, patterns and anything else. So the VM can’t add a line that would make ssh trust another host, or trust a key for another name.
  • Each connection is its own. The entries set ControlMaster no, so a session never rides on a connection that another program opened. Of Lima’s own ssh settings for the VM, devvm copies only the address, port, user and login key, because Lima’s settings turn host key checks off.
  • The entries turn off everything else your ssh could share with the VM. They set ForwardX11 no, ForwardX11Trusted no, Tunnel no, PermitRemoteOpen none, AddKeysToAgent no, ProxyJump none, ProxyCommand none, UpdateHostKeys no and HashKnownHosts no, whatever your own Host * says. That turns off X11, tunnels, remote SOCKS forwards and adding keys to an agent. PermitRemoteOpen needs OpenSSH 8.7 or newer (ssh -V), and an older ssh refuses the entries.
  • Your agent is forwarded only as the VM’s SSH agent choice says. devvm’s own connections to a VM follow the same choice, the one the VM’s current start was made with, and each carries that VM’s agent alone. devvm finds the VM’s agent socket, which is yours, devvm’s own or none, and gives it to the backend’s start of that VM, to its shell and to the commands that set it up, such as the setup devvm sends and the devcontainer.json commands. The backend’s other commands get no agent, and neither do the reads of a VM’s host keys, the self-check’s probe or the checks of a --clone VM’s clone. devvm never changes its own environment, so when one run reaches several VMs, such as a group’s links, no VM gets another VM’s agent. devvm’s background processes, such as the proxy and the port forwarder, start without an agent, and its own ssh to a VM uses the VM’s login key alone. devvm limactl runs without your agent too, because Lima’s ssh shares one connection per VM, kept open after the command ends, and an agent forwarded over it is the agent of whichever command opened it. With your agent, a devvm limactl shell could open that connection and pass your agent to devvm’s later sessions of a VM whose choice is devvm’s agent or none.

A session carries the VM’s connections through your machine only where your ssh asks for it. The entries can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours without also refusing an ssh -R you type, so a RemoteForward still applies. The VM’s sshd allows local forwarding (-L and -D, which VS Code uses), and it allows remote forwards only on addresses in 127.77.0.0/16, which devvm keeps for links between VMs, so a remote forward on the VM’s localhost, as ssh -R asks by default, is refused. It allows no tunnels or X11. Root in the VM can change all of that, so it’s your ssh that decides, and remote forwards you add says what’s left open.

Secrets stay on the host

devvm saves secrets in the macOS Keychain, or elsewhere in files only you can read, and it never puts a secret in a process’s arguments (where secrets are saved). A VM uses only the Claude Code token, when its image has claude, and the secrets you bind to it. On every tier, a VM’s secrets and its agents’ logins stay on your machine, and its proxy puts them only into requests for their own hosts.

The secrets work only for that VM. Its proxy needs the VM’s own password, and the VM’s placeholders end in a random value of the VM’s own, which isn’t the password, so a placeholder that the VM sends elsewhere gives nothing away. Another VM, or a program on the host that reaches the proxy’s port, gets no secret. The password is in files only you can read, and never in a process’s arguments or in devvm’s run logs, and only you can read the proxy’s logs.

Each VM’s proxy reads traffic to the hosts it puts secrets in for with the VM’s own CA, which devvm keeps in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/ca/ (the VM’s CA). Your machine never trusts it, but inside its VM it vouches for any site, and no other VM trusts it. Only you can read the keys, they never leave this machine, and devvm keeps them out of Time Machine. Each CA lasts 30 days, and the next one, which the VM already trusts, takes over a week before the current one ends. The certificates that the proxy makes never outlast their CA. What a copy of a key could do, and for how long, is under the proxy’s CA keys.

Set-id files on Linux hosts

Root in a VM can set the set-user-id and set-group-id bits on files in the project folder. On macOS these bits don’t reach the host, because virtiofs drops them, but on Linux they do. A file that a Lima VM writes is yours, so a set-user-id file runs as you for anyone else on the machine who runs it. A set-user-id file that your machine’s root owns runs as root for anyone who runs it, you included, and since the VM’s writes are yours, such a file came from something else on this machine.

devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, by devvm stop or found stopped at a launch, but not at a launch into a running VM, because the search reads every file’s metadata and takes about a second for 200,000 files. It skips .git folders, which hold most of a big project’s files and whose files nothing runs by their path. It lists root’s files apart with setid_root_files, and you shouldn’t run them but delete them with sudo rm. It lists the rest with setid_files, and chmod u-s,g-s FILE clears their bits.

What it doesn’t protect

Each defense on this page leaves something open, such as what allowed hosts and secrets permit, open VMs, files the VM writes into the project folder, links between VMs, and escapes from the VM itself through bugs in Lima, Apple’s Virtualization framework or QEMU. Attack vectors keeps the one list of them, under Narrowed, not closed and Left to you, and each entry there links back to its mechanism.

Found a way out of a VM? See SECURITY.md.

item.title: Backends
item.description:
This page explains how a backend gives devvm what it needs to run a VM, what devvm does when a backend lacks something, and how devvm names VMs. devvm runs its VMs on Lima, and another backend would plug in the same way, through the features below (how a backend plugs in).

What a backend does

A backend has four roles, and every backend has all of them:

  • The host: it says what it needs that this machine lacks, which devvm doctor reports, how long a VM’s name can be, where its VMs live, and which folders hold their disks, so devvm can check the free space before a step that writes them.
  • Images: it builds images and the shared tools’ images, keeps the images, and names the files of its own that it puts into base, which base’s key hashes.
  • Machines: it makes, starts, stops, renames and deletes VMs, runs commands and shells in them, and says how ssh and devvm’s port forwarder reach them. It also says how a VM runs now: which start it’s on, whether that start is confined to the VM’s proxy, and the file the VM’s proxy and forwarder follow, which ends them when the process that runs the VM ends.
  • Housekeeping: it says how much disk its VMs and caches take for devvm space, lists the VMs with devvm’s label that this devvm has no state for, and lists and deletes devvm’s share of its own caches for devvm gc --caches. A backend that can’t tell one of these returns nothing, so devvm shows no size or deletes nothing.

A backend may also keep files of its own for a VM besides the VM, which devvm gc --orphans deletes once the VM is gone. Lima keeps none.

Features

Each thing devvm needs from a backend is a feature, such as building images, mounting the project folder or confining a VM to its proxy. devvm doctor lists them as “features” too, but they aren’t the base image features you choose with devvm setup. Each backend declares how it has each feature:

  • native: the backend does it itself.
  • emulated: devvm builds it from other parts of the backend.
  • none: the backend can’t do it.

A backend lists every feature, the ones it lacks too, and devvm refuses to use a backend that leaves one out, so a new feature makes each backend say how it has it. Some features are built on others: ports-all on ports, agent-toggle on agent-forwarding, and link on ssh. A backend has such a feature no better than the one it’s built on, so the feature is emulated wherever its base is emulated, and none wherever its base is none.

devvm uses an emulation only once its review has passed, and until then it refuses the emulation. A review takes a design note, a threat check with the security-audit skill, and end-to-end checks that prove the guarantee.

devvm doctor lists Lima’s features, and devvm doctor --json those of every backend devvm has. Both show an emulation whose review hasn’t passed as unreviewed.

The feature table

Feature What it is Lima
build-image build images from the layer and feature scripts native
build-confinement builds reach the internet but not the host’s loopback, or nothing native: Seatbelt on macOS. On Linux, QEMU’s restrict=on confines a build with no network, but a build with the internet reaches the host’s loopback (details)
from base from a container image (--from) native: devvm converts the image to a disk
clone a project VM from an image native: an APFS copy-on-write copy on macOS, and a qcow2 overlay on Linux (details)
project-mount the project folder, read-write native: virtiofs on macOS, and 9p on Linux
agent-folders agents’ host folders, read-only native: read-only mounts, enforced by the host
tools-share the shared tools, read-only native: a read-only mount, enforced by the host
egress-proxy network traffic only through devvm’s proxy native: Seatbelt on macOS, and on Linux QEMU’s restrict=on with a guestfwd to the proxy (details)
ssh ssh for editors native: Lima’s ssh forward and config
ports the listed ports forwarded to the host’s loopback emulated (reviewed): devvm’s forwarder over Lima’s ssh, for the listed ports alone, with Lima’s own forwards off (details)
ports-all every port forwarded, servers on the VM’s loopback included emulated (reviewed): the same forwarder, for whatever listens in the VM from port 1024 up, and never a port the host has (details)
agent-forwarding ssh-agent forwarding, chosen when the VM is made native
agent-toggle turning a VM’s ssh-agent forwarding on or off later native
cpus a VM’s CPUs native
memory a VM’s memory native
disk a VM’s disk size native: it grows but never shrinks
docker-layer the docker layer: Docker’s engine running in the VM native
nix-layer the nix layer: Nix’s daemon and its store in the VM, with builds in Nix’s sandbox native (details)
link links between VMs: a program in one VM reaches a port another VM publishes, by name native: a link session of devvm’s own over Lima’s ssh, with remote forwards to 127.77.0.0/16 alone (details)

egress-proxy is what every network tier but open needs. The open tier needs no feature of its own: every backend must let a VM on its own network (NetDirect) reach a port on the host’s loopback and set the guest’s proxy settings from the confinement (Confinement.GuestProxy, ProxyURL), which the conformance suite checks (checkProxyURL), because every VM’s proxy carries its requests. So a backend without egress-proxy still has open VMs, and devvm refuses every other tier on it in one line (net_tier_backend).

What each backend emulates

On Lima, devvm emulates forwarding ports, both the listed ones and every one, through its forwarder, and the emulation is reviewed (port forwarding). Everything else on Lima is Lima’s own.

The forwarder is devvm’s own on every backend, never a backend’s. A backend that has ports turns its own forwards off, and devvm’s forwarder reaches a running VM’s sshd the way the backend’s SSH says, which is a user, a key and a port. devvm refuses that target unless it’s on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, with the same check it uses for links and the ssh config (vmssh.FromTarget). devvm reads which ports the VM forwards from its state, chooses which of them are free, pins the VM’s host keys for its current start and starts the forwarder, which follows the backend’s lifeline for the VM.

Missing and unreviewed features

devvm checks each feature an image or a VM needs this way:

flowchart TD
need["a feature the image<br>or the VM needs"] --> how{{"how the backend has it"}}
how -- "native" --> ok["allowed"]
how -- "emulated, reviewed" --> ok
how -- "emulated, unreviewed,<br>or none" --> np{{"egress-proxy, for<br>a new open VM?"}}
np -- "no" --> refused["refused: devvm stops<br>and names the VM,<br>the feature and the backend"]
np -- "yes" --> warned["the VM is made open,<br>as asked"]

Before devvm builds an image, makes or starts a VM, or changes a VM’s settings, it checks that the backend has every feature the image or the VM needs. The backend itself is behind the same check: every time devvm asks it to build an image or the shared tools, make a VM or start one, devvm checks the features that request needs before the backend sees it, so a request that skipped the first check is refused too. When the backend lacks one, devvm stops and names the VM, the feature and the backend (backend_lacks). It does the same for a feature the backend only emulates when that emulation’s review hasn’t passed (backend_unreviewed). devvm never falls back to something weaker, so a VM on a confined tier never starts with an open network.

To get the feature, use a backend that has it. A VM keeps its backend, so that means making a new VM.

A new VM’s tier is the one exception, because allowlist is the default, and When a backend lacks something says what devvm does instead.

What a start changes

A backend makes a VM as devvm asks, and then changes it only when it starts. Each time devvm starts a stopped VM, it tells the backend what the VM’s state asks for, which is its size, the agent folders in devvm’s agent store and whether it forwards your SSH agent, together with how the VM is confined. The backend compares that with the VM it has and changes only what differs, so a start that changes nothing leaves the VM’s config as it was. Nothing changes a stopped VM’s config between starts, so devvm size and devvm ssh-agent save what you ask for in the VM’s state, and the VM gets it when it next starts.

A running VM is left as it is, and devvm says what changes when it next starts. Its ports aren’t the backend’s, so devvm ports changes them at once, and a running VM’s forwarder starts again with the new ones (port forwarding). A disk can’t shrink, so a start that asks for a smaller disk than the VM has fails before the backend changes anything (disk_shrink).

Which ports a VM forwards stays in the VM’s state alone, and the backend never hears of them. The backend keeps only what it needs for the start it made, such as Lima’s record of the hostagent it started confined (confinement).

VM names

A project VM’s name is devvm-<folder>-<hash>. The folder part is up to 20 characters of the folder’s name, in lowercase, with characters other than letters and digits turned into dashes, and the hash part is 14 hex digits of a hash of the folder’s path. devvm takes a name as a project VM’s only when it has that form, so a name in a state file or a backend’s list whose folder part has any other character, or starts or ends with a dash, isn’t a project VM’s.

A backend may need shorter names, and then devvm cuts the folder’s part to fit. When fewer than 4 characters of it would fit, devvm refuses (vm_name_no_room). On Lima the room for a name depends on the Lima home’s path, because Lima keeps each VM’s ssh socket under it, so there the fix is a shorter Lima home (lima_home_too_long, limits).

Only a new VM gets a name, which fits the limit of the backend that makes it. devvm finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder’s path, in the VM’s folder in devvm’s data folder (vms/<hash>/, named by the hash that ends the VM’s name), so an existing VM keeps the name and the backend its state records, whichever backend new VMs get, and keeps them when its folder moves (a moved folder).

Which backends a launch asks

A launch asks a backend about its VMs only when some VM’s state names that backend. It asks them to write the ssh config and to check the SSH agent’s folders. So a backend that no VM uses never runs during a launch, even when it isn’t running or isn’t installed (a VM’s backend).

item.title: devvm clone
item.description:
Show or change whether this folder’s VM has its own clone of the repo

Synopsis

Show whether this folder’s VM has its own clone of the repo, on, or mounts this folder, off. devvm clone on and devvm clone off make the VM again from its image, after asking in a terminal without –no-input, then open a shell in it, and devvm keeps its home folder and its settings, while everything else on its disk is lost. On copies the repo’s branches into the new clone, and off first offers to fetch the clone’s work into this repo, unless you give –no-clone-check.

devvm clone [on|off] [flags]

Examples 

 devvm clone # show whether the VM has its own clone of the repo
 devvm clone on # make the VM again with its own clone of the repo, after asking
 devvm clone off # fetch the clone's work, then make the VM again with this folder mounted
 devvm clone on --force # make it again without asking, as a script must

Options 

 --clean-home give the VM the image's home folder instead of keeping its own
 -f, --force don't ask to confirm, which devvm needs without a terminal or with --no-input
 -h, --help help for clone
 --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside
 --json print it as one JSON object, for scripts
 --no-clone-check don't check a --clone VM's clone for unfetched commits and uncommitted changes first, which are lost
 --no-export don't export the agents' history first
 --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm clone explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm: Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first

item.title: Settings and files
item.description:
devvm writes nothing into your project folders. It keeps the settings you edit in ~/.config/devvm and everything it writes itself in ~/.local/share/devvm, and it reads a few environment variables. Your settings lists the files you edit, devvm’s data folder lists the ones devvm writes, and Overview explains how devvm keeps them.

Your settings

~/.config/devvm ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devvm) holds what you edit, and it’s the only folder of devvm’s that you should change by hand. devvm never rewrites a file of yours there. It reads config.toml and your own layers and CAs, it creates a new layer’s files when you run devvm layer new, it changes single lines of policy when you add or remove a rule for every VM, and it writes version when the folder has none and when it changes its folders to a newer layout.

File What it holds Written by
config.toml the defaults that new VMs get and the retention settings, which win over what devvm’s commands save, the company proxy and an Ubuntu mirror (config.toml) you
policy your network rules for every VM devvm network allow -g, deny -g, rm -g, or you
layers/ your own layers and their allowlists devvm layer new, then you
agents/ your agents’ settings in devvm’s agent store, one folder for each agent devvm agent import, devvm agent save, or you
ca/ your company’s CA certificates, which VMs and builds trust you
version the folder’s layout version, which says how devvm keeps its files here devvm, when it’s missing or older

Edit the files in ~/.config/devvm, and never edit the ones in ~/.local/share/devvm. devvm writes those itself and rewrites them whole, so a change you make there can be lost, or can stop devvm from reading the file. To set a default by hand, put it in config.toml instead.

Upgrading devvm keeps this folder as it is. Back it up, such as in a dotfiles repo, to keep your settings and layers.

config.toml

~/.config/devvm/config.toml sets the defaults that new VMs get, the retention settings, the company proxy, an Ubuntu mirror and the release check, in a file you write by hand. devvm reads it and never writes it. Every key is optional, and devvm has no config.toml until you write one. This example sets every key:

# The network tier new VMs get: open, internet, allowlist or none.
network = "allowlist"

# The ports new VMs forward: all, none, or ports and ranges.
ports = "5173,8000-8010"

# The features base gets, in the order they run, or [] for none.
features = ["cli-tools", "fzf", "omb"]

# The coding agents new VMs get, or [] for none.
agents = ["claude", "codex"]

# The layers new VMs get, bottom first, or [] for none.
layers = ["docker"]

# A mirror of Ubuntu's archive that base's first build tries first.
ubuntu-mirror = "http://mirror.example.com/ubuntu-ports"

# Whether a launch checks once a day for a newer devvm release.
release-check = true

# New VMs' CPUs, and their memory and disk in GiB.
[size]
cpus = 4
memory = 8
disk = 100

# What devvm deletes on its own, with the keys devvm retention takes.
[retention]
logs.runs = 20
history.age = "90d"
history.count = 10
tools.unused-age = "30d"
orphans.age = "30d"
nix-cache.size = "20G"

# The company proxy, when the shell you run devvm in sets none.
[proxy]
https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com"

Each key takes what its command takes. network is a tier, open, internet, allowlist or none, as devvm network -g sets it (choosing a tier). ports is all, none or a list, as devvm ports -g takes it (size and ports). features lists the features that base gets, agents the coding agents that new VMs get, and layers the layers that new VMs get, bottom first. cpus is a whole number, and memory and disk are a number of GiB, such as 8, 8.5 or "8G", as devvm size -g takes them. The [retention] keys are the retention settings, with a duration such as "90d" or a size such as "20G" in quotes, and a count as a number.

The [proxy] table is the company proxy that every VM’s proxy, builds and devvm’s own downloads go through when the shell you run devvm in sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, whatever the VM’s tier. No VM gets the company proxy’s settings itself. That shell’s settings win over the whole table. https and http take what HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY take, an http:// URL or host:port, and no-proxy takes what NO_PROXY takes. A URL never holds a password, and devvm refuses one that does, so put only the user in it and save the password with devvm secret set proxy. No command saves the proxy, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

An Ubuntu mirror

ubuntu-mirror is a mirror of Ubuntu’s archive, such as one your company or university runs, which the first build of base gets its packages from before it tries Ubuntu’s own. It must mirror the archive for this machine’s architecture: archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu on an Intel or AMD machine, or ports.ubuntu.com/ubuntu-ports on an Apple silicon Mac or another arm64 machine. Give it as an http:// or https:// address without a user, a query or spaces, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). A package that the mirror doesn’t have, or a mirror that doesn’t answer, falls back to Ubuntu’s archive for that file.

A mirror can’t give base a package that Ubuntu didn’t publish. apt checks every list and package against Ubuntu’s archive key whichever server sends it, and refuses one that doesn’t match, and devvm checks them against that key again on this machine before it keeps any package. A mirror that’s behind, or one that’s lying, can still serve lists older than Ubuntu’s, because Ubuntu’s signed lists don’t expire. devvm refuses lists more than a day older than the Ubuntu cloud image base starts from, and it names the mirror and keeps none of the build’s packages (old package lists). devvm compares the lists with the cloud image’s date, not with today’s, so a mirror that fell behind after that date can still give base packages older than Ubuntu’s, and you should only set a mirror you trust to keep up. Only the first build of each base uses the mirror, because a later build of the same base installs the packages devvm kept from that first build (base). VMs don’t use it, and neither do layers or a --from base. No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The release check

When you run devvm in a terminal, it checks at most once a day for a newer devvm release, and when one is out it says so in one line before it opens the VM, naming the release, the version you have and devvm upgrade. devvm never installs anything on its own, so you upgrade with devvm upgrade when you choose to. release-check = false turns the check off, and so does setting DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 in the environment, as CI can. release-check must be true or false, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The check reads only where GitHub’s latest devvm release is, over HTTPS, and sends nothing about you or your machine. The latest release is never a prerelease, so the check never announces one (trying a prerelease). It runs beside the launch, so it never makes devvm wait, and when you’re offline it says nothing and tries again the next day. The line comes from what the last check found, so a release that came out since then shows up at the launch after the next check. devvm keeps what the check found in ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/release.json, and devvm doctor shows it. devvm says nothing without a terminal, with --no-input, for a devvm built from its source, or for a copy that neither the install script nor Homebrew installed, which devvm upgrade can’t upgrade.

Where a default comes from

For each default, devvm uses the first of these that sets it:

  1. A flag for one VM, such as --ports or --cpus.
  2. config.toml.
  3. What devvm’s commands saved: devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json.
  4. devvm’s own default.

A command that would save a default that config.toml sets refuses, names the file and the key, and changes nothing, because the value in config.toml would still win. To change that default, edit it in config.toml, or delete it there to let devvm’s commands set it again. In a terminal, devvm setup doesn’t ask about what config.toml sets, and it says so.

devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention show where each value came from, after a #. They show config.toml’s path for a value from config.toml, devvm: settings.json for one that a command saved, and devvm: default for devvm’s own:

$ devvm ports -g
5173,8000-8010 # /Users/you/.config/devvm/config.toml
$ devvm network -g
allowlist # devvm: default

With --json, the same commands add source, or sources for each value of devvm size -g and devvm retention, which is config.toml, settings.json or built-in.

When devvm can’t read it

devvm reads all of config.toml each time it needs a default, and it checks every key and value. A key it doesn’t know, such as a typo, a value that a key can’t take, and a file that isn’t TOML each stop the command, and devvm names the file and the line. Fix the line, and run the command again. config.toml has no key for the backend, because every new VM runs on Lima, so a backend key stops the command as an unknown key.

devvm setup

devvm setup chooses what new VMs get. In a terminal, it asks five questions, each starting from the current choice, and saves each answer in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json, as the command for that setting saves it. It skips a question that config.toml answers, saying so, and it refuses a flag that would change what config.toml sets.

  1. The features that base gets.
  2. The CPUs and memory that new VMs get, as devvm size -g saves them.
  3. The network tier that new VMs get, as devvm network -g saves it: open, internet, allowlist, which is the default, or none. Each new VM’s summary shows that tier, and when you customize the VM in a terminal, devvm asks for its tier, with Enter keeping the one the summary showed (what a new VM gets). --network TIER chooses for one VM and wins over the saved choice.
  4. The coding agents that new VMs get.
  5. The layers that new VMs get.
devvm setup # asks all five questions
devvm setup --features fzf,omb # base's features, without asking
devvm setup --features none # base gets no features
devvm setup --agents claude,codex # new VMs' coding agents, without asking
devvm setup --layers docker # new VMs' layers, without asking

devvm setup has three flags of its own, and each one chooses without asking anything. --features LIST chooses base’s features, as a comma-separated list or none for none, and devvm refuses an empty --features ''. --agents LIST chooses new VMs’ coding agents in the same way, and --layers LIST chooses new VMs’ layers. With any of the flags, what the flags leave out stays as it is. Without a terminal and without flags, devvm setup asks nothing and keeps base’s features, saving every feature when none was chosen yet. To change new VMs’ size without asking, use devvm size -g (choosing new VMs’ size), and to change their network tier, use devvm network -g (choosing a tier).

Coding agents for new VMs

The coding agents you choose in devvm setup are the ones a new VM gets unless you choose others for it. The summary devvm shows before it makes the VM names each of them as coming from devvm setup, and when you customize the VM, they’re checked in the list (what a new VM gets). --agents chooses others for one VM. The choice is for new VMs only, so a VM that exists keeps its agents, and devvm tools changes them.

devvm asks for them on its first run in a terminal, together with the size and base’s features, until you’ve chosen them. Until then, and when you choose none, new VMs get no agents by default. devvm setup --agents claude,codex and devvm setup --agents none choose them without asking, and devvm refuses a name that isn’t an agent’s, suggesting the closest.

Layers for new VMs

The layers you choose in devvm setup are the ones every new VM gets unless you choose others for it. They can be devvm’s built-in layers, desktop, docker and nix, and your own, which is how you give every new VM an extra of your own (extras of your own). The summary devvm shows before it makes a new VM names each of them as coming from devvm setup. When you customize the VM in a terminal, they’re already chosen under Layers in the list, and you can leave any of them out of that VM (what a new VM gets).

devvm setup --layers docker,desktop # every new VM gets docker, with desktop on top
devvm setup --layers none # new VMs get no layers
devvm --layers nix # this VM gets nix alone, not setup's layers
devvm --layers none # this VM gets no layers

devvm setup --layers takes the layers bottom first, in the order the image’s name joins them, so --layers docker,desktop gives new VMs the image docker+desktop. It refuses a name that isn’t a layer’s, suggesting the closest, and changes nothing. Until you choose some, new VMs get no layers by default, and devvm doesn’t ask for them on its first run. In a terminal, devvm setup asks for them last, after the coding agents. To set them by hand, use the layers key in config.toml, which devvm setup --layers then refuses to change.

--layers on devvm is the exact list of one VM’s layers, so it replaces setup’s layers, and --layers none makes a VM without any. A devcontainer.json’s layers go on top of setup’s (devcontainer.json).

The choice is for new VMs only. A VM that exists keeps the layers it was made with, and devvm setup says so when it saves the choice. To give that VM more layers, run devvm layer add in its folder (adding layers to a VM), and to take some out, devvm layer rm (taking layers out of a VM).

When a layer of yours that you chose in devvm setup has no script in ~/.config/devvm/layers, such as after you delete it, a new VM is made without it, and devvm warns, naming the layer. Run devvm setup --layers to choose the layers again. When the VM’s backend can’t run a layer you chose, such as docker on a backend without Docker’s engine, devvm makes no VM and names the layer. Then choose other layers for that VM with --layers, or change new VMs’ layers with devvm setup --layers.

Retention

devvm keeps what it makes until you delete it, and the retention settings tell it to delete some of it on its own. Every setting is off until you set it, so first run devvm space to see what each one would free: its RETAIN column shows each setting that’s on, beside the row it applies to, with what it would delete now (devvm space).

devvm retention shows every setting and its value, and off for each one that isn’t set. devvm retention KEY=VALUE... sets them, and devvm retention KEY=off turns one off, for example devvm retention history.age=90d tools.unused-age=30d. devvm refuses a key or value it doesn’t know, and a key with no value such as history.age=, and then it writes nothing. devvm saves the settings in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json. The [retention] table of config.toml sets them too, and a setting there wins over the saved one, so devvm retention refuses to change it. Each line that devvm retention shows ends with where its value came from, after a #. When devvm can’t read a file that sets them, it names the file, and the line for config.toml, and applies none of them.

Key What devvm deletes
logs.runs the run logs beyond the newest this many, which is 20 when it’s off
history.age the exports of agents’ history written this long ago or more, such as 90d
history.count the exports of agents’ history beyond the newest this many
tools.unused-age the current shared tools that no VM has had for this long, counted from when devvm first found that no VM has them. While a VM is being made or is getting new shared tools, retention deletes none of them in that run, because that VM may not list the tools it picked yet, and it still applies the other settings
orphans.age what devvm keeps for VMs that their backend no longer has, once their state hasn’t changed for this long, as devvm gc --orphans does
nix-cache.size the shared Nix cache’s least recently used files, while it takes more than this, such as 20G; it’s 10 GiB when it’s off

Ages are durations, a whole number of minutes, hours, days or weeks, such as 30m, 12h, 30d or 2w. Sizes are a whole number of K, M, G or T, each 1024 of the one before, such as 500M or 20G, as devvm space shows them. The shared Nix cache also keeps to its size while VMs fill it, because a VM’s proxy deletes the cache’s least recently used files before a new file would take it past that size. A size you set applies to each VM from its next start. devvm applies the settings at the start of a command, at most once a day, except for orphans.age, which needs to ask each backend about its VMs, so only devvm gc --retention applies it. devvm gc --retention applies all of them at once. When it deletes something, devvm says what in one line. Retention never deletes a VM, an image, a shared tool that any VM’s state lists, or anything in the backends’ own caches, which only devvm gc --caches frees. In cache/, the folder in devvm’s data folder that holds what devvm makes again when it needs it, retention deletes only the shared Nix cache’s files. When two devvms start at once, only one of them applies the settings.

devvm retention –json

devvm retention --json prints the settings as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. settings has every key with its value as you wrote it, and off for each one that isn’t set. sources has every key with where its value came from: config.toml, settings.json for one that devvm retention saved, or built-in for one that’s off. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses a KEY=VALUE with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "settings": {
 "history.age": "90d",
 "history.count": "off",
 "logs.runs": "off",
 "nix-cache.size": "off",
 "orphans.age": "off",
 "tools.unused-age": "30d"
 },
 "sources": {
 "history.age": "config.toml",
 "history.count": "built-in",
 "logs.runs": "built-in",
 "nix-cache.size": "built-in",
 "orphans.age": "built-in",
 "tools.unused-age": "settings.json"
 }
}

A company’s CA

Some company networks inspect TLS through a proxy, such as Zscaler or Netskope, that shows its own certificates, signed by the company’s certificate authority (CA). This machine trusts that CA, but VMs and the VMs that devvm builds images in don’t, so their TLS connections fail. To make them trust it, put the CA’s certificate in ~/.config/devvm/ca:

mkdir -p ~/.config/devvm/ca
cp company-root.pem ~/.config/devvm/ca/

devvm reads every *.pem and *.crt file in that folder each time you open a VM, each time it builds an image and each time it resolves the shared tools’ versions, and it leaves other files alone. A file can hold one certificate or several, in PEM, the text form that starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. devvm accepts only CA certificates. When a file holds anything else, such as a private key, a certificate devvm can’t read or a certificate that isn’t a CA’s, devvm refuses the whole folder and names the file. It sends only the certificates it read out of a file, never the rest of the file. devvm doesn’t follow links there, so copy each certificate into the folder rather than linking to it. When a *.pem or *.crt file is a link, or the folder itself is one, devvm refuses the whole folder and names the link, because a link into a project folder would let that project’s VM replace the CA that every VM, build and proxy trusts. devvm also refuses the folder, naming the file, when it can’t read a file there or the folder itself.

Every project VM trusts these CAs in its system’s store from its next launch, and so does every VM that devvm builds an image or shared tools in. devvm takes them out of a build VM before the image is finished, so images never keep them, and adding or removing a CA rebuilds nothing. A layer script of yours that copies the system’s CA bundle somewhere else does keep that copy. On every network tier, the VM’s proxy also trusts them for the connections it makes itself, and so does the refresh of a coding agent’s login that the proxy makes on this machine when the login is due, so a company proxy that inspects TLS doesn’t make the refresh fail. devvm also resolves the shared tools’ versions on this machine, with a mise of its own that it downloads once, and that download trusts these CAs as well as this machine’s own store, and on Linux so does that mise. On macOS, mise trusts them for most of its connections, but the part of it that checks where each tool’s release was built trusts only the CAs that macOS trusts, which Keychain Access shows. So on macOS, a company’s CA that mise needs has to be there too, where a Mac that your company manages usually has it already. When mise doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, devvm says so and names this folder. devvm’s other connections from this machine, such as checking an image’s registry or Ubuntu’s image, trust this machine’s own store, as your other programs here do. When you take a certificate out of the folder, VMs stop trusting it at their next launch, and stores that copy the system’s CAs, such as Java’s cacerts, drop it too.

Most tools read the system’s store, among them apt, apk, curl, git and Python’s ssl module. For those that don’t, every VM’s environment points them at it:

Variable Value For
NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS /etc/ssl/devvm.pem, which holds only devvm’s CAs and is empty when there are none Node, npm and Bun
SSL_CERT_FILE /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, the system’s bundle Go programs, and Rust programs that read the system’s roots
REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, PIP_CERT the system’s bundle Python’s requests and pip, which use their own CA list otherwise
UV_SYSTEM_CERTS 1 uv

A CA in the folder can read every TLS connection a VM makes, as it can this machine’s, so put only CAs there that you trust as much as this machine does. How it works › Network tiers explains how the CAs reach VMs, and Images and caching how builds use them.

devvm’s state

~/.local/share/devvm ($XDG_DATA_HOME/devvm) holds what devvm makes and keeps for you, and devvm writes everything in it, so don’t edit it by hand. It holds the defaults that devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save in settings.json, below config.toml’s, and a folder for each VM in vms/, with the VM’s state, its own allowlist and its network logs. It also holds the images and the shared tools, the run logs, the agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm save, the ssh config for your VMs, and devvm’s own Lima home (lima/), where the Lima backend’s VMs and images live. devvm’s data folder lists each file and folder in it, with how each one is cleaned up.

On Linux hosts this folder also holds your secrets, in files under secrets/ that only you can read, so keep that in mind when you back it up. On macOS they’re in the Keychain.

devvm’s Lima home is its own, whatever LIMA_HOME says, so Lima settings meant for other VMs never reach devvm’s. Set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to move it, for example to a sandbox or to a shorter path.

Only you can read devvm’s files, in either folder, because each time devvm runs, it makes both folders yours alone (devvm’s data folder). When devvm can’t read one of its files, it names the file and the line (a file devvm can’t read).

Project folders devvm refuses

A VM mounts its project folder read-write, so devvm refuses to make a VM for a folder that would give the VM more than the project. It refuses a folder that is or holds your home folder, ~/.config/devvm, ~/.local/share/devvm or devvm’s Lima home. It also refuses a folder inside one of devvm’s own folders, because a VM there could rewrite the scripts that every image build runs, or the files that devvm runs on this machine.

When devvm refuses a folder, make the VM in a project folder inside it, or keep the project somewhere else. A --clone VM mounts nothing from the folder, so devvm doesn’t refuse its folder.

Warning

If you mean to give the VM the whole folder, pass --unsafe-folder when you make the VM, and devvm warns you that the VM gets read-write access to it (only the project folder).

Colors

In a terminal, devvm colors the labels and links around its messages, while the messages’ own text stays in your terminal’s usual color. The values a message fills in, such as a VM’s name, a path, a port or a count, are bold, so they stand out from the words around them. An error’s devvm: label is red and a warning’s is yellow, a doc link is blue and underlined, and the ==> before what devvm did is bold. When a step fails, the end of the run log that devvm prints is dim, and so is the log’s latest line on the status line and each line that -v shows. The mark a slow step leaves when it’s done is green.

The tables that devvm ls, devvm images, devvm space and devvm doctor print are colored too. Each table’s header row and the totals row are bold, and a state is green when it’s good, such as current, Running or native, yellow when it needs your attention, such as stale, unused, Stopped or emulated, and red when something is wrong, such as an unenforced tier or an unreviewed emulation. Digests, image keys and a feature a backend doesn’t have, which devvm doctor lists as none, are dim, and names, paths, sizes and counts stay in your terminal’s usual color. The columns line up the same with colors or without.

devvm uses only your terminal’s 16 base colors, so your theme picks shades that read well on its background, light or dark. It never sets a background color.

devvm decides for standard output and standard error apart, and colors one only when it’s a terminal, so output you pipe or redirect to a file stays plain, tables included. What a command prints with --json is plain even in a terminal, and the run log is never colored. These environment variables change when devvm colors, and the first one that applies decides:

  • NO_COLOR, set to anything but an empty value, turns colors off.
  • FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE, set to anything but 0, turns them on even when the output isn’t a terminal.
  • TERM=dumb turns them off.

Environment

NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR, CLICOLOR_FORCE turn devvm’s colors off, or on when the output isn’t a terminal (details)
DEVVM_LIMA_HOME move devvm’s own Lima home (details)
DEVVM_FROM the container image that the base of new VMs and builds starts from when there’s no --from (details)
DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK=1 don’t check for newer shared tools once a day (details)
DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 don’t check for a newer devvm release once a day (details)
DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE the Keychain service devvm saves and reads secrets in, instead of devvm (details)
CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN the Claude Code token that VMs get, over the saved Claude Code login, whichever it is (details)

item.title: devvm code
item.description:
Open this folder’s VM in VS Code over Remote-SSH

Synopsis

Get this folder’s VM ready as devvm host does, then open its folder in VS Code over Remote-SSH, with VS Code’s code command.

devvm code [flags]

Examples 

 devvm code # open this folder's VM in VS Code
 devvm code --ssh-config # the same, adding devvm's Include line to ~/.ssh/config without asking

Options 

 -h, --help help for code
 --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside
 --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own
 --ssh-config add devvm's Include line to ~/.ssh/config without asking

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm code explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm: Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first

item.title: Lima
item.description:
This page explains how devvm runs its VMs on Lima: the Lima home it keeps them in, how it builds images and clones VMs from them, what it sets in each VM’s config, how it confines VMs and builds, and how it forwards their ports. Lima covers what you need to run it, devvm limactl and Lima’s limits.

A Lima home of its own

Lima merges _config/default.yaml and _config/override.yaml from its home into every VM it creates or starts. A network you set there for your own VMs would give a devvm VM a second network card with a route around its proxy, and an extra mount set there would go unnoticed. So devvm keeps its VMs in a Lima home of their own, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima, whatever LIMA_HOME says (devvm’s Lima home says what that means for you).

devvm refuses to start a VM while that home holds either file (lima_global_config), and it refuses a VM that has a network devvm didn’t give it (vm_has_networks).

devvm runs limactl from its own data folder. When a config is invalid, Lima writes lima.REJECTED.yaml into the folder it runs in, and a project folder belongs to the VM to write.

Clones and overlays

An image is a stopped VM in devvm’s Lima home, named devvm-img-<key>. devvm makes base’s from Ubuntu’s cloud image with base.yaml, base’s size as --cpus, --memory and --disk, and --mount-none, and it gives limactl create the template on its standard input (-), from the binary, so no copy of base.yaml is on disk. With --from, it makes base’s from the converted disk instead, and boots its kernel and initrd directly (details). A layer’s image is a clone of its parent’s, also made with --mount-none, so a build mounts nothing from the host. A project VM is a clone of its image’s VM, which devvm makes while the image is stopped.

  • macOS: the clone’s disk is an APFS copy-on-write copy. It shares the image’s blocks until the VM writes them, so du overcounts it.
  • Linux: Lima’s disks are qcow2 files, and a clone would be a full copy. So a project VM’s disk is a qcow2 overlay of its image’s, readable only by you, which shares the image’s blocks and holds only the VM’s changes. An image’s disk is read-only once it’s built, and devvm can’t delete an image while VMs’ disks are overlays of it (image_in_use). devvm reads each VM disk’s backing file with qemu-img info -U, which shares the disk with the QEMU of a running VM, because that QEMU’s write lock refuses qemu-img info otherwise.

What devvm sets on a VM

devvm sets these in each VM’s Lima config:

  • Mounts: the project folder (read-write), agents’ folders (read-only), and the shared tools at /mnt/devvm-tools (read-only). Each folder but the tools is mounted at its host path. devvm mounts nothing else, and it leaves out the home folder that Lima’s templates mount. On macOS, where Lima runs VMs with vz, the project folder’s mount names the folder by the device and inode that devvm recorded when it made the VM, as location: /.vol/<device>/<inode> with mountPoint set to the folder’s path. macOS’s /.vol opens a folder by its device and inode, so Virtualization.framework shares the folder devvm made the VM for, wherever that folder is when the VM starts, and never follows a link put at its path (an existing VM). Virtualization.framework then serves the share by the path the folder had at the start, so a folder moved back while the VM runs answers “Operation not permitted” in the VM until its next start. QEMU’s 9p on Linux has nothing like /.vol, so there the mount is by the folder’s path.
  • ssh: agent forwarding on or off, and the host port. devvm chooses the port when it makes the VM and records it, so no other VM’s forwarded ports take it. The port changes only when another program on the host has it, on any address, while the VM is stopped, or when the VM lists it to forward.
  • Ports: none, because Lima’s own forwards are off and devvm’s forwarder forwards the VM’s ports instead (below).
  • Size: CPUs, memory and disk.
  • Guest environment: Lima’s env:, which Lima writes to /etc/environment at every boot. On every tier it holds the VM’s proxy’s address and its settings, and Lima doesn’t pass the host’s proxy settings in. A confined VM reaches the proxy as Lima’s host address on macOS and as QEMU’s guestfwd address on Linux, and an open VM reaches it at Lima’s host address on both, which is this machine’s loopback as Lima’s network has it, with host.lima.internal added to its NO_PROXY. limactl edit sets the proxy’s URL with a stand-in for the password (devvm-proxy-password), and devvm then replaces the stand-in in the VM’s lima.yaml, which it rewrites with mode 600, so the password is in no process’s arguments. Its NO_PROXY and no_proxy name the VM alone, and never its links, which its HTTP clients reach through the proxy, so links never change it. A start runs limactl edit only when the environment differs from the one the VM has, because it compares them first. That edit gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot, as any edit does, and devvm forgets a VM’s host keys at every start and pins them again once it runs, so devvm’s ssh config, its own connections and your editors keep working.

Lima changes only a stopped VM’s config, so a change you make while the VM runs applies at its next start. When devvm makes a VM, the clone gets its mounts, agent forwarding, ssh port, ports rules and environment, and devvm then edits the VM’s size where it differs from its image’s. Each start of a stopped VM compares the VM’s config, as limactl list shows it, with what the VM’s state asks for and with how the VM starts. That covers its size, its project folder’s path, which changes once the folder moved (a moved folder), and on macOS the device and inode its mount names, its agents’ folders, its agent forwarding, its ssh port, its environment, Lima’s proxy settings, DNS and its ports rules. devvm then changes whatever differs in one limactl edit, and runs none when nothing does, because each edit gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot. Lima can’t shrink a disk, so a start that asks for a smaller disk than the VM has fails before it changes anything (disk_shrink).

devvm leaves Lima’s mountInotify off, so file watchers in the VM see only the changes made in the VM (file watchers). With it on, Lima’s hostagent watches the project folder on the host and, for each change there, changes the file’s times in the guest as root, which raises an inotify event for the guest’s watchers. The hostagent can’t tell the VM’s own writes from the host’s, so it does this to every file the VM writes too, and on macOS the guest then sees such a file as root’s for a moment. A command that writes a file and then changes its mode fails in that moment, and in a test on macOS, git init in the project folder failed 13 times in 30 with it on and never with it off. Lima also passes on no deletions, and it marks the setting as experimental.

Confinement

A VM on a confined tier, internet, allowlist or none, reaches nothing but its proxy on the host, which applies its tier’s rules, and even root in the VM can’t get around that. Direct connections, DNS, UDP and connections to the host’s own services fail at once, while forwarded ports, mounts and ssh keep working.

On each host, the VM’s traffic passes through one process that devvm confines:

flowchart TD
subgraph linux["Linux"]
vm2["the VM"] --> q["QEMU,<br>restrict=on"]
end
q -- "only to<br>192.168.5.4:3128" --> proxy["its proxy"]
subgraph mac["macOS"]
vm1["the VM"] --> ha["its Lima<br>hostagent,<br>sandboxed"]
end
ha -- "allowed" --> ok["its ssh port<br>its proxy<br>its Lima sockets<br>its SSH agent"]
ha -. "denied" .-> no["everything<br>else"]

On macOS, devvm starts the VM’s Lima process, its hostagent, under a macOS sandbox. That’s sandbox-exec with a Seatbelt profile, sandbox.sb in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/.

  • The profile lets the process connect to the VM’s ssh port and its proxy on the host’s loopback, to the unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder (ssh’s control socket and the VM’s network), and to the ssh agent the VM forwards, which is yours or devvm’s own. It connects nowhere else, so other sockets on the host, such as Docker’s, stay out of reach even if the Lima process were compromised.
  • The profile lets the process listen only on the VM’s ssh port, over TCP, and on unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder, so it can’t open a port of the VM’s on the host even if Lima ignored its rules (ports).
  • Names resolve in the proxy, so Lima’s own DNS server for the VM is off, the guest’s DNS points at an address that nothing listens on, and lookups fail at once. The guest reaches the proxy at 192.168.5.2, which is the host as Lima’s network sees it.

On Linux, Lima starts QEMU through a wrapper that devvm writes (~/.local/share/devvm/run/qemu/) and that runs devvm. The wrapper adds QEMU’s restrict=on to Lima’s network, so no traffic goes in or out but Lima’s own forwards. It also adds one address, 192.168.5.4:3128, which QEMU connects to the VM’s proxy. If Lima’s QEMU arguments aren’t the shape devvm expects, with one -netdev user,id=net0,… and no other network, the wrapper refuses to start QEMU (qemu_refused), so QEMU never runs unrestricted. DNS points at an address that nothing listens on, so lookups fail at once.

An open VM isn’t confined: on macOS its hostagent runs without a profile, and on Linux QEMU runs without the wrapper, so without restrict=on and without the guestfwd. Its guest reaches its proxy at 192.168.5.2 and the proxy’s own port on both hosts, because Lima’s user-mode network, vz’s and QEMU’s alike, reaches the host’s loopback at that address. Its NO_PROXY adds host.lima.internal and 192.168.5.2, which the proxy on the host couldn’t resolve as the VM does, Lima’s DNS stays on, so names resolve in the VM, and propagateProxyEnv is off, so the guest gets no proxy settings of the host’s.

A process can’t leave its sandbox, so devvm records the hostagent it started (started in the VM’s run folder) and checks that the VM still runs on it (the self-check). A VM started another way, such as with limactl start, runs unconfined, and devvm ls shows it as unenforced. The VM’s proxy follows the hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid in the VM’s Lima folder) and exits with it. devvm writes the record only once limactl start returns, while the hostagent runs on its own from early in the start, so an interrupt during the start stops the VM (how long a proxy runs). Interrupted before the hostagent answers, the VM is one Lima reports as Broken, which limactl stop refuses, so devvm stops a broken VM with limactl stop --force. A hostagent that runs without its driver yet is still starting QEMU, which writes its pid file only once it runs, and that can take seconds on a slow host, such as one with nested virtualization. Stopped with --force then, the hostagent would go and the QEMU it started would run on without it, so devvm waits up to 30 seconds for the driver first and then stops the VM as Lima reports it. A VM whose QEMU still runs without its hostagent holds its disk, so no new QEMU can start on it, and a start stops such a VM with --force first.

Builds are also confined, because they run code devvm didn’t write. On macOS a build’s Lima process runs under a profile that reaches either the internet but not the host’s loopback, where other VMs’ proxies and dev servers listen, or nothing at all. Behind a company proxy, a build with the internet also reaches one port of the host’s loopback, its own proxy’s (a company proxy). On Linux only a build with no network is confined.
