QEMU can’t keep the internet while dropping the host’s loopback, so other builds reach services on the host’s localhost. Builds forward no ports.

sandbox-exec is deprecated. If macOS drops it, devvm needs another way to confine the hostagent, and until then the self-check catches a VM that runs unconfined.

Ports

devvm’s forwarder forwards a Lima VM’s ports by the rules that Port forwarding sets out. On Lima this is an emulation, and it’s reviewed (design). devvm doesn’t use Lima’s own forwards because they listen with SO_REUSEADDR, and on macOS such a forward takes 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program on the host has *:PORT, along with that program’s localhost connections.

So Lima forwards nothing. Each VM’s portForwards are rules that ignore every guest port, TCP and UDP, on 127.0.0.1 (which also covers ::1), 0.0.0.0 and ::. Lima’s own ssh is its VM driver’s forward, not a rule, so it keeps working. devvm sets the rules when it makes the VM, and a start sets them again only where they differ, because any change gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot. On macOS, a confined VM doesn’t rely on the rules alone, because its sandbox refuses the Lima process every port but its ssh port (confinement).

Which ports a VM forwards is in the VM’s state, which devvm’s forwarder reads, so devvm ports changes the state and never the VM’s Lima config, and the backend never hears of them. Its process and files lists the forwarder’s files and its log.

The forwarder isn’t Lima’s, and it runs only for project VMs. What Lima gives it is how to reach a running VM: Lima’s ssh port on this machine’s loopback, Lima’s user, and Lima’s key (_config/user in devvm’s Lima home), which every VM there authorizes. The forwarder connects there with the host keys devvm pinned for the VM’s current start, which the VM’s ssh config checks too. Its lifeline is the VM’s hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid), so it ends when the hostagent does, and devvm rm deletes its files.

item.title: Working on a clone
item.description:
devvm --clone gives the VM its own clone of the repo instead of mounting your folder, so nothing in the VM can touch your working tree or .git. Use it when you don’t trust what runs in the VM, such as an agent working unattended, and on Linux hosts, which have no .git protection. Files the VM writes lists what --clone keeps away from this machine.

devvm --clone # create the VM, copy your branches into it and open a shell in its clone
git fetch devvm # later, on this machine, fetch the VM's work as devvm/<branch>
git log -p main..devvm/main
sequenceDiagram
participant R as Your repo
participant V as The VM's clone
R->>V: devvm --clone pushes<br>every local branch
Note over V: you or an agent<br>commit in the VM
V->>R: git fetch devvm gives<br>devvm/#lt;branch#gt;
Note over R: review,<br>then merge
R->>V: devvm rm looks for<br>commits not fetched
V->>R: fetched into<br>saved/devvm/#lt;branch#gt;
Note over R,V: the VM is deleted,<br>and its remote removed

Requirements

  • The folder is the top folder of a git repo that has at least one commit and a branch checked out, not a detached HEAD.
  • The repo is the folder’s own, or the folder is a worktree that git worktree add made. devvm refuses a .git that points into another repo, because the push would copy that repo’s branches into the VM. That includes a .git file that isn’t a worktree’s, a worktree whose link back to this folder doesn’t match, a commondir that leads to another repo, and objects or refs that are symlinks, or that sit in a folder that is one. devvm also refuses a repo that borrows objects from another repo through objects/info/alternates. To use such a repo, run git repack -a -d in it, then delete that file.
  • git is installed on this machine. The VM’s images already have it.
  • You choose --clone when the VM is created, and once a VM is a --clone VM you don’t need to pass --clone again. devvm refuses --clone for an existing VM that mounts its folder, and devvm clone on switches that VM instead (switching a VM that exists).

What’s copied

From this machine, the VM mounts only the shared tools and its agents’ config folders. Once the VM is running, devvm creates a repo in it at the same path as your folder and pushes every local branch into it. When the folder is a git worktree, devvm pushes only the worktree’s branch and that branch’s upstream, if it has one, and leaves the repo’s other branches on this machine. The push goes over ssh to the VM itself and checks the host keys devvm pinned for it. No setting in your repo’s config, such as a url.*.insteadOf that rewrites the VM’s URL, can send the push anywhere else (how the push connects). devvm checks out your current branch in the clone, and your shell opens there.

Apart from a worktree’s upstream, which can be a remote-tracking branch such as origin/main, devvm copies only your local branches. Tags, uncommitted changes, and untracked or ignored files such as .env and node_modules stay on this machine. devvm warns you about uncommitted changes, so you can commit them and send them later with git push devvm BRANCH.

If the copy fails, for example because the VM can’t be reached, devvm tries again the next time you run it in the folder.

The remote

devvm adds a git remote for the VM to your repo. It’s named devvm, or devvm-<folder> if devvm is already taken, or the VM’s full name if both are. The remote’s URL is the VM’s full name followed by the clone’s path, so git connects through devvm’s ssh config, and fetching needs two things:

  • Your ~/.ssh/config needs devvm’s Include line (SSH access by name). devvm offers to add it when it creates the clone, and again when you run devvm host or devvm code. Until the line is there, or when devvm had no terminal to ask in, fetch with GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -F ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config' git fetch devvm.
  • The VM must be running. A stopped VM has no SSH entry, so git fetch fails because it can’t resolve the name. Run devvm or devvm host in the folder first.

Fetching the VM’s work

Fetching runs nothing from the VM on this machine. git only receives objects and updates the devvm/* branches, or creates new saved/devvm/* branches when devvm rm does the fetch. The commits themselves are untrusted, though, so treat them as you would a contributor’s branch and review them before you merge them, check them out or run anything they change.

Subfolders

When you run devvm in a subfolder of the repo’s folder, devvm uses the --clone VM as it uses any parent folder’s VM (a subfolder). The clone is at the repo folder’s path, so the subfolder’s path in the VM is the same subfolder in the clone. When the clone has that subfolder, the shell opens there, and devvm host and devvm code give it as the folder to open. When the clone lacks it, for example because the subfolder is untracked or ignored and so never copied, they use the clone’s top folder instead.

devvm --clone in a subfolder never uses a parent folder’s VM. It makes a new --clone VM for the subfolder, as devvm --here does, and doesn’t take --parent, so the subfolder must be the top folder of a repo of its own.

Several agents in one VM

Several agents can work in one --clone VM, each on a branch of its own in a git worktree of its own, so each agent edits its own copy of the files. Put the worktrees inside the clone, such as in .worktrees/NAME, because the clone’s parent folders in the VM belong to root, and so git worktree add ../NAME fails there. In the VM, in the clone:

echo .worktrees/ >> .git/info/exclude # once, so git status in the clone leaves the worktrees out
git worktree add -b agent/api .worktrees/api # a worktree on a new branch, agent/api
cd .worktrees/api # then start the agent here

Every worktree shares the clone’s repo, so the agents’ branches are all in it. One git fetch devvm on this machine brings every agent’s branch back, such as devvm/agent/api, and you review each one as you would any of the VM’s work (fetching the VM’s work). Before devvm rm deletes the VM, it also checks each worktree inside the clone for uncommitted changes (deleting the VM).

Install each worktree’s dependencies in that worktree, and never share one node_modules folder between worktrees, because each branch can need different packages, and two agents installing at once can break it. pnpm and bun keep one package store in the VM and hard-link packages from it into each worktree’s node_modules when both are on the same disk, so another worktree costs little download or disk.

The agents also share the VM’s ports, so two servers on the same port collide. Give each worktree’s server a port of its own, such as with PORT=3001. A VM that forwards every port, as new VMs do by default, forwards each of them to this machine’s localhost (ports).

The agents in one VM share its network tier and rules, its secrets, and its CPUs, memory and disk, and each agent can read and change every other agent’s worktree. When the agents need different network tiers or rules, secrets or sizes, or when one agent mustn’t reach another’s work, give each agent a folder of its own on this machine, such as a separate clone of the repo, and run devvm --clone in each, so each gets a VM of its own.

Deleting the VM

Before devvm rm deletes a --clone VM, it checks the clone for work you’d lose. It starts a stopped VM for the check as a launch does, so the VM’s confinement is checked first:

  1. If the clone has branches with commits this repo hasn’t fetched, devvm names them and offers to fetch them into new local branches named saved/devvm/<branch>. It skips a branch whose name git on this machine refuses and names it, and that branch goes with the VM. To keep such a branch, rename it in the VM with git branch -m before you run devvm rm.
  2. If the clone or a worktree inside its folder has uncommitted changes, devvm lists the first 20 of them in all, with each worktree’s changes under its path, and asks before deleting them along with the VM. devvm skips a worktree whose folder is gone or that git would prune, and it doesn’t check worktrees outside the clone’s folder. When the clone has more than 100 worktrees, devvm checks the first 100 and asks before deleting the VM, even if none of them has changes.

If either check finds something and there’s no terminal to ask in, or you give --no-input, devvm refuses and keeps the VM. These questions are asked only in a terminal, because only you can judge the work, so --force never answers them (questions devvm asks).

Once the checks pass, devvm deletes the VM. If the remote still points at the VM, devvm then removes it with git remote remove, which also deletes its devvm/* branches and their upstream settings. Before it does, devvm keeps every devvm/* branch that has commits no other branch has as a new local branch under saved/devvm/, whoever fetched it. devvm names each branch it creates, and they’re yours to review, merge or delete, as with git branch -D saved/devvm/main.

The saved branches are named after the remote, as saved/<remote>/<branch>, and devvm never overwrites a branch. When a branch is in the way, devvm uses saved/<remote>-2, then -3 and so on, and if it finds no free name, devvm rm refuses and keeps the VM (saved branches).

devvm rm --force skips only the question whether to delete the VM at all, and both checks still run. devvm rm --no-export skips the export of the agents’ history, and it also leaves both checks as they are.

devvm rm --no-clone-check skips both checks, so the VM goes with the commits this repo hasn’t fetched and the uncommitted changes, and devvm warns you of that first. Use it when a check can’t read the clone, such as when git in the VM is broken, and devvm refuses and keeps the VM. Use it too when the VM doesn’t start for the check, such as when its tier isn’t enforced, because devvm then says what kept it from starting and keeps the VM. devvm still asks whether to delete the VM unless you also give --force, and it still keeps the devvm/* branches you fetched as saved/devvm/ branches.

Switching a VM that exists

devvm clone shows whether this folder’s VM has its own clone of the repo, which is on, or mounts the folder, which is off. devvm clone on and devvm clone off switch the VM by making it again from the image it has, as devvm layer add does, and then open a shell in it:

devvm clone # show on or off
devvm clone on # make the VM again with its own clone of the repo, after asking
devvm clone off # fetch the clone's work, then make the VM again with this folder mounted

The VM keeps its home folder and its settings, as a VM made again does, and everything else on its disk is lost. So in a terminal devvm asks first, with no as the default, and without one it refuses unless you give --force. --no-export skips the export of the agents’ history, and --clean-home gives the VM the image’s home folder instead of its own, as for devvm layer add. When the VM is in the mode you ask for already, devvm says so and changes nothing.

devvm clone on needs a folder that --clone takes (requirements), and devvm refuses before it changes anything when the folder isn’t one. Your work is in the folder, so only the VM’s disk is lost. The new VM mounts nothing of the folder, and as it starts, devvm copies your branches into its clone and adds the remote, as for a new --clone VM (what’s copied). Once the new VM is ready and the old one is deleted, devvm takes the .git locks off the folder, because no VM mounts it any more. First it names what the old VM changed that the locks can’t stop, as a launch does (when devvm reports .git).

devvm clone off loses the clone, which is on the VM’s disk, so first it checks the clone as devvm rm does (deleting the VM). It offers to fetch the branches this repo hasn’t fetched into saved/devvm/<branch> branches, and it asks before the clone’s uncommitted changes go. Only a terminal can answer these questions, and --force never does, so without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm refuses and keeps the VM as it is. devvm clone off --no-clone-check skips the check after a warning, and the clone’s unfetched commits and uncommitted changes are lost. The new VM mounts the folder again with .git protection as a new VM gets it, which is on on macOS and off on Linux hosts. Before the new VM first starts, and before devvm locks .git, it removes the remote and keeps each devvm/* branch that has commits no other branch has as a saved/devvm/ branch, as devvm rm does. If the switch is then undone, devvm adds the remote back.

When a step fails, or you press Ctrl+C, before the new VM has its home folder, devvm puts the old VM back as it was, in its old mode, as it does for any remake.

A --clone VM keeps its clone on its own disk, so devvm layer add, devvm layer rm and devvm update refuse it. To change its layers or bring it up to date, run devvm clone off, then that command, then devvm clone on.

devvm clone –json

devvm clone --json prints one JSON object with clone, which is on or off, as output for scripts describes. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses on or off with it, and the flags that go with them.

{
 "version": 1,
 "clone": "on"
}

item.title: devcontainer.json
item.description:
devvm supports the Dev Container specification, so a project’s devcontainer.json sets up its VM. When you run devvm in a folder with a .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, or else a .devcontainer.json at the folder’s root, the new VM gets that file’s settings by default, as far as devvm supports them. To make the VM without reading the file, run devvm --no-devcontainer.

The settings devvm supports are the container image to start from, the features devvm has layers for, the ports, the environment and the commands. devvm says in one line which file it read.

{
 "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/javascript-node:22",
 "features": { "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/docker-in-docker:2": {} },
 "forwardPorts": [3000],
 "remoteEnv": { "PATH": "${containerEnv:PATH}:${containerWorkspaceFolder}/bin" },
 "postCreateCommand": "npm ci",
 "postStartCommand": "npm run db:start"
}

When it’s read

  • When the folder’s VM is made, and again by devvm update. Comments and trailing commas are allowed. devvm reads the file only within the folder, so it doesn’t follow a link out of the folder, and it reads only a regular file of up to 1 MiB. devvm never writes anything to the project folder.
  • What you give on the command line wins. --from wins over image, which wins over $DEVVM_FROM, and --ports wins over forwardPorts, and devvm says so in one line for each. The new VM gets the toolchains and layers that the features map to, which its summary shows, and when you customize the VM, they’re already chosen in its list, each row naming the file, so you can leave them out there. --tools and --layers replace them, as they replace any part’s default (what a new VM gets).
  • An existing VM changes only when devvm makes it again. Its state records the file’s SHA-256. When the file differs from it on a launch, or is gone, or has appeared since, devvm warns once and names devvm update. devvm doesn’t check a VM made with --no-devcontainer, and devvm update doesn’t read the file for it.

A new VM takes each of these from the first place that sets it.

flowchart TD
subgraph ports["Its ports"]
direction TB
flag["--ports"] -- "or else" --> fwd["your ports, with<br>forwardPorts added"]
end
subgraph base["Its base starts from"]
direction TB
from["--from"] -- "or else" --> image["the file's image"]
image -- "or else" --> env["$DEVVM_FROM"]
env -- "or else" --> ubuntu["Ubuntu's cloud image"]
end

When devvm refuses something in the file, it stops with one line that names the file, before it makes anything. For invalid JSON, it names the line and column.

Updating a VM from the file

When you change the file, run devvm update. devvm reads the file as it is now, and before it changes anything, it refuses what it would refuse for a new VM. Then it asks to make the VM again from the file, keeping its home folder, the project folder and its settings, as for an outdated VM, and everything else on the VM’s disk is lost. devvm update --force doesn’t ask, and without a terminal devvm refuses unless you give --force.

devvm replaces only what the file gave the VM, and it keeps what you chose:

  • Toolchains and layers. The ones the file’s features gave the VM go when the file no longer has those features, and the ones the file’s new features map to are added. The ones you chose yourself stay, whether you gave them with --tools or --layers, devvm setup chose them, or the folder’s other files call for them. One you left out in the list, or took out later, stays out.
  • The container image. The VM’s base starts from the file’s new image, pinned as for a new VM. When the file no longer has one, the base starts from $DEVVM_FROM, or else from Ubuntu’s cloud image. A VM made with --from keeps its base, and devvm says that it ignores image.
  • The ports. The ports the file added go when the file no longer lists them, and the ones it lists anew are added, as devvm ports add adds them. The ports you added with devvm ports add stay, and one of the file’s that you took out with devvm ports rm stays out. A VM made with --ports gets the ports the file lists anew, but not the ones --ports won over.
  • The environment and the commands. They’re the file’s new ones, and the commands that run once run again on the new disk.

When the file is gone, devvm makes the VM again without it, so what the file gave goes, and so do its environment and commands. When a file appears for a VM made without one, devvm makes the VM again as the file says, as it would a new VM.

Properties

Property What devvm does
image The VM’s base starts from it, as with --from. devvm uses only an image that its registry gives anyone who asks anonymously, pinned to that digest. It never uses an image only Docker has, one only your registry login reaches, or one on this machine or its network, which is localhost or a registry whose address is loopback, private or link-local, by name or as it resolves.
features ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/docker-in-docker is devvm’s docker layer. A feature under ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/ named after one of devvm’s toolchains, such as ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node, is that shared toolchain. devvm ignores their options and says so in one line. It refuses docker-outside-of-docker, which is this machine’s Docker, and every other feature. devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script.
forwardPorts devvm forwards numbers, localhost:N and 127.0.0.1:N to this machine’s localhost alone, adding them to your ports as devvm ports add does (ports). With every port forwarded, which is the default, they’re among them already. devvm ports rm takes one out, as for any port. It ignores other hosts’ ports and says so in one line.
containerEnv, remoteEnv The VM’s environment, which login shells and the commands below get. remoteEnv wins over containerEnv, and devvm’s own variables, such as LANG and secrets, win over both. A remoteEnv of null sets nothing.
onCreateCommand, updateContentCommand, postCreateCommand They run once, in that order, once the VM is made and set up (commands).
postStartCommand It runs at each start, on the first launch after the VM started.
initializeCommand It never runs, because it would run on this machine, and devvm says so in one line.
build, dockerFile, dockerfile, dockerComposeFile Refused, because devvm starts a VM only from an image.
postAttachCommand, privileged, capAdd, securityOpt, mounts, runArgs, workspaceMount, workspaceFolder, remoteUser, containerUser, updateRemoteUserUID, init, shutdownAction, overrideCommand, hostRequirements, appPort, portsAttributes, otherPortsAttributes, userEnvProbe, waitFor, overrideFeatureInstallOrder, context, service, runServices Ignored, and named in one line.
name, customizations, $schema Ignored.
anything else Ignored, and named in one line.

Commands

A command is a string, which devvm runs with sh -c, an array, which it runs as it is, or an object of named commands, which it runs one by one, sorted by name. The commands run in the VM, as its user, in the project folder, in a login shell, and never on this machine. Their output goes to the run log.

When a command fails, devvm names it in one line, and the commands after it that would run once, or at that start, don’t run. devvm keeps the VM and opens it, because the command is the project’s and not devvm’s. The commands reach only what the VM’s network tier allows, like anything else in the VM.

Variables

Variable
${containerWorkspaceFolder}, ${containerWorkspaceFolderBasename} the project folder, at the same path in the VM, and its name
${containerEnv:NAME} in a string command and in containerEnv and remoteEnv, the VM’s own NAME
${localEnv:NAME}, ${env:NAME} refused, because devvm never puts this machine’s environment in a VM
${localWorkspaceFolder}, ${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}, ${devcontainerId}, ${containerEnv:NAME} elsewhere refused

devvm leaves any other ${…} as it is, for the VM’s shell, such as ${HOME} in a command.

Security

The file belongs to the project, so a VM can rewrite it for the folder’s next VM, or for itself when you run devvm update, and devvm never lets it run anything on this machine, reach this machine’s files or environment, add a mount or weaken confinement. An image from it can still be any public container image, whose own code runs as root while devvm builds the VM’s base, as with --from (security model).

Its forwardPorts open ports on this machine, even when you’ve narrowed your ports with devvm ports -g or devvm ports. devvm forwards them only to this machine’s localhost, never to its other addresses, and never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, just as for devvm ports add. Anything on this machine that connects to such a port reaches what the VM serves there, including a web page in your browser, so for a repo you don’t trust, check its file first, or run devvm --ports none or devvm --no-devcontainer (ports the VM listens on).

item.title: devvm completion
item.description:
Print the shell completion script for bash, zsh or fish

Synopsis

Print the script that completes devvm’s commands, flags, image names and shared tools in SHELL, which is bash, zsh or fish. Load it from your shell’s startup file.

devvm completion SHELL [flags]

Examples 

 source <(devvm completion bash) # in ~/.bashrc, with the bash-completion package installed
 source <(devvm completion zsh) # in ~/.zshrc, after compinit
 devvm completion fish | source # in ~/.config/fish/config.fish

Options 

 -h, --help help for completion

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm completion explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm: Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first

item.title: devvm desktop
item.description:
Open this folder’s VM’s desktop in a VNC viewer

Synopsis

Start the desktop of this folder’s VM, which needs the desktop layer, and serve it on this machine’s 127.0.0.1 with a password of the VM’s own until you press Ctrl+C or the VM stops. On macOS, Screen Sharing opens it and asks for the password, which devvm shows.

devvm desktop [flags]

Examples 

 devvm desktop # open the VM's desktop in Screen Sharing
 devvm desktop --clipboard # the same, sharing the clipboard both ways
 devvm desktop --no-open # show the address and password for a VNC viewer of your own

Options 

 --clipboard share the clipboard between this machine and the VM, both ways
 -h, --help help for desktop
 --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside
 --no-open show the address and password without opening Screen Sharing
 --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm desktop explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm: Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first

item.title: Links between VMs
item.description:
A link lets a program in one of your VMs reach a TCP service in another by name, as in postgres://db:5432/app or fetch("http://api:3000"). The VM with the service is the target, and you publish its port in its folder. The VM that reaches it is the client, and you add the link in the client’s folder. Links work on every backend, whatever the two VMs’ network tiers, as long as the target’s tier is the client’s or a stricter one. devvm carries each connection over ssh through this machine, so neither VM’s network changes, and How it works › Links between VMs explains how.

For a database in ~/code/db and an app in ~/code/app, both with VMs:

cd ~/code/db && devvm link publish 5432 # offer the database's port to links
cd ~/code/app && devvm link add db 5432 # programs in app's VM reach it as db:5432

Programs in the app’s VM then reach the database as db:5432 and as db.devvm.internal:5432. A link joins the two VMs’ trust, so add one only between VMs you’d trust with each other’s reach (below). To link several VMs to each other at once, put them in a group.

Publishing a port

Links reach only the ports a VM publishes, so you publish a port in the target’s folder before any VM can link to it:

devvm link publish # what this folder's VM publishes: none, or a list
devvm link publish 5432 # offer port 5432 to links
devvm link publish 8000-8010 # offer a range
devvm link unpublish 5432 # stop offering it
  • devvm link publish takes ports and ranges as devvm ports does, such as 5432,8000-8010, but not all or none. A port you publish is offered to links from any of your VMs, and each link is still made in its client’s folder with devvm link add.
  • devvm link unpublish takes ports as devvm link publish lists them, and it refuses a port that isn’t published. The server in the VM keeps running. When other VMs link to a port you take out, devvm names them, and their next connections to that port are refused, while connections that are open stay until they close. To remove those links, run devvm link rm in their folders.
  • A change applies at once, whether the VM is running or stopped.
  • Publishing forwards nothing to this machine, and it doesn’t change the ports the VM forwards.

A link connects to the target’s own 127.0.0.1, so the server in the target has to listen there or on all its addresses. A server that listens on ::1 alone isn’t reached.

Adding a link

In the client’s folder, devvm link add TARGET PORT links its VM to PORT of the VM that TARGET names, once that VM publishes the port:

devvm link add db 5432 # reach port 5432 of the VM for the folder db as db:5432
devvm link add db 5432 --as pg # reach it as pg:5432 instead
devvm link add ../api 8080 # name the target by its folder's path
devvm link add devvm-api-71a99b1076d92c 8080 # or by its VM's name

TARGET takes one of four forms:

  • A folder’s name, as VM names have it, such as db for devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c. devvm matches it against the folder that each VM was made for, so a VM whose backend needed a shorter name still matches its whole folder name. When more than one VM has a folder of that name, devvm refuses and lists each VM with its folder, so you can give the VM’s name or the folder’s path instead.
  • A folder’s path, which starts with . or holds a /, such as ../api or /Users/you/code/api.
  • A VM’s name, as devvm ls lists it.
  • A VM’s ssh alias, such as devvm-db, as you’d give it to ssh (SSH access by name).

devvm refuses a target that has no VM, the client’s own VM, and a port that the target doesn’t publish. It also refuses a link that the two VMs’ tiers don’t allow. When devvm makes the link, it says what the client reaches it as, and that the link joins the two VMs’ trust.

Names

Programs in the client reach a link at NAME:PORT and NAME.devvm.internal:PORT. NAME is the target’s folder name, as VM names have it, unless you give --as NAME. .internal is reserved for private networks, so NAME.devvm.internal never names a host on the internet, and it’s the name to use when the short one could clash with a name your network resolves.

  • A client has one name for each VM it links to. The first link to a target sets the name, and later links to that target take it too, so after devvm link add db 5432 --as pg, devvm link add db 8000 reaches pg:8000. To change the name, remove that target’s links and add them again.
  • A name is one DNS label, made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, which starts and ends with a letter or a digit and isn’t all digits. devvm refuses localhost, the client’s own hostname and a name that another of the client’s links has. When the target’s folder name isn’t a valid name, or it’s taken, give another with --as NAME.
  • A link is reached only by its names, never at the client’s localhost, so localhost:5432 in the client stays the client’s own.
  • A link’s name hides the same name from anywhere else in the client, such as a host db under your network’s search domain.

Ports

The client reaches the target’s port on the same port number, so devvm link add web 80 gives web:80, and ports below 1024 work like any other. Two targets can publish the same port, because the client reaches each one by its own name.

Links carry TCP over IPv4 alone. Each name resolves to an IPv4 address, so a program that connects only over IPv6 doesn’t reach it, and UDP isn’t carried.

Which VM a link reaches

A link stays with the VM it was made for, because devvm records the target VM’s identity with the link. A VM made again in the target’s folder after devvm rm, or another VM with the same folder name that appears later, isn’t the linked target. devvm layer add, devvm layer rm and devvm update keep the target’s identity as they make the VM again, so its links still reach it (adding layers to a VM).

A link joins the two VMs’ trust

Code in the client can often run code in the target through the target’s own service, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM. It then has whatever the target has: its network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. devvm doesn’t stop that, because it’s what the service itself allows. So add a link only between VMs you’d trust with each other’s reach, and publish only the ports that you mean other VMs to use. Network tiers explains what this means for each tier.

Links and network tiers

A client links only to a target on its own network tier or a stricter one, because a link to a target on a lower tier would let the client reach more through the target. So an allowlist client links to allowlist and none targets, but not to internet or open ones, and an open client may link to any target. When devvm can’t read a client’s or a target’s tier, because that part of its state was changed by hand, it refuses the link rather than take it as open (a file devvm can’t read).

devvm checks this rule when you add a link, at each launch of the client and on every connection. For a client on a confined tier, on every connection the target’s tier must also be in force as the target runs. If you move the target from open to a confined tier while it’s running, devvm ls shows it as unenforced until the target starts again behind its proxy, and devvm refuses the client’s connections to it until then, so start the target again with devvm restart in its folder. devvm also warns you of such a target when you add a link to it, when you publish a port in its folder that the client links to, and each time the client starts. The warning names the target and refuses nothing, and devvm doesn’t warn of a stopped target, because its tier applies when it next starts.

While such a link exists, devvm refuses to give the target a tier lower than a client’s, such as devvm network open in its folder, and names the clients that link to it, and it refuses to give the client a tier higher than a target’s, such as devvm network allowlist for a client that links to an open VM. Remove those links with devvm link rm first, or give the target the client’s tier.

Every VM has its proxy, so a program that uses the VM’s proxy settings, such as curl, sends its requests for a link to the VM’s proxy, and the proxy carries a request for one of the link’s names and its port, such as db:5432 or db.devvm.internal:5432, to the link. Other programs reach the link by its name directly. The proxy passes a link’s connection on as it is, so it doesn’t look into it and puts none of your secrets into it.

The network rules don’t apply to links. The allowlist doesn’t allow or block a link’s connections, and devvm network deny db doesn’t stop the link db. The rule above and the published ports decide which connections a link carries, and devvm network log shows them (the link log). To stop a link, remove it with devvm link rm, or unpublish its port in the target’s folder.

Listing links

devvm link lists this folder’s VM’s links, with one row for each port:

NAME PORT TARGET FOLDER STATUS APPLIES
db 5432 devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db Running yes
db 8000 devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db Running unpublished

STATUS is the target’s status as its backend reports it, such as Running or Stopped, and it’s empty when devvm can’t tell. APPLIES is yes for a link that works while the target runs, or else it says why the link doesn’t apply:

  • gone: the target VM no longer exists.
  • replaced: the target’s folder has another VM, made again since the link was.
  • unpublished: the target doesn’t publish the port.
  • policy: the target is on a lower network tier than the client.
  • ungrouped: a group made the link, and the two VMs aren’t in that group together any more. You can remove such a link with devvm link rm.

devvm ls shows how many links each VM has, in its LINKS column.

devvm link –json

devvm link --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the links has its name, its port, the target VM, the target’s folder as target_folder and its status as target_status, both "" when devvm doesn’t know them, applies, which is true or false, and reason, which is why the link doesn’t apply, as APPLIES shows it, or "" when it does.

{
 "version": 1,
 "links": [
 {
 "name": "db",
 "port": 5432,
 "target": "devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c",
 "target_folder": "/Users/you/code/db",
 "target_status": "Running",
 "applies": true,
 "reason": ""
 }
 ]
}

devvm link publish –json

devvm link publish --json prints what the VM publishes as one JSON object, and it only shows, so devvm refuses a list of ports with it. ports is none or a list of ports and ranges, written as devvm link publish takes it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "ports": "5432,8000-8010"
}

Removing a link

devvm link rm TARGET PORT removes one of this folder’s VM’s links, where TARGET is the link’s name or anything that devvm link add takes:

devvm link rm db 5432 # stop reaching db:5432
devvm link rm pg 5432 # by the name given with --as

The link’s next connection is refused, while connections that are open stay until they close.

When links change

A change of links reaches a running client at once and a stopped one when it next starts, and devvm says which. On a running client, the names resolve at once, because devvm rewrites the client’s /etc/hosts, and a link’s port answers within a few seconds. The VM’s proxy reaches a new link as soon as its port answers, so the programs that use the VM’s proxy settings also reach it, including those that were already running. Nothing in the VM restarts, and the VM’s environment doesn’t change, whatever its tier.

When a target stops or goes

devvm never starts a VM for a link. A connection to a stopped target fails, and each launch of the client warns about each stopped target, until you start it with devvm in its folder. The client’s links then work again without any change to the client. When the target stops, the connections that were open through it end. A link also needs both VMs’ backends to carry links, which every backend of devvm’s does, and when one can’t, each launch of the client says so.

devvm rm of a target removes every link to it from your other VMs and names the clients that lost one. A VM that you make again in that folder isn’t linked, so publish its ports and add the links again. devvm rm of a client removes its links, and devvm stop of a client ends its links’ connections.

A link can’t listen when a program in the client already holds its port in a way that covers the link’s address, such as a server of the client’s own on all its addresses with the same port. That link alone doesn’t work, devvm says so, and the client’s other links work. Stop that program, then run devvm restart.

Groups

A group is a set of your VMs that reach each other’s published ports by name, without a devvm link add for each pair. You join each VM in its own folder, and devvm makes the links between them, so every VM in the group gets a link to each port that every other VM in it publishes. A VM is in one group at a time.

For a database in ~/code/db, an API in ~/code/api and an app in ~/code/app, each with a VM:

cd ~/code/db && devvm link publish 5432 && devvm group join web
cd ~/code/api && devvm link publish 8080 && devvm group join web
cd ~/code/app && devvm group join web

Programs in the app’s VM then reach db:5432 and api:8080, programs in the API’s VM reach db:5432, and programs in the database’s VM reach api:8080. The links a group makes are links like any other, so what this page says about names, ports, network tiers, the link log and stopped targets holds for them too, and devvm link lists them.

Joining a group

devvm group join NAME puts this folder’s VM in the group NAME. The first VM to join makes the group, and devvm says so. A group’s name is made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starts and ends with a letter or a digit, and isn’t all digits.

devvm group join web # join the group web
devvm group join web --as api2 # join it as api2 instead of this folder's name
devvm group # the group, its VMs and the ports each one publishes
devvm group leave # leave it

When the VM joins, devvm makes the group’s links in it and in each of the group’s other VMs, and it names the links that each VM gains. The links reach a running VM at once and a stopped one when it next starts, as When links change describes. devvm refuses a VM that’s in another group already, so run devvm group leave first, and it refuses a VM whose backend can’t carry links. A VM made again in a folder isn’t in the group that the folder’s old VM was in.

devvm group shows the group this folder’s VM is in, with one row for each of its VMs:

NAME VM FOLDER PUBLISHED
api devvm-api-0f3c2a91b7d4e6 /Users/you/code/api 8080
app devvm-app-5e1d7c08a2b9f4 /Users/you/code/app none
db devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db 5432

NAME is what the group’s other VMs reach that VM by, and PUBLISHED is the ports it publishes, or none. When this folder’s VM isn’t in a group, devvm says so.

Ports in a group

The group’s links reach every port that a VM in it publishes, so you publish and unpublish ports in each VM’s folder, as Publishing a port describes. A port that you publish reaches the links of every other VM in the group, and a port that you take out goes from them, at once on a running VM and at its next start on a stopped one. devvm names the links that each VM gains or loses. A range that you publish gives a link for each port in it.

Names in a group

The group’s other VMs reach a VM by its folder name, as VM names have it, unless it joined with --as NAME. The name follows the rules for link names, and devvm refuses localhost.

  • Two VMs in a group can’t have the same name, so when another VM in the group has the name this VM would join as, devvm refuses the join until you give this VM another with --as NAME. devvm also refuses a name that’s another VM’s folder name, because that’s the other VM’s own hostname. To change a VM’s name in its group, leave the group, then join it again with --as NAME.
  • A VM’s folder name is its own hostname, so devvm refuses to put a VM in a group where another VM’s name is this VM’s folder name, whatever --as NAME you give, because the name would reach the joining VM itself. For two folders with the same name, such as ~/work/api and ~/old/api, have the VM that’s in the group leave it and join again with another name, such as devvm group join web --as api1, then join the other with --as api2. A VM whose folder has a name of its own needs neither.
  • The links that you make with devvm link add take precedence over the group’s. When you link to a VM in the group yourself, the group’s links to that VM take the name your link gives it, and a port that you linked gets no link from the group. When one of your links has the name of another VM in the group, the group’s links to that VM go, and devvm warns you of it, until you remove your link with devvm link rm.

A group joins the trust of all its VMs

A group joins the trust of every VM in it, as a link joins the two VMs’ trust, because code in any of them can often run code in the others through the ports they publish. A VM that joins later gets the same reach into every VM in the group, and they get the same reach into it, so devvm says so on every join. Put VMs in a group only when you’d trust each of them with the others’ reach.

Groups and network tiers

A group’s VMs are all on one tier. devvm refuses to put a VM in a group whose VMs are on another tier, and it names both tiers. It checks joins one at a time, so when two VMs join a group at once, the second is checked against the first, and a devvm that waits for another says so. While a VM is in a group, devvm refuses to change its tier with devvm network, so run devvm group leave first.

Because every VM in a group is on one tier, the group’s links keep the rule that a client links only to a target on its tier or a stricter one. Each of their connections is still refused while the target’s tier isn’t in force as it runs, and devvm warns you of such a target when the group makes a link to it.

Leaving a group

devvm group leave takes this folder’s VM out of its group. It removes the links that the group made, in this VM and in the group’s other VMs, and names the links that each VM loses. The links that you made with devvm link add stay. devvm link rm doesn’t remove a link that the group made, so leave the group, or unpublish the port in its target’s folder.

devvm rm of a VM takes it out of its group, and when the group’s last VM leaves, the group is gone.

devvm group –json

devvm group --json prints the group as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. group is the group’s name, or "" when the VM is in none, and members is [] then. Each of the members has its name in the group, its vm, its folder, and the ports it publishes as published, written as devvm link publish lists them, or none.

{
 "version": 1,
 "group": "web",
 "members": [
 {
 "name": "db",
 "vm": "devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c",
 "folder": "/Users/you/code/db",
 "published": "5432"
 }
 ]
}

Containers in the VM

A container that the docker layer runs in the client has a network of its own, so it neither resolves a link’s names nor reaches its address. Run it with --network host, as in docker run --network host IMAGE, so it shares the VM’s network and reaches the links as the VM does.

The link log

devvm network log in the client’s folder shows its links’ connections, whatever its tier. A line has the time, link for a connection devvm carried or REFUSED for one it refused, the link’s name and port, and the target VM, with why devvm refused it:

2026-11-01T10:00:00Z link db:5432 to devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c
2026-11-01T10:05:00Z REFUSED db:5432 to devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c: it isn't running

When the client is on a confined tier and the target’s isn’t in force yet, the line says unenforced, as Links and network tiers describes.

A client has at most 256 of its links’ connections carried at once, and devvm refuses and logs the next one. devvm network log –json describes the events in JSON.

item.title: A VM's desktop
item.description:
A VM has no screen of its own, but with the desktop layer it gets an Xfce desktop, which devvm desktop opens in a window on this machine. This page covers adding the desktop, opening it, its password and the clipboard, and what it costs. The desktop explains how devvm keeps it to this machine.

Adding the desktop

The desktop is one of devvm’s built-in layers, so only the VMs you choose it for get it, and base and the other VMs stay without it. To add it to a new VM, check desktop under Layers in the list devvm shows when you customize a new VM, or name it with --layers:

devvm --layers desktop # a VM of base with the desktop
devvm --layers docker,desktop # the desktop on top of the docker layer

devvm builds the desktop image the first time a VM needs it, and VMs that choose it share that image. --layers is the exact list of the VM’s layers, so name every layer you want the VM to have.

To give every new VM the desktop, choose it with devvm setup --layers desktop, or add it to the layers you already chose, such as devvm setup --layers docker,desktop. New VMs then get it unless you leave it out when you customize them or give --layers without it (layers for new VMs). VMs that exist keep the layers they were made with.

A VM made without the desktop has none, and devvm desktop says so. To give it one, run devvm layer add desktop, which makes the VM again from an image with the desktop on top of its own layers, such as docker+desktop. The VM keeps its home folder, the project folder and its settings, and loses the rest of its disk, such as the packages you installed, so devvm asks first (adding layers to a VM). devvm layer rm desktop takes the desktop out again in the same way (taking layers out of a VM).

devvm layer add desktop # make this folder's VM again with the desktop, after asking
devvm layer rm desktop # make it again without the desktop

The desktop works on base, and on a base made --from a Debian, Ubuntu or Alpine image.

Opening it 

devvm desktop # serves this folder's VM's desktop and opens it in Screen Sharing
devvm desktop --no-open # only shows its address and password
devvm desktop --clipboard # shares the clipboard both ways, for this run

devvm desktop gets the VM ready as devvm host does, and starts it if it’s stopped. Then it starts the VM’s desktop, unless it’s running already, and shows its address and password:

devvm-website-0123456789abcd's desktop is at
vnc://127.0.0.1:41234
Password: k3mxq7tw
It stays there until you press Ctrl+C.

On macOS, devvm opens the address in Screen Sharing, which comes with macOS and asks for the password. Screen Sharing can keep the password in your keychain, and the address stays the same each time. On Linux, open the address in a VNC viewer of your own, such as TigerVNC’s vncviewer or Remmina.

The desktop stays at that address until you press Ctrl+C, or until the VM stops, and then devvm desktop ends. The desktop goes on running in the VM, so the windows you left open are there the next time you run devvm desktop. It’s 1600 by 1000 pixels.

The desktop is only ever on this machine, and only while devvm desktop runs:

  • devvm serves it on this machine’s 127.0.0.1 alone, so nothing else on your network reaches it. Each VM keeps its port, which no other VM and no program on this machine has. When a program has taken it, devvm chooses another one and keeps that.
  • In the VM, the desktop listens on no port at all, so a VM that forwards every port never forwards it.
  • On a confined network tier, the VM still reaches only its proxy while you use its desktop.

Browsers

The desktop has no browser of its own, so install the one you want in the VM, such as Google Chrome, Chromium or Firefox. Browsers reach the web through the VM’s proxy without asking you for a password, and so do the desktop’s other programs. Browsers ask for a proxy’s password rather than read it from the VM’s proxy settings, so the desktop’s programs use the VM’s local proxy instead. The local proxy is a small proxy in the VM, at http://127.0.77.1:3128, which adds the VM’s password to each request and sends it on to the VM’s proxy. A browser follows the desktop’s proxy settings unless you’ve given it one of its own.

The local proxy changes nothing about what the VM may reach. A host that the VM’s network tier doesn’t allow is still blocked, and a plain http:// page shows the proxy’s reason and the devvm network allow command that allows it. An https:// page shows the browser’s own error instead, such as Chrome’s ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED, so run devvm-why in the desktop’s terminal to see what was blocked.

The local proxy listens on the VM’s loopback alone, and devvm never forwards it to this machine, even on a VM that forwards every port. It starts with the desktop and runs until the VM stops.

The password

Each VM has its own password of eight lowercase letters and digits. devvm makes it the first time you run devvm desktop and keeps it with the VM’s state on this machine, so devvm rm deletes it. The password never goes into the VM, and it isn’t in devvm’s run log. devvm checks it on this machine before a viewer reaches the VM, whatever the VM’s own desktop asks for.

Other users and programs on this machine can also connect to 127.0.0.1, so the password is what keeps them out. VNC passwords are eight characters at most, and devvm lets a viewer try one password a second, so guessing it would take thousands of years.

The clipboard

The clipboard isn’t shared unless you add --clipboard. With sharing on, what you copy on this machine goes into the VM, where a coding agent can read it, and what the VM copies lands on this machine’s clipboard. Without --clipboard, devvm keeps this machine’s clipboard out of the VM, even when something in the VM has changed its desktop’s settings, and the VM’s desktop doesn’t send its clipboard.

--clipboard turns sharing on in both directions for that run, and the next run without it turns sharing off again. devvm can’t stop a VM whose desktop was changed from sending its clipboard to Screen Sharing, so when you don’t want the VM’s clipboard on this machine, also turn off Use Shared Clipboard in Screen Sharing’s Edit menu.

What it costs

  • About 370 MB of disk for the desktop image, which every VM with the layer shares, while base and the VMs without the layer stay that much smaller.
  • About 500 MB of the VM’s memory while its desktop runs, which it does from your first devvm desktop until the VM stops. A VM whose desktop you never open uses none.

When the desktop doesn’t open

  • The VM has no desktop: it was made without the desktop layer. Run devvm layer add desktop to make it again with the layer, as adding the desktop explains.
  • The desktop didn’t start: devvm shows the end of its run log. The desktop’s own log is ~/.cache/devvm-desktop.log in the VM.
  • Screen Sharing didn’t open: open the address devvm shows in Screen Sharing yourself, by typing it into Finder’s Go > Connect to Server, or in another VNC viewer.
  • Screen Sharing says the password is wrong: use the password devvm desktop shows for this VM. Each VM has its own.

item.title: Design notes
item.description:
For contributors: why devvm is built the way it is, what was tried and dropped, and what’s still open. How each part works is on its own page; the layout and rules are in AGENTS.md.

Emulated features

When devvm builds a backend feature from other parts of the backend, the feature is emulated, and it gets a note here before its review. The note says what the feature is built from, the guarantee it keeps, what could break it, and which end-to-end checks prove it. The threat check comes next, and only then is the feature marked reviewed. Every feature Lima has is native except its ports, which devvm’s forwarder emulates (below).

ssh into VMs

ssh for editors is native on Lima, so it isn’t an emulation, but its sessions keep a guarantee of devvm’s own: ssh and editors reach a VM by name through the entries devvm writes (security model), and a session gives the VM no way out it doesn’t already have, on a confined tier nothing past its proxy, whatever the VM runs as sshd.

What keeps a session from carrying the VM out. An ssh session can carry the VM’s traffic only through channels the host’s ssh asks for: remote forwards (-R, RemoteForward, a remote SOCKS forward), X11, a tunnel and the agent; OpenSSH’s client refuses a channel the server opens unasked. Root in the VM runs whatever sshd it likes, so the guarantee is the host’s ssh’s: devvm’s entry (first in ~/.ssh/config, so its options win over a Host *) sets ForwardX11 no, ForwardX11Trusted no, Tunnel no, PermitRemoteOpen none (so devvm needs OpenSSH 8.7 or newer; no IgnoreUnknown for older ones, as its first value wins and would replace a user’s Host * one, such as macOS’s for UseKeychain), ForwardAgent as the agent choice the VM’s current start was made with says, AddKeysToAgent no (no key of the host’s lands in an agent the session forwards), ProxyJump none and ProxyCommand none (no hop through something else), UpdateHostKeys no (the VM can’t add host keys; devvm reads them itself) and HashKnownHosts no. A RemoteForward can’t be turned off without refusing ssh -R on the command line too, so it isn’t (Not covered). VS Code’s Remote-SSH uses local and dynamic forwards (-L, -D) and is unaffected. Then sshd’s own settings, a defence for an honest VM (assets/layers/base.sh, /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-devvm.conf, first so it wins; Lima’s own forwards are local; it applies only where the image’s sshd_config includes sshd_config.d, as Ubuntu’s and Debian’s do, so for some --from images not at all, which only an honest VM’s defence loses):

  • Local forwarding (-L, -D, -W) is allowed: the VM itself connects, from its own network, which its tier confines like any other connection of the VM’s (checked). VS Code’s Remote-SSH reaches its server this way.
  • Remote forwards bind only 127.77.0.0/16, the range devvm keeps for links between VMs, and remote socket forwards are refused. A remote forward makes the host connect on the VM’s behalf, so one the host’s ssh asked for by mistake could reach anything the host reaches, its loopback services and sockets (docker.sock, agents) included, around the VM’s confinement. GatewayPorts clientspecified binds the address a request names, and PermitListen 127.77.*:* matches that address as text, so a request for localhost (ssh’s default), 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0 or ::1 is refused. Only devvm on the host asks for a forward in that range, always by number. X11 and tunnels are refused too.
  • Agent forwarding is allowed: the entry decides it from the SSH agent choice the VM’s current start was made with (ForwardAgent, devvm’s own agent too); refusing it would break devvm ssh-agent on in editors.

These settings guard against the host’s ssh asking for a forward that devvm’s entry doesn’t pin (a RemoteForward under Host *, ssh -R), and only while root in the VM leaves sshd as it is. They’re a safeguard for an honest VM, and the boundary is the host’s ssh, which accepts a channel only for a forward it asked for.

What it relies on: OpenSSH’s client refusing unrequested channels, and devvm’s Include line first in ~/.ssh/config, so its entries’ options win.

What could break it: host ssh settings that come before devvm’s entries.

Not covered:

  • A remote forward you ask for (ssh -R, a RemoteForward of yours): remote forwards you add lists what it leaves open.
  • Sessions see the proxy’s password, as devvm’s own shells do, and VS Code relays what VS Code describes.

Ports on Lima

The guarantee: when a VM forwards every port, each TCP port from 1024 up that a server in it listens on, on its loopback or on all its addresses, is forwarded to the same port on the host’s loopback, and only to its loopback. When a VM lists its ports, only those are forwarded, however many it lists, by the same rules. The forwarder never takes a port that a program on the host has on any address when the forward is made, or a port devvm records for another VM. Forwarding gives the VM no way out that it doesn’t already have, because every connection starts on the host. Lima’s own forwards listen with SO_REUSEADDR, so on macOS, whenever a server in the VM starts, Lima takes 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program on the host has *:PORT, and that program’s loopback connections go with it. That’s why Lima forwards nothing and devvm’s forwarder forwards the VM’s ports instead. On macOS, a confined VM doesn’t depend on Lima for that, because its hostagent’s sandbox refuses it every port but its ssh port, so Lima can’t forward a port of the VM’s even if it ignored its rules. The emulation is reviewed, with the threat check’s findings fixed or listed below, which is why the host key read is capped, reports are paced and the log is limited, and the end-to-end checks prove the rest.

What it’s built from:

  • Lima’s forwards off. Each VM’s portForwards holds three ignore rules, each for every guest port and protocol (any, which is TCP and UDP). They’re on 127.0.0.1, which Lima also matches for ::1, on 0.0.0.0 and on ::, which together match servers on all addresses. They come ahead of Lima’s own last rule, which forwards everything. CreateVM sets them with limactl clone --set. Start sets them only where limactl list shows other rules, because an edit gives the VM new host keys at its next boot. Lima’s ssh is its VM driver’s forward (ssh.localPort), not a rule, so the ignore rules leave it alone, and they cover the guest’s own ssh port like any other.
  • The sandbox’s binds (macOS, confined tiers). The hostagent of a confined VM runs under a Seatbelt profile (confinement) that denies every network bind but two kinds. It may bind the VM’s ssh port over TCP, which devvm chooses and records in the VM’s state (the ports section’s host.ssh), and unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder, which hold the hostagent’s own socket (ha.sock), the VM’s network (default_ep.sock, default_fd.sock) and ssh’s control socket. Seatbelt matches a bind by its port alone, on any address, even when the rule names localhost, and it can’t allow an ephemeral bind (port 0) without allowing every port. It matches a unix socket by its path with links resolved, so a link in the Lima folder doesn’t let the hostagent bind a socket elsewhere. Lima’s host resolver binds two ephemeral ports for its DNS server, so a confined VM starts with the resolver off and 127.0.0.1 as its DNS server, as on Linux, where nothing listens and lookups fail at once. The hostagent reaches the guest agent over vsock, which needs no bind. This list comes from starting a VM under a profile that reported every bind, then under one that denied the rest: Lima logs a forward it’s refused (failed to listen) and carries on, while a refused resolver ends the start.
  • Which ports. Which ports each VM forwards, all, none or a list, is in its state (ports.forward), and the backend never hears of them: neither Start’s Want nor any other call of the backend’s has them. vmssh.Forwards.Start, the one owner of the forwarder, reads them from the VM’s state each time it starts one, after a start of the VM and when devvm ports changes a running VM’s ports, without editing Lima’s config. A stopped VM’s change is its state’s alone, because its next start reads it. When the VM lists ports, the forwarder forwards those less the ports a program on the host has, which the owner leaves out with a ports_taken warning. When none is left, no forwarder runs.
  • A forwarder per VM, on the host. The forwarder is vmssh.Forwarder, which isn’t a backend’s. Its owner, vmssh.Forwards, runs it detached as devvm _ports, one per VM, for project VMs alone, because only a project VM’s start goes through it, and builds’ starts don’t. The owner starts it once the backend’s Start returns, and again on a running VM when its ports change, each after stopping any forwarder the VM had, which ends the connections open through it. devvm finds that one by its pid file, which it checks against the process’s arguments, as it does for the proxy. It sends that forwarder SIGTERM and kills it if it hasn’t ended within 2 s, so its ports are free before devvm asks which listed ports a host program has. devvm holds a lock of the VM’s own (ports.lock, beside its pid file ports.pid in the VM’s run folder) from stopping the old forwarder until the new one has started, so two devvm runs at once, such as a start and devvm ports, leave one forwarder, the one its pid file names. The owner waits up to 10 s for the forwarder to say it forwards while it runs. The forwarder says so in a status file of its own beside its pid file (ports.status), which holds its pid and which devvm removes before each start. If it doesn’t, devvm warns with ports_forward_failed, naming its log, and leaves it to keep trying while the VM runs on.
  • Reaching the VM. The forwarder makes one ssh connection, a master (ssh -F none -M -S <socket>), to the VM’s sshd on Lima’s ssh port on the host’s loopback. Lima’s SSH gives the port with the user and the key, the first IdentityFile of Lima’s ssh config, and devvm refuses that target unless the config names 127.0.0.1 (vmssh.FromTarget, the check links and the ssh config use too). It logs in as Lima’s user with Lima’s key alone (IdentitiesOnly, IdentityAgent=none), _config/user in devvm’s Lima home, which every VM there authorizes, and never with the user’s agent. The master reads none of the user’s configuration and forwards nothing either way, with ClearAllForwardings, PermitRemoteOpen none, ProxyCommand none, and no agent, X11 or tunnel. The VM’s sshd allows local forwarding, and remote forwards only to 127.77.0.0/16 for links (base.sh), and -W is local forwarding. Its control socket is in ~/.local/share/devvm/run (mode 700) and is named by a hash of the VM’s name, because a socket’s path is at most 104 characters. When the connection is lost, the forwarder closes its forwards and makes the connection again every 2 s while the lifeline holds.
  • What listens. The master’s session runs ports.sh (assets/guest/ports.sh) as the VM’s user (sh -s). It prints the local addresses of the VM’s listening TCP sockets, which are the state 0A lines of /proc/net/tcp and tcp6, whenever they change and every 10 s regardless, so it ends soon after the connection does. The forwarder treats the report as untrusted. A line over 128 bytes or a report over 4096 lines ends the connection, and anything that isn’t a hex address and port is skipped. Reports are applied at least 500 ms apart, and one that comes sooner waits, holding up the VM’s ssh channel with it, so the VM can’t make the forwarder bind, dial and read devvm’s state at its own pace. The VM can make the forwarder write to its log, with ports coming and going and with the session’s stderr, so the log takes 200 writes at once and then one every 10 s. Each write is at most 512 bytes, without control characters but newlines and tabs, C1 included, and a start empties the log once it’s over 1 MiB. A forwarded port’s connections go to 127.0.0.1 for a server on all IPv4 addresses or on that address, and to ::1 for a server on all IPv6 addresses or on that address. A server on another 127.x address alone gets its connections there. Servers on other addresses alone aren’t forwarded.
  • How many. With every port, the forwarder takes ports from 1024 up, because the ports below are the host’s system services. With listed ports, it takes those alone (-only), a listed port below 1024 included, because the user asked for it, and a bind the host refuses is logged. Either way the forwarder takes at most 256 ports at once. It reads the reserved ports (below) again with each report, and while it can’t read them, it takes no new port and keeps those it has. A port it has that has since become reserved, such as one another VM’s start has chosen, is given up at that report, though the VM still listens on it. A port the forwarder couldn’t take is tried again only once the VM’s server on it goes and comes back.
  • Listening. The forwarder listens on 127.0.0.1 and ::1, or on IPv4 alone on a host without IPv6. It binds without SO_REUSEADDR (platform.ListenExclusive). With that option, which Go and Lima set, macOS lets a socket take 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program has *:PORT, and that program’s loopback connections go with it. Without the option, the bind is refused when another program has the port on any address. This was checked on macOS for a program on 0.0.0.0, on :: (IPv4 and IPv6 at once, as Node’s and Go’s servers listen), on IPv6 alone and on 127.0.0.1, each with and without SO_REUSEADDR of its own. A port held only by ended connections (TIME_WAIT, with nothing answering on it) is taken as usual, so a server that restarts gets its forward back. When a bind is refused, the forwarder dials the port and takes it only if the dial is refused. A full backlog times out, which counts as taken. A port the forwarder took on 127.0.0.1 but finds in use on ::1 is given up, so localhost never reaches two programs. On Linux, SO_REUSEADDR stays on. Linux refuses that bind with the option too while another socket listens on the port, and without it, the forwarder’s own ended connections (TIME_WAIT) would keep anyone from listening on the port for a minute, its next forwarder included.
  • Each connection. Each forwarded connection is a channel of the master’s (ssh -S <socket> -W HOST:PORT), with one process per connection and at most 256 at once. The VM’s sshd opens it to the VM’s own loopback from inside the VM. The channel’s ssh has the master’s options. If the master is gone, ssh connects on its own, and it then reaches the VM’s sshd the same way, never the host’s.
  • Reserved ports. The forwarder never takes the VM’s own Lima ssh port, which Lima’s SSH names, or its proxy port, which its state records, and the owner passes both as -reserve. It also never takes the ssh, proxy and desktop ports devvm chooses and records in any VM’s state, or other VMs’ listed ports (ports.Used). Every Lima VM’s ssh port is one of those, whatever its tier: devvm chooses it when it makes the VM, sets it with limactl clone --set .ssh.localPort, and records it in the VM’s ports section before the clone (ports.Allocator.SSH). One allocator, ports.Allocator, chooses every host port devvm chooses, the ssh, proxy and desktop ports, and records it while it holds the VM’s lock and then the claims lock (run/claims.lock, state.VM.Claim) until the VM’s state is written, so two devvm commands making or starting VMs at once never choose the same one. A build VM has no state, so devvm chooses its ssh port too, on every host, through the same allocator (ports.Allocator.Build), under the claims lock alone (state.Claims), and on macOS the build’s Seatbelt profile names that port. It records the port by the build VM’s name (run/build-ports/<name>), where ports.Used reads it, until limactl start returns, and by then Lima has bound the port or the start has failed. The devvm that starts the build holds a file lock on that record until then, and the kernel lets go of the lock when that devvm ends, even when it’s killed. Each time devvm chooses a port, under the claims lock, it first deletes the records whose lock no process holds and that are over 15 minutes old. The age matters because a killed devvm leaves its limactl start running, which may still bind the port for up to Lima’s 10 minutes of waiting for the VM’s ssh. So a devvm killed while its build VM starts reserves that port for 15 minutes, and then only until the next port is chosen. A stopped VM gets a new one only when a program on the host has its port on any address, even one that accepts no connections, or when the VM lists it to forward, and its start then sets it with an edit. Lima binds the port only once the VM boots, a few seconds after its start, so a port Lima picked itself would be free for another VM’s forwarder in that window, and Lima’s own ssh, which checks no host key, would then reach the other VM (the threat check below).
  • The host key. devvm keeps one record of a VM’s host keys for each of its starts, vms/<hash>/run/known_hosts (vmssh.PinHostKeys). It removes the record before each start and reads the keys after it, through limactl shell, at most 64 KiB for at most 30 s, keeping only lines whose key decodes and names its own type (vmssh.ParseHostKeys). The record’s first line names the start it was read for (backend.Run.ID), so a record of another start, such as one before a limactl start outside devvm, is read again, and keys read while the VM started again aren’t recorded. The forwarder checks the VM against that record, with HostKeyAlias and StrictHostKeyChecking yes, as the ssh config, links’ sessions and a --clone VM’s git do. All of them reach the VM through one function, vmssh.Checked, which checks the backend’s ssh and adds the record: the forwarder and the ssh config pin the keys when the record is another start’s, and links’ sessions and git take only a record of the current start. The pin keeps the forwarder from talking to a program on the host that takes the ssh port. It doesn’t guard against the VM itself, which is already the other end of the connection.
  • Its lifeline. The forwarder follows the hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid, the lifeline Lima’s Running gives), as the proxy does, and exits once the file is gone, holds anything else, or its process is gone. devvm stop stops it with the VM, and devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop it before they delete its files with the VM’s folder. A VM that stops some other way, such as when its self-check fails or a restart stops it, ends its forwarder through the lifeline, and the next start stops any forwarder that’s left before it starts its own.

What keeps a forward from carrying the VM out: every connection starts on the host. A program connects to the forwarder’s port, and the forwarder asks the VM’s sshd to connect to the VM’s loopback. The VM opens nothing to the host through the forwarder, because the master asks for no remote forward, agent, X11 or tunnel, and OpenSSH’s client refuses a channel that the server opens unasked, whatever sshd root in the VM runs. The only remote forwards devvm asks a VM for are a client’s links, on a link session that is a connection of its own, never the forwarder’s master (links). What the VM sends back goes to the program that connected, as with any forward. On a confined tier, the VM’s own connections stay confined by Seatbelt or QEMU’s restrict=on, while the forwarder runs on the host as devvm, outside the hostagent’s sandbox.

What it relies on: OpenSSH’s client refusing unrequested channels and honoring -F none, the kernel refusing a bind without SO_REUSEADDR where another socket has the port (checked on macOS), and devvm’s state listing every VM’s ports. It also relies on Lima binding its ssh forward on the host’s loopback alone, on the host key that devvm pins at the start, and on Lima honoring the ignore rules ahead of its own rule. On macOS, a confined VM relies on Seatbelt refusing the hostagent’s binds instead of on the rules, and on the Virtualization framework’s own process, which runs outside the profile, binding nothing: the VM’s network goes through the hostagent’s unix sockets.

What could break it: a Lima release that forwards despite the ignore rules, or that forwards from somewhere other than portForwards. On macOS, a confined VM keeps the guarantee even then, because its sandbox refuses the binds. An open VM, and every VM on Linux, where QEMU’s restrict=on doesn’t cover the hostagent’s own binds, still relies on Lima honoring the rules. A Lima release that needs a new bind for a confined VM, such as a resolver that can’t be turned off, fails its start closed, and Lima’s log names the refused bind. The end-to-end checks look at the rules, and use lsof or ss to check that the hostagent has no TCP or UDP port of the VM’s and that a host program keeps its port. A program on the host could take Lima’s ssh port while the VM is stopped, and the pinned host key refuses it. Lima’s key logs in to every VM in devvm’s Lima home, as it does for Lima’s own ssh, but public key authentication never sends the key to the VM.

Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, its local IPC companion; the sandbox’s binds and the ssh port). Leads, each confirmed and fixed, ruled out, or listed:

  • Another VM answering for this one’s ssh: confirmed, fixed. An ssh port that Lima picks at a VM’s start, and binds once the VM boots, is one devvm doesn’t record, so no forwarder reserves it. Another VM forwarding every port, with a server on that port in the window, has its forward take it. Lima then carries on with its other ssh forward and waits on the port (seen with a host program holding it), and Lima’s own ssh checks no host key (StrictHostKeyChecking no), so limactl shell, the host keys devvm reads and pins after the start, and devvm’s setup and shell would reach the other VM. The fix: each VM’s ssh port is devvm’s, whatever its tier, recorded before the clone and reserved by every forwarder. It’s unit-tested and checked by the CLI tests, and end to end, the port a VM’s state records is the one Lima listens on.
  • A guest port bound around the rules: ruled out on macOS on a confined tier. Lima forwards a port only by binding it on the host, and the sandbox refuses every port but the ssh port. End to end, with Lima’s own rule put back for one start inside the sandbox, Lima tries the guest’s TCP and UDP ports, is refused (operation not permitted), and has no port but its ssh port, while devvm’s forwarder forwards the TCP port.
  • The ssh port on every address: listed. Seatbelt allows the ssh port on any address, so a Lima that bound it on 0.0.0.0 would put the VM’s sshd on the network, where it still takes only keys. Lima binds it on 127.0.0.1, and the end-to-end checks look at the hostagent’s listeners. The rule allows the port over TCP alone, so the guest’s UDP server on that port number can’t get a forward from it; checked end to end.
  • A program holding a stopped VM’s ssh port: ruled out, but for a race. A start looks for the recorded port with a bind on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 as well as a connection, so a program that has the port on any address, even one that accepts no connections, gives the VM a new port. Only a program that takes the port between that check and Lima’s bind, a few seconds later, gets Lima’s ssh, which is listed under not covered below. End to end, a VM whose port a host program holds starts on a new one, recorded, and the program keeps its own.
  • Two VMs choosing the same ssh port: confirmed, fixed. Without a lock, two devvm commands making VMs at once could each choose the same port from the ports other VMs record, and the second VM’s Lima would wait on a port that the first one’s has. devvm chooses and records a port while it holds the claims lock, run/claims.lock in its data folder, after the VM’s own lock (locks).
  • A build VM’s ssh port: confirmed, fixed. A port that Lima picked at a build’s start would be one that no VM’s state records, so another VM forwarding every port could take it in the window before Lima binds it, and Lima’s ssh would then run the build’s scripts in that VM. The fix: devvm chooses every build VM’s ssh port, on macOS and Linux, under the claims lock, and records it in run/build-ports/<name>, which every forwarder reserves, until the build VM’s start returns. A record that a killed devvm leaves is deleted the first time devvm chooses a port once the record is 15 minutes old, because no process holds its lock, and until then it keeps the port from any VM while the start that the killed devvm left may still bind it. Builds carry no credentials, an image is the build VM’s own disk, and a tool build writes its images through a folder that only its own VM mounts, so even a VM that reached a build’s ssh another way could break that build but couldn’t learn a secret from it or choose what an image or a tool image holds. It’s unit-tested on both systems, and the CLI tests check that a build’s start sets the port.
  • What a failed start or create leaves: ruled out. A VM whose create fails, other than by an interrupt, keeps its state, and with it its recorded port, until devvm rm deletes it, so the port stays reserved and nothing else takes it. devvm rm deletes the state, which frees the port.
  • Unix sockets: ruled out as a way out. The hostagent binds them only in the VM’s Lima folder, which only Lima’s own commands and devvm use.
  • DNS around the proxy: ruled out. With Lima’s resolver off, the guest’s DNS server is 127.0.0.1, where nothing listens, and Lima’s network’s DNS address and the host’s address on it answer nothing even when root asks them directly, because the sandbox denies the hostagent the host’s DNS service and every connection but the proxy’s; checked end to end.
  • A compromised hostagent: listed. The bind rules stop a Lima that misbehaves, not code an attacker runs in it, which the profile still lets read and write your files.
  • Starts without the sandbox: listed. Only confined starts on macOS run under it. A build keeps Lima’s host resolver, so its binds aren’t denied, and an open VM starts unconfined.
